apidx.location: src/haute/pipeline.py:360 (run, `return outputs[order[-1].name]`) and src/haute/pipeline.py:409 (score, same)
apidx.title: run()/score() silently return the LAST topological node, not a declared output — fan-outs return the wrong DataFrame
apidx.description: Both run() and score() end with `return outputs[order[-1].name]`, i.e. they return whichever node sorts last in topological order. For any graph that is not a strict linear chain this is a silent footgun. Empirically confirmed: a pipeline with `src -> out` (the real result, an @output node) AND `src -> sink` (a @data_sink that writes a side file) returns the SINK's frame, because `sink` happens to sort after `out`. The user gets a wrong-but-plausible DataFrame with no error, no warning, and no way to see that the result they got is not the one they intended. The library already has a first-class `@pipeline.output` node type and a NodeType.OUTPUT, and `to_graph()` even falls back to labelling the last node OUTPUT — but the execution path ignores all of that and trusts topo position. Topological order among leaves is not deterministic across equivalent graphs (graphlib's static_order depends on insertion order), so the 'returned' node can change merely by reordering decorators. This is the kind of silent-wrongness the project explicitly wants to avoid.
apidx.recommended_fix: Make the returned frame explicit. Resolve output as: (1) if exactly one node has NodeType.OUTPUT (or is a sink leaf with no consumers), return it; (2) if multiple terminal/output nodes exist, raise a HauteError naming them and instructing the user to mark one (e.g. via an `output=True` kwarg or by being the sole @output node); (3) only fall back to a single leaf when unambiguous. At minimum, define 'output' as the unique node with no outbound edges and raise loudly when there is more than one terminal node, rather than silently picking topo-last. Do NOT silently disambiguate — fail loudly (per CLAUDE.md).

apidx.location: src/haute/pipeline.py:54-68 (Node.__call__), specifically the `dfs[0]` single-input path (line 67) and the `dfs[: self.n_inputs]` slice (line 64)
apidx.title: Node.__call__ silently drops extra wired inputs (single-param node fed two edges uses only the first)
apidx.description: Node.__call__ decides how many inputs to pass purely from the function signature's parameter count, then SLICES the incoming dfs to that count: a single-param node uses `dfs[0]` (line 67) and a multi-param node uses `dfs[: self.n_inputs]` (line 64). If the user wires MORE edges into a node than its function accepts, the surplus inputs are silently discarded. Empirically confirmed: `@p.polars def t(df): return df` with `p.connect('a','t').connect('b','t')` runs successfully and silently uses only `a`, dropping the `b` edge entirely — no error, no warning. This is a classic wiring footgun: the user believes both inputs participate (they explicitly called connect twice), but one is dropped. It is especially dangerous for edge_join / merge-style logic where dropping an operand changes results without failing. The signature-vs-edges contract is never validated.
apidx.recommended_fix: Validate edge count against the node's declared arity at run/score time (or at connect/finalisation). When `len(dfs) > n_inputs` for a non-source node, raise a HauteError naming the node, the number of connected inputs, the number the function accepts, and the offending extra source(s). Only slice when counts match. This makes over-wiring fail loudly instead of silently truncating.

apidx.location: src/haute/pipeline.py:62-68 (Node.__call__ multi-param branch) vs the explicit guard at 58-61
apidx.title: Under-wiring a multi-param node raises a raw `TypeError: fn() missing 1 required positional argument` instead of a Haute-framed, actionable error
apidx.description: Node.__call__ has a friendly Haute-authored message for the zero-input case (lines 58-61: "Node '...' expects N input(s) but received none"). But when a multi-parameter node receives FEWER dfs than it needs (e.g. a two-param join with only one edge connected), the code calls `self.fn(*dfs[: self.n_inputs])` which forwards too few positional args and lets Python raise a bare `TypeError: need_two() missing 1 required positional argument: 'right'` (confirmed empirically). That traceback names the raw Python function and parameter, not the Haute node, says nothing about edges, and gives no remedy. So the SAME class of mistake (wrong number of inputs) produces a polished message in one sub-case and a leaked interpreter traceback in another — inconsistent and unactionable. Contrast run()'s nice 'has no inbound edges. Use pipeline.connect() to wire it up.' message for the no-edge case.
apidx.recommended_fix: Before invoking, compare `len(dfs)` to `self.n_inputs`; when fewer inputs are supplied than required, raise a HauteError like "Node '<name>' expects <n_inputs> input(s) but only <len(dfs)> edge(s) are connected; wire the remaining input(s) with pipeline.connect(...)." Keep the existing no-edge and zero-input messages consistent with it.

apidx.location: src/haute/pipeline.py:132-134 (api_input decorator) and Node.is_deploy_input at :36-39 (reads config['api_input']); used by score() seed logic at :379-388
apidx.title: `@pipeline.api_input` decorator does NOT mark a node as the live API input — you must also pass `api_input=True`; the decorator name and the seeding flag collide
apidx.description: There are two unrelated meanings of 'api_input' that share a name and trap users. (1) `@pipeline.api_input` (the type-decorator, line 132) only sets `_node_type=NodeType.API_INPUT`. (2) score()'s seeding logic keys off `Node.is_deploy_input`, which reads `config.get('api_input')` (the boolean kwarg), NOT the node type. Confirmed empirically: a node decorated with bare `@p.api_input` has `is_deploy_input == False` and config `{'_node_type': API_INPUT}` — so score() will NOT seed it as the live input. To actually get seeding you must write the redundant, surprising `@p.api_input(api_input=True)` — which is exactly what every test does (test_pipeline.py:644,699,703,720). A user who writes the obviously-named `@pipeline.api_input` and calls score(df) will silently fall into the 'no deploy inputs -> seed ALL sources' branch and get different behaviour than intended. The decorator's own name strongly implies it designates the API input; it does not.
apidx.recommended_fix: Unify the two meanings: have the `api_input` decorator set `is_deploy_input` (i.e. mark the node as the live/deploy seed) by default, OR rename the boolean discriminator so it cannot be confused with the decorator (e.g. `deploy_seed=True`), and make `is_deploy_input` derive from NodeType.API_INPUT rather than a separate kwarg. Whichever direction, the obvious spelling `@pipeline.api_input` must do the obvious thing without a redundant `api_input=True`.

apidx.location: src/haute/pipeline.py:379-388 (score, `seed_all = len(deploy_inputs) == 0  # fallback: seed every source`)
apidx.title: score() silently seeds EVERY source with the input df when no api_input is marked — a guess-fallback that violates 'fail loudly'
apidx.description: When no source node is marked as a deploy input, score() sets `seed_all = True` and feeds the single input `df` into ALL source nodes (line 380, comment literally says 'fallback: seed every source'). This is a silent behavioural fork: the same call `pipeline.score(df)` means 'seed only the marked live input' on one pipeline and 'overwrite the output of every data_source — including static rating tables — with this one frame' on another, decided implicitly by whether any node carries `api_input=True`. For a pricing pipeline this is dangerous: a user who forgets the marker and calls score() will have their static reference tables (rating tables, lookup data) silently replaced by the scoring payload, producing wrong prices rather than an error. CLAUDE.md explicitly forbids 'unnecessary fallbacks ... a fallback which is incorrect and hard to notice'; this is precisely that. The branch is documented in the docstring but the docstring is not visible at the call site.
apidx.recommended_fix: Require an explicit live input for score(). If zero sources are marked, raise a HauteError instructing the user to mark exactly one (or pass an explicit mapping of which source(s) to seed). If a true 'seed all' mode is genuinely wanted, make it an explicit opt-in parameter (e.g. `score(df, seed='all')`) rather than an implicit fallback inferred from missing metadata.

apidx.location: src/haute/pipeline.py:488-503 (class Submodel) and its docstring `Usage::` block; contrast Pipeline.run/score/to_graph/submodel which Submodel does not have
apidx.title: Submodel exposes all 21 node decorators and connect() but has no run/score/to_graph — its docstring implies a usable workflow it cannot complete
apidx.description: Submodel subclasses NodeRegistry and therefore inherits every decorator (data_source, polars, model_score, ...) plus connect(), nodes, edges. Its docstring (lines 494-502) shows a full `@submodel.external_file(...) / submodel.connect(...)` workflow, strongly implying a Submodel is an executable unit. But confirmed empirically: `Submodel` has no `run`, no `score`, no `to_graph`, no `submodel`/`submodel_files`. So a user can fully build and wire a Submodel and then discover there is no way to execute or inspect it as a graph — the only way it participates is by being re-registered into a Pipeline via `pipeline.submodel('file.py')`, which is NOT visible from the Submodel class or its docstring. The class body is empty (only a docstring), making it look like a stub. This is a discoverability cliff: the public surface advertises authoring affordances with no terminal action, and the relationship to Pipeline.submodel() is undocumented at the type.
apidx.recommended_fix: Either (a) give Submodel a clear, documented role — e.g. a method/property that lets it be inspected (to_graph) and a docstring line stating 'A Submodel is not executed directly; register it into a Pipeline via pipeline.submodel("<file>.py")', or (b) factor the executable methods so the difference is obvious. At minimum, the docstring must tell the user how a built Submodel is actually run, and the empty class body should carry that contract rather than `...`/nothing.

apidx.location: src/haute/pipeline.py:219-221 (instance decorator -> registers as NodeType.POLARS) executed by Node.__call__ at :54-68; docs/building-models/nodes/instances.md:17-22 declares instanceOf/inputMapping 'Required'
apidx.title: `@pipeline.instance` is a public decorator whose core semantics (instanceOf/inputMapping) the standalone run()/score() executor silently ignores
apidx.description: The public `instance` decorator (line 219) maps to NodeType.POLARS and stores `instanceOf`/`inputMapping` in config. Per the docs these are REQUIRED and the whole point is 'reuse another node's logic with remapped inputs'. But Node.__call__ (the only execution path for Pipeline.run/score) just calls the literal decorated function body with positional dfs in edge order; it never reads `instanceOf` to fetch the original node's logic, and never reads `inputMapping` to remap inputs. So an `instance` node in a standalone-run pipeline does NOT behave as an instance at all — it runs whatever empty/placeholder body the function has, with inputs in raw connect() order. This only works when executed through the separate executor (_builders), not through the public Pipeline.run/score the decorator is attached to. A user reading `pipeline.instance` and the instances doc will reasonably expect run()/score() to honour it; it silently does not. (This is adjacent to, but distinct from, the known passthrough-body cluster for optimiser/modelling/etc.: here the gap is that an explicitly-named convenience decorator on Pipeline has no honouring code in Pipeline's own execution.)
apidx.recommended_fix: Either honour instanceOf/inputMapping in Node.__call__/run (resolve the referenced node and apply input remapping) so the public decorator means what it says, or remove `instance` from the Pipeline/NodeRegistry public surface if it is only meaningful to the canvas/executor — do not expose an authoring decorator that the same object's run() cannot execute. If kept as canvas-only, document loudly that standalone run()/score() does not resolve instances.

apidx.location: src/haute/__init__.py:16 (`__all__ = ["HauteError", "Pipeline", "Submodel"]`) and :19-24 (__getattr__ only resolves Pipeline/Submodel)
apidx.title: Top-level package leaks none of the types users must reason about: NodeType and the ConfigError/ExecutionError/etc. subclasses are not importable from `haute`
apidx.description: `__all__` exports only HauteError, Pipeline, Submodel. Confirmed empirically: `haute.ConfigError`, `haute.NodeType` raise AttributeError — they live only in the underscore-internal `haute._types` and in `haute.errors`. Two concrete DX gaps: (1) The error hierarchy is designed for granular catching ('All Haute-specific exceptions inherit from HauteError so callers can catch the whole family' — errors.py docstring), and run()/score() raise specific failures, yet a user who wants `except haute.ConfigError` cannot get the subclass from the top-level package and must know to import from `haute.errors`. Only the ROOT is exported, defeating the granularity the hierarchy was built for. (2) NodeType is described in _types.py as the 'canonical node-type identifiers' and is what a user needs to interpret `to_graph()` output or reason about node types — but it is reachable only via a private (`_types`) module, so there is no supported import path. The package is under-exporting the very vocabulary it expects users to use.
apidx.recommended_fix: Export the documented public vocabulary from `haute`: at minimum the concrete error subclasses (ConfigError, ExecutionError, DeployError, SchemaMismatchError, ContractMismatchError, FeatureMismatchError) and NodeType, wired through the existing lazy `__getattr__`/`__dir__` mechanism. Promote NodeType to a non-underscore public module (or re-export it) so there is a supported import path. Keep truly-internal types out, but stop forcing users into `haute.errors` / `haute._types`.

apidx.location: src/haute/pipeline.py:103-128 (_register_node) and the 21 decorators at :132-221, all signed `(fn=None, **config: Any)`
apidx.title: Every node decorator accepts arbitrary **config with no key validation — typo'd config keys are silently stored and ignored
apidx.description: All 21 type-specific decorators delegate to `_register_node(fn, _node_type=..., **config)` which stores `config` verbatim on the Node with zero validation. The codebase already defines precise per-node TypedDicts (DataSourceConfig, ModelScoreConfig, etc.) and explicit *_CONFIG_KEYS tuples in _types.py — but the decorators ignore them. Confirmed empirically: `@p.data_source(pathh='data.parquet')` (typo for `path`) is accepted and stored as `{'_node_type': dataSource, 'pathh': 'data.parquet'}` with no error. The intended `path` is simply absent, so the source will later fail far downstream (or silently mis-load) with an error that does not point back to the typo. Because config is `**Any`, the IDE cannot autocomplete or type-check keys either, so the rich TypedDicts provide no protection at the one place users actually type config. This turns every config typo into a latent, hard-to-trace failure.
apidx.recommended_fix: Validate decorator config against the known key set for that node type at registration (the *_CONFIG_KEYS tuples already exist), raising a HauteError that names the unknown key and lists valid keys for that node type (the same pattern connect() uses for unknown node names). This catches typos at definition time with an actionable message and makes the TypedDicts load-bearing.

apidx.location: src/haute/_project.py:193 and src/haute/_project.py:231 (surfaced via haute run/lint/deploy)
apidx.title: Resolver errors tell users to pass `--file <path>`, but no command has a `--file` flag (positional arg only)
apidx.description: `resolve_pipeline_file` is the canonical resolver behind `haute run`, `haute lint`, and the no-toml branch of `haute deploy`. When a directory contains more than one discoverable pipeline (no main.py, no [project].pipeline), `_resolve_default_in` raises FileNotFoundError with the message 'Multiple pipeline files found in <root>: a.py, b.py. Pass one explicitly with --file <path>, or rename the intended entry point to main.py.' (line 231; the docstring at line 193 repeats the same `--file <path>` instruction). But none of the commands expose a `--file`/`--pipeline` option — every one of them accepts the pipeline path as a POSITIONAL argument (`@click.argument("pipeline_file", required=False)` in _run.py:85, _lint.py:92, _deploy.py:223). A user who literally follows the advice and runs `haute run --file motor.py` gets Click's 'Error: No such option: --file' (exit 2) — a second, more confusing failure on top of the first. The ambiguous-multiple-pipelines case is a routine real-world scenario (a repo with several pipeline modules at the root), so this dead-end is hit in practice. The advice should name the actual interface, e.g. 'Pass the path as an argument (haute run <path>), or rename the intended entry point to main.py.'
apidx.recommended_fix: Change both message sites in _project.py (the ambiguity branch at ~line 231 and the docstring at ~line 193) to reference the real positional usage instead of `--file <path>` — e.g. 'pass the file path as an argument (haute run <path> / haute lint <path>), or rename the intended entry point to main.py'. Alternatively add a `--file` option to the commands if that flag form is desired, but the message must match whatever interface actually exists.

apidx.location: src/haute/cli/_train.py:119 (also docstring at line 13-19 'as generated by haute export')
apidx.title: `haute train --help` references a non-existent `haute export` command
apidx.description: The `train` command's help text states: 'The script should define a TrainingJob instance named `job` with a `.run()` method (as generated by `haute export`).' No `export` command is registered on the CLI group (src/haute/cli/__init__.py adds only deploy, impact, init, lint, run, serve, smoke, status, train — there is no `export`; the only `export` symbols in the codebase are the unrelated `export_script` HTTP route and `export_trace`). Compounding this, the `haute init` scaffold never mentions `haute train` or produces a training script anywhere (verified: no 'haute train'/'export' strings in _scaffold.py), so a user reading `haute train --help` is pointed at a command that does not exist, with no discoverable path to obtaining the TrainingJob script the command requires. This makes the command feel broken/abandoned and gives the user no actionable way to produce valid input.
apidx.recommended_fix: Either (a) implement the `haute export` command and register it, or (b) correct the train help to describe how a TrainingJob script is actually produced today (e.g. point at the modelling/export HTTP route or the GUI export affordance, or show a minimal hand-written `job = TrainingJob(...)` example). Also add a one-line pointer in the `haute init` 'Next steps' / scaffold so training has a discoverable entry point.

apidx.location: src/haute/cli/_impact.py:56 (get_project_root() call)
apidx.title: `haute impact` crashes with a raw ConfigError traceback in a haute.toml project that is not a git repo
apidx.description: handle_impact guards only `toml_path.exists()` (line 50) before calling `project_root = get_project_root()` at line 56. `get_project_root` (src/haute/_project.py:81-86) imposes an ADDITIONAL requirement beyond haute.toml existence: the project must be inside a git repository, otherwise it raises `ConfigError('haute.toml found but not inside a git repository; run git init', ...)`. ConfigError is a plain `HauteError(Exception)`, not a `click.ClickException`, and the call is not wrapped in try/except — so Click lets it propagate as a full Python stack trace with a non-1 exit. This is inconsistent with every sibling command, which surface a clean `click.echo('Error: ...', err=True); raise SystemExit(1)`. A user who has run `haute init` but has not yet `git init`-ed (or is in a subdir) gets a stack trace from `impact` while `smoke`/`deploy`/`status` in the same directory print actionable one-liners. (Note: the ConfigError message text itself is good — 'run git init' — but it should be shown as a clean CLI error, not a traceback.)
apidx.recommended_fix: Wrap the `get_project_root()` call (and ideally the whole impact body) so HauteError/ConfigError is caught and re-emitted as `click.echo(f'Error: {exc}', err=True); raise SystemExit(1)`, matching the pattern in _status.py:47-49 and _deploy.py:100-107. The git-repo precondition should produce the same clean message as a missing haute.toml.

apidx.location: src/haute/cli/_train.py:74 (read_user_text(filepath) inside the only UnsafeCodeError try-block)
apidx.title: `haute train <directory>` (or unreadable file) crashes with a raw IsADirectoryError/PermissionError
apidx.description: handle_train checks only `filepath.exists()` (line 64) — which is True for a directory — then calls `validate_user_code(read_user_text(filepath), allow_imports=True)` at line 74. `read_user_text` (src/haute/_io.py:461) does `Path(path).read_text(...)`, which raises `IsADirectoryError` for a directory and `PermissionError` for an unreadable path. The surrounding try/except only catches `UnsafeCodeError` (line 75), so these I/O errors propagate as a raw traceback rather than a clean message. So `haute train rating/` or `haute train somedir` exits with a stack trace instead of an actionable 'not a file' error. Unlike run/lint/deploy (which funnel through resolve_pipeline_file and at least handle directories deliberately), `train` takes the raw `@click.argument("training_script")` and feeds it straight to read_user_text, so it has no equivalent guard.
apidx.recommended_fix: Add an explicit `if not filepath.is_file(): click.echo(f"Error: Training script is not a file: {filepath}", err=True); raise SystemExit(1)` after the existence check, and/or broaden the try around read_user_text to catch OSError and emit a clean message. A `.py`-suffix check would also make the 'as generated by ...' contract clearer.

apidx.location: src/haute/cli/_serve.py:275-285 (_warn_if_non_loopback) vs src/haute/_logging.py:43 (configure_logging called only in server.py:336)
apidx.title: The documented host-exposure security warning is emitted before logging is configured, so it does not reach stderr as the documented structured event
apidx.description: The _serve module docstring and `_warn_if_non_loopback` promise that binding off-loopback 'logs a loud structured warning via structlog so the choice is auditable in server logs' on stderr. The warning fires inside `handle_serve` -> `_warn_if_non_loopback` (line 522, via logger.warning('server_bind_non_loopback', ...)) BEFORE `uvicorn.run` boots the app — and `configure_logging()` (which installs the stderr StreamHandler + ConsoleRenderer and sets WARNING routing) is only ever called in the server lifespan (server.py:336), never on the CLI path (verified: configure_logging has no caller under src/haute/cli/). At the moment the warning is emitted, structlog is in its UNCONFIGURED default state (PrintLogger to stdout, not the stdlib->stderr pipeline the module advertises). The practical effect: the security warning's destination stream and rendering are not what the docstring claims (it is not the structured stderr event until the server later reconfigures logging), and in a non-TTY/redirected context the operator may not see the loud warning where they expect it. For a safety affordance whose entire purpose is auditability, this gap undermines the guarantee.
apidx.recommended_fix: Call `configure_logging()` once at the start of `handle_serve` (or in the `serve` Click entrypoint) before `_warn_if_non_loopback`, so the exposure warning renders through the documented stderr structlog pipeline. Alternatively, emit the exposure warning via `click.echo(..., err=True)` like every other user-facing CLI message, reserving structlog for in-server events.

apidx.location: src/haute/cli/_run.py:67 vs src/haute/cli/_run.py:70
apidx.title: `haute run` writes per-node FAILURE lines to stdout but the failure summary to stderr
apidx.description: In handle_run, the per-node result loop prints both success and failure lines via `click.echo(...)` to STDOUT (line 64 for the ✓ line, line 67 `click.echo(f"  ✗ {nid}: {res.error ...}")` for the ✗ failure line). Only the trailing summary `click.echo(f"\n{errors} node(s) failed.", err=True)` (line 70) goes to stderr. So the actual diagnostic — which node failed and why — lands on stdout while the count lands on stderr. A caller that captures stderr to surface errors (a common CI/script pattern) sees 'N node(s) failed.' with no indication of WHICH node or the error text, and a caller that greps stdout for results gets the failures intermixed with the data preview. The split is internally inconsistent and degrades scriptability.
apidx.recommended_fix: Route the per-node failure line (line 67) to stderr (`err=True`) so the failing-node diagnostics and the failure summary share the same stream, while keeping the ✓ success lines and the final data preview on stdout. This matches the stdout=data / stderr=diagnostics convention the other commands follow.

apidx.location: src/haute/errors.py:3-7 (and ~15 class defs across src/, e.g. modelling/_train_config.py:41, _rating.py:299, executor.py:161, routes/_optimiser_limits.py:11, _model_explainability.py:15, _worker_isolation.py:49, _databricks_io.py:87-95, deploy/_request_limits.py:23-72)
apidx.title: errors.py docstring promises 'catch the whole family with a single except', but ~15 domain exceptions root at stdlib types outside HauteError; only one `except HauteError` exists in all of src/
apidx.description: errors.py opens with: 'All Haute-specific exceptions inherit from HauteError so callers can catch the whole family with a single except.' That contract is materially false. A `git grep '^class .*Error'` over src/ finds ~40 exception classes, and roughly 15 of them are genuine Haute domain errors that deliberately subclass stdlib types rather than HauteError: TrainingConfigError(ValueError) [a *config* error], RatingTableMissError(ValueError), PreviewProjectionError(ValueError), FrontierComputeBudgetExceededError(ValueError), TrainingConfigError(ValueError), ModelExplanationError(RuntimeError), OptimiserApplyTraceError(RuntimeError), the eight IsolatedWorker* classes (base IsolatedWorkerError(RuntimeError)), WaterfallReconciliationError/WaterfallUnavailableError(ValueError), plus the three RequestBody*Error(ValueError) and three CacheArtifact* classes. Consequently a consumer (CLI, server, embedding app, or test) that writes `except HauteError` to handle 'any Haute failure' silently misses all of these. The proof that nobody actually relies on the promised affordance: a grep for `except HauteError` across the entire src/ tree returns exactly ONE hit (codegen.py:415). The hierarchy that exists (HauteError -> ConfigError/ParseError/ExecutionError/DeployError/...) is well-designed but under-populated, so the taxonomy is effectively 'ad-hoc stdlib exceptions everywhere' for ~40% of domain errors despite a clean root being available.
apidx.recommended_fix: Re-root every Haute domain exception under the correct HauteError branch: TrainingConfigError -> ConfigError, RatingTableMissError/PreviewProjectionError/ModelExplanationError/IsolatedWorker*/FrontierComputeBudgetExceededError -> ExecutionError, DatabricksConfigError -> ConfigError, etc. Where an existing `except ValueError`/`except RuntimeError` call-site must keep working during migration, use a mix-in (e.g. `class TrainingConfigError(ConfigError, ValueError)`) so both `except HauteError` and `except ValueError` catch it. Then either update the docstring to match reality or (better) add a test that asserts every concrete Error subclass defined under src/haute is a subclass of HauteError, so the promise is enforced going forward.

apidx.location: src/haute/_config_builder.py:409-418
apidx.title: Generic 'Failed to load node config; check that the path exists and contains valid JSON' headline masks the precise sidecar validation message, which is demoted to a cause= parenthetical
apidx.description: load_node_config() failures are caught with `except (FileNotFoundError, json.JSONDecodeError, OSError, ValueError)` and re-raised as a single ConfigError whose headline is always 'Failed to load node config; check that the path exists and contains valid JSON, or create the file.' with the real diagnostic shoved into a context kwarg `cause=str(exc)`. The problem: this conflates three very different failure classes under one misleading headline. When the JSON parsed perfectly but a *field value* is invalid - e.g. expand_rating_step_config_from_sidecar raises ValueError('ratingStep tables[2].factors[0] must be a column name') or _banding_config raises ValueError('breakpoint rule \'18\' must map to a non-empty value') - the user is told to 'check that the path exists and contains valid JSON', which is actively wrong (the path exists and the JSON is valid) and sends them debugging the wrong thing. The genuinely actionable message ('tables[2].factors[0] must be a column name') only appears as a trailing `(cause=...)` fragment after the wrong headline. The ValueError catch is also so broad it cannot distinguish 'file missing' from 'JSON malformed' from 'field invalid', so the headline can never be accurate.
apidx.recommended_fix: Split the handling: keep the 'check the path / valid JSON' headline only for FileNotFoundError/OSError/json.JSONDecodeError; for a ValueError raised by the schema/sidecar validators (which means the file loaded and parsed but content is invalid), lead with the underlying message and ADD node context, e.g. raise ConfigError(str(exc), func_name=func_name, config_path=normalised_path) from exc. Even simpler: have the sidecar validators raise a typed ConfigError/SchemaMismatchError themselves (see related finding) so _config_builder can let it propagate with just `exc.context.setdefault('config_path', ...)` enrichment, mirroring the codegen.py:415 idiom.

apidx.location: src/haute/_rating_step_config.py:23-353 and src/haute/_banding_config.py:24-205
apidx.title: Sidecar config validators raise raw ValueError with no node label/file path, while the directly-adjacent data-source schema validator uses typed SchemaMismatchError(..., path=, missing=, available=)
apidx.description: Two sibling validation paths for user-edited config handle errors in opposite styles. _io.py (data-source schema) raises the typed SchemaMismatchError with rich structured context on every failure - e.g. SchemaMismatchError('Source projection references columns missing from the source schema.', missing=sorted(missing), available=schema_columns) and SchemaMismatchError('Declared source schema mismatch.', path=path, missing=missing, mismatches=mismatches). By contrast _rating_step_config.py and _banding_config.py - which validate the *same kind* of user-authored JSON sidecar - raise bare ValueError with a string-prefixed context like 'ratingStep tables[0].factors must be a list' or 'breakpoint rule \'x\' must map to a non-empty value'. These have a within-table coordinate (tables[N]) but crucially NO node label and NO file path, so a user with five rating-step nodes who gets 'ratingStep tables[2].factors[0] must be a column name' has no idea which of the five nodes (which JSON file) to open. The vocabulary is also inconsistent (typed+structured vs raw+string-concatenated) for what is conceptually one error family (invalid declared schema/config), which forces every caller and every test to handle two shapes.
apidx.recommended_fix: Make the sidecar validators raise the same typed error the rest of the I/O boundary uses - ConfigError or SchemaMismatchError - carrying structured context (table_index, factor, the offending value) instead of pre-formatted strings, and thread the node label / config path through (the caller _config_io.load_node_config knows the path; _config_builder knows func_name). At minimum, pass the node label/path as **context so it appears in str(err). This unifies the vocabulary and gives 'which node' for free.

apidx.location: src/haute/routes/_optimiser_service.py:1188-1189, 1211-1212, 1233-1234 (root cause: raw ValueError used for user-config validation at e.g. lines 1381-1404, 1505-1511)
apidx.title: User-fixable optimiser config errors surface to the API as HTTP 500 because raw ValueError is indistinguishable from genuine internal failures
apidx.description: The optimiser route validates user config with raw ValueError - e.g. 'frontier_min must be less than or equal to frontier_max.', 'frontier_ranges must provide min and max for each constraint', 'Unable to estimate frontier ranges from an empty scenario frame.' - and the request handlers catch `except ValueError as exc: raise HTTPException(status_code=500, detail=str(exc))`. A 500 Internal Server Error tells the client 'the server is broken', when in fact the user supplied bad constraint ranges and should get a 4xx ('fix your input'). Because the validation errors are the SAME raw ValueError type as a genuine internal bug, the handler has no way to tell a user error (should be 400/422) from an internal error (should be 500), so it blankets everything as 500. This is the concrete downstream cost of the missing typed hierarchy: with a ConfigError/validation type, the handler could map user errors to 400 and only unexpected exceptions to 500. (Note: the artifact-handle validators at 990-1020 are server-generated handles, so their 500 mapping is more defensible; the finding is about the genuinely user-authored config paths.)
apidx.recommended_fix: Raise a typed user-error (ConfigError, or a dedicated request-validation error) from the config validators, and in the route map that type to HTTPException(status_code=422/400, detail=str(exc)) while keeping `except Exception -> 500` for truly unexpected failures. This makes the HTTP status honest and gives API clients a machine-distinguishable signal for 'fix your request' vs 'server bug'.

apidx.location: src/haute/_banding_config.py:50 (also mirrored at :64, :123, :188)
apidx.title: Banding map-form rules raise 'must be a list' when the real problem is an unsupported banding type, telling the user to do the opposite of the fix
apidx.description: In _expand_rule_map, after the categorical and breakpoints branches, the fall-through is `raise ValueError(f'{banding_type} banding rules must be a list')`. But this function is only reached when rules is a *dict* (normalise_banding_rules dispatches dict->_expand_rule_map, list->deepcopy). So when a user provides map-form rules under, say, a 'continuous' banding factor, they get 'continuous banding rules must be a list' - which is misleading twice over: (a) they provided a dict, and the message implies the dict shape is the problem when actually map-form is a supported shape for categorical/breakpoints, and (b) the true cause is that map-form rules are only supported for banding types categorical/breakpoints, not that 'a list' is required. The same copy-pasted message appears in _compact_rule_map (:123) and the list-path fall-throughs (:64, :188), so the wording is reused even where the input genuinely was/ wasn't a list, making it unreliable as a diagnostic.
apidx.recommended_fix: Distinguish the two causes. In the dict-handling functions, the fall-through should say something like f"map-form (object) banding rules are only supported for 'categorical' and 'breakpoints' banding; banding type {banding_type!r} requires a list of rule rows" - naming the actual constraint and the supported types. Keep 'must be a list' only on the true 'unexpected type' fall-through where the value was neither dict nor list.

apidx.location: src/haute/executor.py:153-158 (PreambleError); contrast with HauteError._render at errors.py:23-29
apidx.title: PreambleError captures source_line as an instance attribute but never renders it, so the line number it carefully records never appears in the error message
apidx.description: PreambleError(HauteError) overrides __init__ to accept and store source_line, but it stores it as a plain attribute (self.source_line = source_line) and calls super().__init__(message) WITHOUT passing source_line into HauteError's **context mechanism. HauteError._render only renders self.message + self.context, so str(PreambleError('preamble failed to compile', source_line=42)) yields just 'preamble failed to compile' - the line number, which is the single most useful piece of context for a user debugging a broken preamble (imports/utility block), is silently dropped from the message and every log line and traceback string. The whole point of the HauteError **context design (per its docstring: 'structured information ... reaches log lines and tracebacks without callers having to format it manually') is bypassed here. Callers that want the line must know to read the .source_line attribute, which defeats the affordance.
apidx.recommended_fix: Pass source_line through the context channel: super().__init__(message, source_line=source_line) (guarding None if a bare message is preferred when unknown), or keep the attribute but also include it in context. Then 'preamble failed to compile (source_line=42)' renders automatically. Consider an assertion/test that PreambleError str() includes the line when provided.

apidx.location: src/haute/_databricks_io.py:87-100 (DatabricksConfigError, CacheNotFoundError, FetchIntegrityError)
apidx.title: Databricks domain exceptions live in _databricks_io.py and subclass HauteError directly instead of ConfigError/ExecutionError, so the semantic branch of the taxonomy is bypassed
apidx.description: DatabricksConfigError, CacheNotFoundError and FetchIntegrityError are defined locally in _databricks_io.py rather than in errors.py, and all three subclass HauteError directly rather than the semantically-correct mid-level type. DatabricksConfigError ('Missing Databricks data credentials...') is conceptually a ConfigError; CacheNotFoundError and FetchIntegrityError are execution/runtime failures that should sit under ExecutionError. The messages themselves are excellent (actionable, name the env vars and the GUI action). But because they bypass the ConfigError/ExecutionError tier, a caller doing `except ConfigError` to handle all configuration problems will NOT catch a missing-Databricks-credentials error, and `except ExecutionError` won't catch a fetch-integrity failure - even though both ARE caught by `except HauteError`. This is the same hierarchy-fragmentation theme as the headline finding, but specifically about skipping the intermediate semantic layer rather than escaping HauteError entirely. Defining them in the module (vs errors.py) also splits the taxonomy across files, making the full set of catchable error types hard to discover from one place.
apidx.recommended_fix: Reparent: DatabricksConfigError -> ConfigError; CacheNotFoundError, FetchIntegrityError -> ExecutionError. Either move them into errors.py alongside the rest of the hierarchy, or (if module locality is preferred) at least import the correct base from errors.py and inherit from it, and ensure they are re-exported so the catchable surface is discoverable. Apply the same reparenting review to the other HauteError-direct subclasses (ApiInputSchemaError, UnsafeCodeError, GitError) to decide whether a mid-level branch fits.

apidx.location: src/haute/_config_builder.py:421-427 (and identical text src/haute/_parser_regex.py:726-732)
apidx.title: Sidecar-required error never names the actual config folder and omits how to fix it
apidx.description: When a user authors a folder-backed node inline (e.g. `@pipeline.banding(column="x", rules=[...])` with no `config=`), `_resolve_node_config` raises `ConfigError("Node config must be stored in a JSON sidecar and referenced with config=\"config/<type>/<name>.json\".")`. The literal placeholder `<type>` is never substituted, yet the real folder frequently differs from the decorator name: `@pipeline.output`->`config/quote_response/`, `@pipeline.model_score`->`config/model_scoring/`, `@pipeline.external_file`->`config/load_file/`, `@pipeline.api_input`->`config/quote_input/`, `@pipeline.live_switch`->`config/source_switch/`, `@pipeline.scenario_expander`->`config/expander/`, `@pipeline.optimiser`->`config/optimisation/`, `@pipeline.optimiser_apply`->`config/apply_optimisation/`. A user has no way to know the correct folder from the message, the mapping lives only in `NODE_TYPE_TO_FOLDER` (already imported into this module), and the error neither says the inline kwargs were discarded nor how to generate the file. This is the first wall a hand-author hits and it dead-ends them.
apidx.recommended_fix: Resolve the real folder from the imported `NODE_TYPE_TO_FOLDER[node_type]` and interpolate the concrete path, e.g. `config="config/quote_response/<name>.json"`. Add that the inline kwargs were ignored and point to a generator (`haute init` writes starter sidecars; codegen can emit one). Apply the same fix to the duplicated string in `_parser_regex.py:727-731` so both parse paths agree.

apidx.location: src/haute/pipeline.py:273 (Pipeline docstring) and 498-499 (Submodel docstring); contradicted by src/haute/_config_builder.py:421-427
apidx.title: Decorator docstrings advertise inline kwargs that the parser rejects with ConfigError
apidx.description: The `Pipeline` class docstring shows `@pipeline.data_source(path="data.parquet")` and the `Submodel` docstring shows `@submodel.external_file(path="models/freq.cbm", file_type="catboost")`. Both `DATA_SOURCE` and `EXTERNAL_FILE` are in `NODE_TYPE_TO_FOLDER`, so copy-pasting either documented example and running `haute lint`/`serve`/`deploy` raises `ConfigError("Node config must be stored in a JSON sidecar...")` — the canonical onboarding examples are broken against the real (AST-parser) execution path. The runtime `Pipeline.run()` path tolerates them, so the example 'works' in a pure-Python `pipeline.run()` smoke test but fails the moment the file is parsed, which is exactly what the product does for serve/deploy. This trains users to write code that cannot be loaded.
apidx.recommended_fix: Make the docstrings show the sidecar form for folder-backed types (`@pipeline.data_source(config="config/data_source/raw_rows.json")`, matching the actual scaffold), reserving inline-kwargs examples for types the parser truly builds inline (polars, edge_join, explore). Even better, make the parser honour the inline kwargs the decorator already accepts (synthesise the sidecar) so docs and behaviour converge.

apidx.location: src/haute/_config_builder.py:82-227 (_build_node_config per-type branches)
apidx.title: Most of _build_node_config is unreachable from both parse paths yet reads like the authoring contract
apidx.description: `_build_node_config` is only ever called by the two parser paths after the `has_config_folder(node_type)` gate (`_config_builder.py:421-429` and `_parser_regex.py:726-739`). Because 14 node types are in `NODE_TYPE_TO_FOLDER`, the branches for API_INPUT, DATA_SOURCE, LIVE_SWITCH, MODEL_SCORE, BANDING, RATING_STEP, OUTPUT, DATA_SINK, EXTERNAL_FILE, MODELLING, OPTIMISER, OPTIMISER_APPLY, SCENARIO_EXPANDER and CONSTANT can never run during real parsing (only POLARS/EDGE_JOIN/EXPLORE/transform survive the gate). Yet this function is the single most authoritative-looking place to answer 'what kwargs does a banding/rating_step/model_score node accept?' — it spells out `factors=[{...}]`, `tables=[{...}]`, `operation`/`op`, `combined_outputs`, etc. A developer extending Haute reads ~110 lines of detailed kwarg-translation logic that is fiction for the path they care about, and may 'fix a bug' in a branch that never executes (the exhaustive review already flagged contract-mismatch divergence here for similar reasons). The real config shape for those types lives in the `expand_*_from_sidecar` helpers and the TypedDicts.
apidx.recommended_fix: Delete the unreachable branches (or guard `_build_node_config` so it only handles the inline-buildable types) and let `_resolve_node_config` route folder-backed types straight to sidecar loading. If the inline-kwargs translation is meant to be a supported hand-authoring affordance, wire it into `_resolve_node_config` *before* the `has_config_folder` raise so it actually runs; today it is exercised only by unit tests.

apidx.location: src/haute/_config_builder.py:111-116 and 184-188
apidx.title: source_type->sourceType is special-cased for only two node types while every sibling key stays as-authored
apidx.description: For MODEL_SCORE and OPTIMISER_APPLY the builder does `decorator_key = "source_type" if key == "sourceType" else key`, i.e. the author writes snake_case `source_type=` but every *other* key in `MODEL_SCORE_CONFIG_KEYS`/`OPTIMISER_APPLY_CONFIG_KEYS` (`run_id`, `output_column`, `registered_model`, `artifact_path`, ...) is passed through verbatim and is already snake_case in both decorator and config. So within one node type the casing rule is 'snake everywhere, except this one key is snake-in/camel-out'. Meanwhile BANDING/RATING_STEP accept BOTH `output_column` AND `outputColumn` (lines 130, 139, 152-153) and emit camelCase, and OPTIMISER/MODELLING pass keys through unchanged. A hand-author cannot predict the casing convention; it varies per node type and per key with no stated rule. (Compounded by the fact these branches are sidecar-dead per the separate finding, but the same camel/snake split is what users must reproduce by hand in the JSON sidecar.)
apidx.recommended_fix: Pick one convention for the user-facing surface (decorator kwargs and sidecar keys) — snake_case is the Python-idiomatic choice and already dominates — and translate to the internal camelCase form in exactly one place. Drop the per-type ad-hoc `source_type`/`sourceType` and dual `output_column`/`outputColumn` acceptance, or document a single explicit alias table so the rule is discoverable rather than per-branch folklore.

apidx.location: src/haute/_scaffold.py:977 (starter body) vs src/haute/cli/_init_cmd.py:407-410 (raw_rows.json sidecar)
apidx.title: Scaffold encodes the source data path in two places that can silently drift
apidx.description: `haute init` writes a `data_source` node whose function body hardcodes `pl.scan_parquet(Path(__file__).parent / "../data/sample.parquet")` (starter_pipeline) AND a sidecar `config/data_source/raw_rows.json` containing `"path": "../data/sample.parquet"`. The two are independent sources of truth for the same fact. The starter test's `_materialise_missing_source_files` (_scaffold.py:1166-1184) reads the *sidecar* `config['path']` to decide what file to synthesise, while `haute run` executes the *body's* `scan_parquet`. A user following the scaffold's own recipe comment ('point the source node's JSON sidecar at it') updates the sidecar path, but the body keeps scanning the old path — so the test (sidecar-driven) and the run (body-driven) silently disagree, and the failure surfaces far from the edit. The scaffold thus teaches a dual-path data-source idiom whose two halves must be kept in lockstep by hand.
apidx.recommended_fix: Make the starter source single-sourced: either drive the body from the sidecar (read `config['path']` in the source loader and have the body call a shared `haute` source-loading helper) or drop the redundant `path` from the sidecar and let the body be the only source of truth. At minimum, update the recipe comment to say 'edit BOTH the body's scan path and the sidecar path' until they are unified.

apidx.location: src/haute/_config_validation.py:99-129 (warn_unrecognized_config_keys); called at src/haute/_config_builder.py:444 without node_label
apidx.title: Mistyped sidecar keys are dropped with only an unattributed log warning and no suggestion
apidx.description: A sidecar author who typos a key (`outputColum`, `combinedColumns`, `default_value` where the schema wants `defaultValue`, etc.) gets it silently ignored: `warn_unrecognized_config_keys` only emits a `logger.warning` and is documented to 'Never raise'. Two ergonomics gaps: (1) it offers no near-miss/'did you mean' hint even though it has the full valid-key set (`VALID_KEYS[node_type]`) in hand, so a one-character typo gives no path to the fix; (2) `_resolve_node_config` calls it as `warn_unrecognized_config_keys(node_type, config)` with no `node_label`, so the warning is keyed by node *type* only — with several banding/rating nodes in a pipeline the user cannot tell which file the dropped key came from. For a CLI user running `haute lint`, a log-level warning is also easy to miss entirely, so the misconfiguration manifests later as a wrong-but-not-failing result (the antithesis of the project's 'fail loudly' guidance).
apidx.recommended_fix: Pass the node label/func name through to `warn_unrecognized_config_keys` so the warning identifies the file, and add a difflib `get_close_matches` suggestion against `VALID_KEYS[node_type]` ('unrecognised key "outputColum" on banding node "foo"; did you mean "outputColumn"?'). Consider surfacing these as `haute lint` findings (non-zero/visible), not just structured log lines, so they are not silently swallowed.

apidx.location: src/haute/_config_builder.py:229-232
apidx.title: instance_of vs of: two names for the same kwarg, generator emits one and hand-author guidance the other
apidx.description: `_build_node_config` accepts both `instance_of=` (checked first) and `of=` (fallback) for instance references, mapping either to `instanceOf`. Codegen, however, always emits `@pipeline.instance(of="...")` (codegen.py:507), so round-tripped pipelines use `of=` while the builder prioritises `instance_of=`. Neither name is documented on the `instance` decorator (`pipeline.py:219-221` has a bare docstring), so a hand-author has no signal which to use, and reading generated code (`of=`) versus reading this builder (`instance_of` first) gives contradictory cues. Two undocumented synonyms with a silent precedence order is a small but real 'which one is canonical?' papercut.
apidx.recommended_fix: Choose one canonical kwarg (the generator already standardises on `of=`), document it on `NodeRegistry.instance`, and either drop the other alias or keep it but document it explicitly as a deprecated synonym. Keeping codegen and the hand-authoring guidance on the same name removes the contradiction.

apidx.location: src/haute/_types.py:178,191,213 (output_column vs outputColumn); :111,129-146,166,182,272-273,386,588-590 (camelCase keys) vs :178,495,517-561 (snake_case keys)
apidx.title: Node-config keys mix camelCase and snake_case with no rule -- the same concept (output column) is `outputColumn` in banding/ratingStep but `output_column` in modelScore
apidx.description: The node-config TypedDicts in _types.py have no consistent key-casing convention. camelCase keys: sourceType, instanceOf, inputMapping, baseInput, joinInput, leftOn, rightOn, maintainOrder, outputColumn, defaultValue, combinedColumn, combinedOutputs, fileType, modelClass, childNodeIds, inputPorts, outputPorts. snake_case keys (often in the SAME dict): output_column, registered_model, experiment_id, run_id, quote_id, scenario_index, scenario_value, max_iter, feature_columns, version_column, optimised_value_column, factor_columns, data_input, banding_source. The split is not merely cross-node: ModelScoreConfig (_types.py:166,178) carries BOTH `sourceType` (camel) and `output_column`/`registered_model` (snake); OptimiserApplyConfig (:386-388) carries `sourceType` (camel) next to `version_column`/`optimised_value_column` (snake). Worst of all, the identical concept 'the name of the column a node writes' is spelled `outputColumn` in BandingFactor (_types.py:191) and RatingTable (:213) but `output_column` in ModelScoreConfig (:178). A new engineer authoring or reading a config cannot predict the casing of any given key and must grep each one; auto-completion and muscle memory are useless. This is the most pervasive naming-coherence defect in the codebase.
apidx.recommended_fix: Choose one canonical casing for config keys (snake_case is the lower-churn choice: it already dominates the optimiser/modelling surfaces and matches Python/JSON norms) and migrate the camelCase keys to it behind a back-compat read shim in _config_validation/_config_io (accept the old key on read, emit only the new one on save) so existing on-disk configs keep loading. Add a CI test that introspects every *Config TypedDict and every Pydantic request/response model and fails if a field name violates the chosen convention (mirroring the existing OPTIMISER_CONFIG_KEYS-style allow-lists). At minimum, unify the output-column key across banding/ratingStep/modelScore to a single spelling, since divergent names for one concept is the clearest footgun.

apidx.location: src/haute/routes/_optimiser_service.py:201,594,4413,4720 (mult_col); src/haute/_builders.py:1444,1462,1479,1490,1618 (mult_col, optimal_scenario_value, optimised_factor); src/haute/executor.py:554 (optimal_scenario_value, optimised_factor); frontend/src/utils/nodeTypes.ts:76 (optimised_value); frontend/src/panels/optimiser/ratebookFactorTables.ts:5 (RATE_COLUMN=optimal_scenario_value)
apidx.title: The optimiser's central output value has ~6 different names across the stack, including the actively-misleading local `mult_col` (implies multiplier)
apidx.description: The one concept 'the per-scenario value the optimiser chooses' is named six different ways depending on layer: (1) config key + input column `scenario_value` (_types.py:336, OptimiserConfig); (2) local variable `mult_col` everywhere in the service and builders (routes/_optimiser_service.py:201, _builders.py:1444) -- 'mult' implies a *multiplier*, a stale mental model that misdescribes the value and will mislead anyone reading the solver code; (3) the actual output column default `optimal_scenario_value` (_builders.py:1462, executor.py:554); (4) the apply-node's frontend default rename target `optimised_value` (nodeTypes.ts:76, `optimised_value_column: 'optimised_value'`); (5) the ratebook synthesized output column `{name}_optimised_factor` (_builders.py:1618) and legacy default-value column `optimised_factor` (executor.py:554); (6) the frontend constant `RATE_COLUMN = 'optimal_scenario_value'` (ratebookFactorTables.ts:5). A developer tracing a value from config (`scenario_value`) to solver code (`mult_col`) to output (`optimal_scenario_value`) to the apply default (`optimised_value`) crosses four names for the same number, with no comment tying them together. `mult_col` is the dangerous one: it asserts a semantic (multiplication) the code does not guarantee.
apidx.recommended_fix: Rename the local `mult_col` -> `scenario_value_col` (and `step_col` -> `scenario_index_col`) throughout _optimiser_service.py, _builders.py, optimiser.py, and _optimiser_apply_explainability.py so the variable matches the config key it reads. Standardise the OUTPUT column on a single name (`optimal_scenario_value` is the most descriptive) and have the ratebook path emit it too instead of `{name}_optimised_factor`; align the frontend apply default (`optimised_value`) and `RATE_COLUMN` to the same string, or document the rename relationship in one place. Add a module docstring in _optimiser_service.py mapping config-key -> internal-var -> output-column for the scenario_value / scenario_index pair.

apidx.location: src/haute/schemas.py:833 (test_rows # validation rows), :836 (diagnostics_set); src/haute/modelling/_training_job.py:176,517 (test_rows=split_result.n_validation); src/haute/cli/_train.py:102 ('Test: {result.test_rows} rows'); frontend/src/api/types.ts:351 (test_rows)
apidx.title: `test_rows`/`test_mb` actually carry the VALIDATION-set counts -- colliding with the train/validation/holdout vocabulary used everywhere else, and the CLI prints 'Test:' for validation rows
apidx.description: Across the modelling stack the canonical split vocabulary is train / validation / holdout: TrainResponse.diagnostics_set is documented '"train" | "validation" | "holdout"' (schemas.py:836), the splitter exposes n_validation / n_holdout (_training_job.py:517-518), and holdout has its own field `holdout_rows`. The ONLY place the word 'test' appears is `test_rows` (schemas.py:833, types.ts:351) and `test_mb`/`testing_mb`-style estimate fields -- and they do not mean a test set at all: _training_job.py:517 assigns `test_rows=split_result.n_validation`, and schemas.py:833 even carries the comment `# validation rows`. The leak reaches the user: cli/_train.py:102 prints `Test: {result.test_rows:,} rows` for what are validation rows. In an insurance/DS context, train/validation/test is a precise three-way distinction; naming the validation count `test_rows` is a silent-misuse trap that will cause an engineer (or actuary reading the CLI) to mis-model their data leakage assumptions. (Distinct from the existing finding about `diagnostics_set` being an untyped str -- this is about the misleading *field name* `test_rows`.)
apidx.recommended_fix: Rename the field to `validation_rows` (and any `test_mb`/`test_*` estimate counterpart to `validation_mb`) end-to-end: TrainResult/_training_job.py, TrainResponse (schemas.py), TrainResponse in types.ts + guards.ts, the ui_contracts fixtures, and the CLI print ('Validation:'). Provide a back-compat alias on the response model for one release if external consumers read `test_rows` (Pydantic `validation_alias`/serialization_alias) and remove it once the frontend migrates. Add a regression test asserting the response exposes `validation_rows == n_validation` and that no field named `test_*` carries validation data.

apidx.location: src/haute/_types.py:191,213 (config: outputColumn) vs frontend/src/types/trace.ts:62,103,123,223,241 (trace detail: output_column) consumed together in frontend/src/trace/bandingRows.ts:13 (outputColumn) & :30,49 (factor.output_column)
apidx.title: A banding factor's output column flips casing between its config payload (`outputColumn`) and its trace-detail payload (`output_column`) -- and one component reads both
apidx.description: The banding node stores its per-factor output column under `outputColumn` (camelCase) in config (_types.py:191; frontend types/banding.ts:8). But the trace-detail surface for the same factor exposes that column as `output_column` (snake_case) in trace.ts:62/103/123/223/241. The collision is not theoretical: frontend/src/trace/bandingRows.ts has to juggle BOTH spellings -- it reads the config shape `outputColumn` (bandingRows.ts:13) and the trace shape `factor.output_column` (bandingRows.ts:30,49) inside the same module to render banding trace rows. So the same logical field has two casings in two payloads the same code path consumes, forcing per-call-site awareness of which spelling applies. This is the cross-wire manifestation of the broader camel/snake config-key split and a concrete maintenance footgun (rename one and the other silently keeps the old value).
apidx.recommended_fix: Make the banding config key and the banding trace-detail key use the same casing for the output column. Simplest: when building the banding trace detail on the backend, emit `outputColumn` to match the config (or, if snake_case is chosen project-wide per the casing fix, migrate the config key to `output_column` and keep them identical).
