frontend-quality.recommended_fix: Broaden the typing/focus guard: also treat tag==="SELECT", el.isContentEditable, and elements with role in {textbox,combobox,listbox,menu,menuitem,radio} (or any focused [contenteditable]) as 'isTyping' for the destructive shortcuts (Delete/Backspace, Ctrl+A, copy/paste). Centralising this in a small isEditableTarget(el) helper keeps the eight shortcut branches consistent.

frontend-quality.title: Heavy bottom-panel surfaces (OptimiserPreview, ModellingPreview, OptimiserDataPreview, ExplorePreview, TracePanel) are eagerly imported into the initial entry chunk despite being conditionally rendered
frontend-quality.description: App.tsx statically imports OptimiserPreview, OptimiserDataPreview, ModellingPreview, ExplorePreview and TracePanel at module top (lines 23-28). Each of these pulls in a large first-party subtree: the optimiser panel pulls FrontierChart, ConvergenceChart, SummaryTab, DetailCard, RatebookRatesTab, RatebookImpactBeeswarm, iterationSummary, ratebookFactorTables; ModellingPreview pulls 9 tab components (GLMCoefficientsTab, GLMRelativitiesTab, LossTab, LiftTab, ResidualsTab, FeaturesTab, AveTab, PdpTab, SummaryTab); TracePanel pulls StepCard, CalculationHero, WaterfallChart and the whole src/trace detail tree. Measured: the modelling + optimiser + trace source subtrees total 355,288 bytes of source, and all of it lands in the entry chunk. The built artifact confirms it: index-*.js is 440.3 KiB raw / 114.8 KiB gzip, and the gate reports initial total 237.4 KiB gzip against a 240 KiB budget -- only ~2.6 KiB of headroom. Yet every one of these panels is rendered conditionally (OptimiserPreview only when getOptimiserPreview(id) exists, ModellingPreview only when getModellingPreview(id) exists, OptimiserDataPreview only for optimiser nodes with preview data, ExplorePreview only for EXPLORE nodes, TracePanel only when traceResult is set). A user who opens the editor and never solves an optimiser, trains a model, or traces a cell downloads and parses all of this code for nothing. The codebase already has the exact mechanism to fix this: src/panels/LazyNodeEditors.tsx wraps config editors in React.lazy(() => import(...)) behind a LazyEditorBoundary Suspense, and NodePanel consumes them that way -- but the preview/trace surfaces were never migrated to it. Note the asymmetry: OptimiserConfig and ModellingConfig ARE lazy (separate 7.5 KiB / 9.8 KiB gzip chunks), while their heavier Preview siblings are eager. The charts are hand-rolled SVG (no d3/recharts/chart.js/plotly anywhere in src -- verified), so the win is purely from deferring first-party JS, with no vendor-dedup risk.
frontend-quality.recommended_fix: Add the five preview/trace panels to the existing lazy pattern. Either extend LazyNodeEditors.tsx (e.g. export const OptimiserPreview = lazy(() => import('./OptimiserPreview'))) or create a sibling LazyPreviewPanels.tsx, and wrap the conditional render blocks in App.tsx's DataPreview ErrorBoundary (and the TracePanel branch in the aside) in a <Suspense fallback={...}> with a lightweight panel-shaped skeleton. Because these only render after an async solve/train/trace completes, the chunk fetch is fully hidden behind work the user already waited for -- there is no perceptible loading penalty. This moves an estimated 60-90 KiB gzip out of the initial entry chunk, restoring real headroom under the 240 KiB budget.
frontend-quality.recommended_fix_note: Add the corresponding chunk-name prefixes (OptimiserPreview, ModellingPreview, OptimiserDataPreview, ExplorePreview, TracePanel) to LAZY_ONLY_MODULEPRELOAD_CHUNK_PREFIXES in check-bundle-size.mjs so a future eager re-import is caught.

frontend-quality.title: Bundle-budget gate's lazy-only modulepreload check cannot detect a heavy panel becoming eager, and the lazy-only allowlist omits the preview/trace panels entirely
frontend-quality.description: The gate has two defenses against eager heavy code: (1) a 240 KiB initial-gzip ceiling, and (2) a LAZY_ONLY_MODULEPRELOAD_CHUNK_PREFIXES check that fails if a known lazy chunk appears as a startup <link rel=modulepreload>. Defense (2) is structurally blind to the most likely regression. When a developer adds a static import of a panel into App.tsx (as already happened for OptimiserPreview/ModellingPreview/TracePanel -- see the companion finding), Rollup MERGES that code into the index entry chunk; it does not emit a separate named chunk, so there is no 'OptimiserPreview-*.js' modulepreload link for the prefix check to flag. The chunk-name guard therefore only catches the narrow case of an already-split lazy chunk being preloaded, never the case of lazy code regressing back to eager. That leaves only defense (1), the size ceiling -- which the live build shows sitting at 237.4 / 240 KiB (~2.6 KiB / ~1% margin). A small future eager import will breach it, but the failure message ('Initial JS gzip size X exceeds budget') gives no hint about WHICH panel regressed, because they are all anonymized inside index-*.js. Compounding this, the allowlist itself omits the very surfaces that are currently eager and should be lazy: it lists CodeMirrorEditor, vendor-codemirror, vendor-layout, the editors, ModellingConfig and OptimiserConfig, but NOT OptimiserPreview, ModellingPreview, OptimiserDataPreview, ExplorePreview or TracePanel -- so even if those were split, the gate would not assert they stay lazy. The analyze:bundle sourcemap tooling exists but is a manual/opt-in script, not part of check:bundle, so it does not enforce per-source attribution in CI.
frontend-quality.recommended_fix: Strengthen the gate so eager-ness of heavy panels is detectable and enforced, not merely size-capped: (a) once the preview/trace panels are code-split (companion finding), add their chunk prefixes to LAZY_ONLY_MODULEPRELOAD_CHUNK_PREFIXES so any re-eager-ing surfaces as a build failure; (b) add a per-source assertion to check:bundle (reuse analyze-bundle-sourcemaps.mjs's contributor analysis) that fails if a source under src/panels/{optimiser,modelling}, src/trace, or the named preview files contributes generated bytes to the index entry chunk -- this catches eager merges that the modulepreload-name heuristic cannot; (c) consider tightening the initial budget back toward the documented ~200 KiB baseline once the panels are deferred, so the ~1% margin is restored to a meaningful operating buffer.
frontend-quality.recommended_fix_note: Defense (b) is the durable fix: it attributes entry-chunk bytes to source paths, so it is robust to chunk-name anonymization that defeats the prefix check.

frontend-quality.location: frontend/src/components/Toolbar.tsx:90-94 (status dot); frontend/src/hooks/useWebSocketSync.ts:174-177, 95 (terminal disconnected state); frontend/src/App.tsx:517-539 (banner region where a disconnect banner is absent)
frontend-quality.title: WebSocket disconnect has no banner and no recovery affordance — live-sync silently dies behind a 2px dot
frontend-quality.description: useWebSocketSync drives three states (connected | reconnecting | disconnected). On terminal failure — connect() throwing (line 205), retries exhausted after MAX_RETRIES=50 with up to 30s backoff (lines 174-177), or never-opened abnormal close — status becomes 'disconnected'. The ONLY place this surfaces is the Toolbar status dot (Toolbar.tsx:90-94): a 2px <span> whose background colour changes to var(--danger) with a hover `title` of 'Server unreachable — restart haute serve'. There is no banner, no toast, and crucially no retry button. Contrast this with the two sibling failure states App.tsx already renders as full-width banners with actions: sessionExpired (App.tsx:518-531, with a Reload button) and syncBanner (App.tsx:533-539). For a tool whose entire premise is reflecting on-disk pipeline edits in real time, a dead socket means the canvas is now silently stale — the user keeps editing and saving against state that no longer round-trips, with zero prominent indication. Because the dot relies on colour + hover-title only, sighted users glancing at the canvas miss it, and (see separate a11y finding) keyboard/SR users cannot perceive it at all. After 50 retries the app also stops trying entirely, with no way to re-initiate a connection short of a full page reload.
frontend-quality.recommended_fix: Render a dismissible/persistent banner in the App.tsx main column (alongside sessionExpired/syncBanner) when wsStatus === 'disconnected' (and optionally a subtler one for prolonged 'reconnecting'). Give it role='alert', a clear message ('Live sync to the server was lost — file changes will not appear until reconnected'), and a 'Retry now' button that resets retriesRef.current=0 and re-runs connect() (expose a reconnect() callback from the hook, or key the effect off a manual retry counter). Keep the toolbar dot as a secondary indicator. This reuses the established banner pattern and removes the silent-stale-editor failure mode.

frontend-quality.title: Connection-status dot is colour-only and not exposed to assistive tech (no role/aria-live, hover-title only)
frontend-quality.description: The WS connection indicator is a bare <span className='w-2 h-2 rounded-full'> whose meaning is conveyed entirely by background colour (success/warning/danger) plus a `title` attribute. There is no `role`, no accessible name, and no aria-live region, so: (1) screen-reader users are never informed of connection state or of transitions to 'reconnecting'/'disconnected'; (2) the `title` tooltip is mouse-hover-only and not reachable by keyboard; (3) colour is the sole visual channel, failing WCAG 1.4.1 Use of Colour. The same colour-only pattern is used for the 'live' source dot (Toolbar.tsx:133-134, 158-160) and the dirty dot (line 89). Given this is the primary (and currently sole) signal that real-time sync is alive, its inaccessibility compounds the missing-banner issue above.
frontend-quality.recommended_fix: Make the indicator a focusable, labelled status element: add role='status' with an aria-live='polite' wrapper (or aria-label that updates with state, e.g. aria-label={wsConfig.title}), and pair the colour with a tiny glyph/text (e.g. a connected/alert icon) so state is not colour-only. At minimum give it an aria-label and ensure the state text is announced when it changes. Apply the same colour-plus-label treatment to the dirty and 'live source' dots.

frontend-quality.title: Preview error state is visual-only — backend/preview failures are not announced to screen readers
frontend-quality.description: When a node preview fails (status==='error'), DataPreview renders the error purely as an AlertCircle icon plus styled text inside a plain <div> (lines 280-286), and the header shows a second visual-only error chip (lines 416-421). Neither has role='alert' nor lives in an aria-live region, so a screen-reader user who triggers a preview and gets a backend error (timeout, contract error, Polars exception) receives no spoken feedback — the panel simply appears to do nothing. This is inconsistent with the codebase's own convention: NodePanel diagnostics (NodePanel.tsx:278, 516), InstanceReferenceDiagnostic, and Toast all correctly use role='alert'. The preview surface is the primary place users see execution failures, so it is the most important place to announce them.
frontend-quality.recommended_fix: Add role='alert' to the error container (DataPreview.tsx:280-286) so the failure message is announced when it appears. Consider also wrapping the status header region in an aria-live='polite' so status transitions (ok/error/loading) are conveyed. Ensure the error text is the accessible content (it already is plain text).

frontend-quality.title: Loading states ('Loading pipeline…', 'Executing pipeline…') are not announced — no role=status/aria-live
frontend-quality.description: The initial app load shows a centered 'Loading pipeline...' <div> (App.tsx:464-470) with no role='status' and no aria-live, so screen-reader users hear nothing while the pipeline loads and get no completion cue when the canvas appears. The same applies to DataPreview's in-flight states: the 'Executing pipeline...' overlay (DataPreview.tsx:276-279) and the header 'Running...' chip (lines 422-424) are animate-pulse text only. The project already knows the correct pattern — EditorLoadingFallback in LazyNodeEditors.tsx:25-34 uses role='status' aria-live='polite' aria-label='Loading editor' — but it is not applied to the two most prominent loading surfaces. Result: SR users cannot tell whether a long-running preview is working, stalled, or finished.
frontend-quality.recommended_fix: Add role='status' aria-live='polite' (with an aria-label such as 'Loading pipeline') to the App.tsx initial-load wrapper and to the DataPreview loading container, mirroring EditorLoadingFallback. This gives a spoken 'Loading…' on entry and an implicit completion cue when the region is replaced by content.

frontend-quality.title: Toasts use assertive role='alert' on every item inside a polite live-region container — conflicting/duplicated announcements
frontend-quality.description: Each ToastItem sets role='alert' (Toast.tsx:38), which carries an implicit aria-live='assertive', while the parent container also declares aria-live='polite' (Toast.tsx:66). This is contradictory: success and info toasts (e.g. 'Saved → file', 'Pipeline updated from file') are announced assertively, interrupting whatever the screen reader is currently saying, which is inappropriate for non-critical confirmations; and nesting an assertive live region inside a polite one yields undefined/duplicated announcement behaviour across AT. The information-severity is not differentiated — a routine 'success' interrupts the user the same way a hard 'error' does.
frontend-quality.recommended_fix: Differentiate by severity: use role='alert' (assertive) only for type==='error' (and possibly 'warning'); use role='status' (polite) for 'success'/'info'. Remove the redundant aria-live from one level — either keep a single polite live region on the container and drop per-item roles, or keep per-item roles and make the container a non-live wrapper. Ensure each toast is announced exactly once.

frontend-quality.location: frontend/src/panels/PanelShell.tsx:5-24 (fixed MIN_PANEL_W=320, px math); frontend/src/index.css (0 @media queries); frontend/src/App.tsx:498-714 (fixed horizontal flex layout)
frontend-quality.title: No responsive breakpoints anywhere — fixed-px three-column layout breaks on narrow/zoomed viewports
frontend-quality.description: The entire frontend contains zero @media queries (grep across src/*.css and *.tsx returns none) and no container-query usage. The shell is a fixed horizontal flex: left palette (LEFT_PALETTE_W=180 / collapsed 40, PanelShell.tsx:6-7), a flex-1 canvas+preview centre, and a right panel whose minimum is MIN_PANEL_W=320 (PanelShell.tsx:5). On a narrow window (or high browser zoom / split-screen), the right panel cannot shrink below 320px and the palette consumes another 40-180px, so the canvas centre is squeezed and the toolbar's many fixed-width controls (Toolbar.tsx) overflow with no wrapping or stacking. Nothing collapses, stacks, or switches to an overlay below a threshold. DataPreview does have internal width tiers (responsiveColumnWidth, DataPreview.tsx:87-91) but the overall page chrome does not adapt. index.html does set a proper viewport meta, so the app advertises responsiveness it doesn't implement. This is a desktop-class tool so the severity is low, but at staff-quality bar the layout should degrade gracefully rather than overflow.
frontend-quality.recommended_fix: Introduce at least one breakpoint: below ~900px collapse the left palette to its icon rail by default and reduce/await MIN_PANEL_W (or convert the right panel to a slide-over overlay rather than an in-flow column). Allow the toolbar control cluster to wrap or move secondary controls into an overflow menu under a width threshold. Even a single 'compact' breakpoint that prevents horizontal overflow would close the gap.

frontend-quality.location: frontend/src/App.tsx:24-26 (eager imports of OptimiserPreview, OptimiserDataPreview, ModellingPreview, ExplorePreview)
frontend-quality.title: Heavy result-preview panels are eagerly imported into App while config editors are lazy — inconsistent splitting, larger initial bundle
frontend-quality.description: App.tsx statically imports OptimiserPreview (824 lines, pulling its whole optimiser/ chart subtree: FrontierChart, ConvergenceChart, SummaryTab, RatebookRatesTab, DetailCard, RatebookImpactBeeswarm), OptimiserDataPreview (768 lines), ExplorePreview (260 lines), and ModellingPreview — all into the initial bundle (App.tsx:23-26). These panels render only conditionally (App.tsx:589-637) when a user opens an optimiser/modelling/explore result, which is a minority of sessions. Meanwhile every NodePanel config editor IS code-split via React.lazy (LazyNodeEditors.tsx:3-23) and elkjs is dynamically imported (utils/layout.ts:14-19), so the project clearly adopts lazy-loading as a pattern — but the largest result-preview surfaces bypass it and load up front for all users. (Note: no recharts/d3 dependency — charts are custom SVG — so this is bundle weight from app code, not a third-party chart lib.)
frontend-quality.recommended_fix: Wrap OptimiserPreview, OptimiserDataPreview, ExplorePreview, and ModellingPreview in React.lazy with a Suspense fallback (reuse the existing LazyEditorBoundary or a small skeleton), matching the NodePanel editor pattern, so their chunks load only when a result of that type is actually displayed. This trims the initial JS for the common edit-only session.

numerical.title: Float32 factor columns canonicalise non-dyadic decimals at f32 precision, so the SAME nominal value yields a different lookup key than a Float64 column or the authored string entry -> silent miss / wrong premium
numerical.description: _rating_key_expr formats a float factor column to its key with `col.cast(pl.Utf8)`, which uses the COLUMN's native dtype precision (shortest round-trippable repr per dtype). A Float32 column therefore produces a different canonical key than a Float64 column for the same nominal value whenever that value is not exactly representable in f32 (i.e. almost every non-dyadic decimal). Because a rating table's entry keys are authored ONCE (as JSON strings after a sidecar round-trip, or as f64 JSON numbers), they can match only ONE float width. Consequence in the engine itself (not just traces): a frame whose factor column is Float32 misses entries that the identical table would match on a Float64 frame. The lookup RESULT depends on the column's float width. The agreement test's Float32 carve-out is explicitly scoped to TRACE ENRICHMENT (`tests/test_rating_key_agreement.py` docstring: 'non-integer Float32 keys are outside the enrichment-agreement guarantee'), and the only Float32 plain-decimal test uses 0.1, which coincidentally has identical f32/f64 shortest reprs, masking the general failure. This is the engine returning a wrong number, distinct from V025 (source-col mutation) and V038/V039 (sidecar string round-trip).
numerical.evidence: Frame x=Float32(0.3333333333333333) canonicalises to '0.33333334'; the rehydrated sidecar entry key is the string '0.3333333333333333' (compact_rating_step_config_for_sidecar -> '0.3333333333333333' -> expand -> [{'x':'0.3333333333333333',...}]). Keys differ -> no join match. Under default onMissing='error' this raises RatingTableMissError blaming the data ('Missing key(s): {x: 0.33333334}'); under onMissing='neutral' the table output is null and _combine_rating_columns multiply neutral-fills it to 1.0 -> the rating factor is SILENTLY dropped, premium understated, no crash. The byte-for-byte identical table on a Float64 frame returns f=[2.0]. Also confirmed for 0.0001 (f32->'0.0001' vs f64 string '0.0001' matches by luck) vs 1/3 and 123.456 (diverge). Decimal(scale=2) columns show the same class: 25.50 canonicalises to '25.50' and misses entries '25.5'/'25'.
numerical.recommended_fix: Make the float key canonicalisation width-independent so a value's key does not depend on whether its column is Float32 or Float64. In _rating_key_expr, for the non-int-like float branch, cast Float32 columns up to Float64 BEFORE the Utf8 cast (`col.cast(pl.Float64).cast(pl.Utf8)`) for both Float32 and Float64 dtypes, so the engine key matches the f64-based normalise_rating_key mirror and the authored f64/string entry. Symmetrically widen on the lookup side. Then strengthen tests/test_rating_key_agreement.py::test_float32_plain_decimal_matches_string_keys to use a non-dyadic value (e.g. 0.3333333333333333 / 123.456) keyed by the f64 string, asserting a match, and add an explicit Float32-frame-vs-string-entry agreement case. (Widening f32->f64 is exact and lossless, so it cannot introduce a new mismatch.)

numerical.title: Stated invariant 'Python rating key == Polars rating key for all dtypes' is only PARTIAL: normalise_rating_key has no Float32 awareness and always widens to Float64, so it disagrees with the engine expression on any non-dyadic Float32 value
numerical.description: normalise_rating_key formats every float via `pl.Series([value], dtype=pl.Float64).cast(pl.Utf8)` — there is no Float32 code path because a Python float is always f64. _rating_key_expr formats using the column's actual dtype. For a non-dyadic Float32 column value these two differ (engine uses 6-7 sig-digit f32 repr; mirror uses the 17-digit f64 repr of the f32-widened value). The mirror feeds trace enrichment (_trace_enrichment._enrich_single_table) and sidecar canonicalisation, so a trace can report matched/default/no_match flags that disagree with what the engine join actually did for Float32 factor columns. The codebase documents this gap for enrichment, so it is partly intentional, but the broad invariant as commonly stated ('Python key == Polars key for ALL dtypes') is not enforced for Float32.
numerical.evidence: v=0.1 -> engine(Float32)='0.1' but mirror(f32-widened float 0.10000000149011612)='0.10000000149011612' (DIVERGE). v=0.0001 -> engine '0.0001' vs mirror '0.00009999999747378752'. v=1/3 -> engine '0.33333334' vs mirror '0.3333333432674408'. All Int/Float64/Utf8/Bool values agree exactly (verified across UInt64 2^63..2^64-1, Int64 extremes, Int128, the 2^63 boundary, and the full _CANONICAL_GRID).
numerical.recommended_fix: Fold this into the fix above by widening Float32->Float64 in _rating_key_expr (which makes engine == mirror for Float32 too), OR if Float32 keys must stay f32-formatted, give normalise_rating_key an explicit dtype-aware entry point used by enrichment so the mirror reproduces the engine's f32 repr. Either way, extend the agreement test grid to include Float32-sourced values (not just inferred-dtype scalars) so the invariant is pinned, not carved out.

numerical.location: src/haute/_rating.py:136-220 (_breakpoints_to_rules), open-ended tail append at 213-218; consumed by _apply_banding:99-100,130-131
numerical.title: A breakpoints factor consisting of only an open-ended breakpoint (empty boundary) silently produces NO output column
numerical.description: _breakpoints_to_rules appends the open-ended tail rule only `if open_ended is not None and prev_boundary is not None`. With a single open-ended breakpoint and no bounded breakpoints, `bounded` is empty, `prev_boundary` stays None, the tail is skipped, and the function returns []. _apply_banding then finds the continuous when/then chain is None (line 130) and returns the frame UNCHANGED — the configured output column is never created. This is a silent passthrough on a misconfigured-but-plausible factor (a single catch-all band), violating the project's fail-loud rule: downstream nodes referencing the band column see a missing column or stale data with no error.
numerical.evidence: breakpoints=[{'boundary':'','label':'everything'}] -> _breakpoints_to_rules(...) == []; _apply_banding(frame, 'x','b','breakpoints',[that]) returns a frame with NO 'b' column ('b' in out.columns == False).
numerical.recommended_fix: When `bounded` is empty but an open_ended breakpoint exists, emit a single unconditional rule assigning the open-ended label to all finite rows (e.g. {'op1':'>=','val1':-inf} is not allowed since non-finite is rejected; instead build a chain that maps everything to the label, or fall back to a categorical-style constant assignment). At minimum, raise a clear ValueError ('breakpoints factor needs at least one numeric boundary') so the misconfiguration fails loudly instead of silently dropping the output column.

numerical.location: src/haute/_rating.py:153-178 (_breakpoints_to_rules boundary/open-ended separation and duplicate guard)
numerical.title: Multiple open-ended breakpoints silently drop all but the last; the duplicate-boundary guard only covers bounded boundaries
numerical.description: The loop assigns `open_ended = bp` on every empty-boundary breakpoint, so if a config contains two or more open-ended breakpoints only the LAST survives and the earlier ones are discarded with no error. The explicit duplicate-boundary rejection (lines 173-178) only checks bounded numeric boundaries via `seen_boundaries`, so it does not catch duplicate/contradictory open-ended tails. A user who accidentally leaves two rows with blank boundaries gets a silently different banding than configured.
numerical.evidence: breakpoints=[{'boundary':'10','label':'lo'},{'boundary':'','label':'A'},{'boundary':'','label':'B'}] -> _breakpoints_to_rules yields the tail rule {'op1':'>','val1':10.0,'assignment':'B'}; label 'A' is silently lost.
numerical.recommended_fix: Reject more than one open-ended breakpoint with a ValueError ('a breakpoints factor may have at most one open-ended boundary'), consistent with the existing duplicate-bounded-boundary rejection. Add a regression test feeding two blank-boundary rows and asserting the error.

numerical.location: src/haute/_rating.py:346-370 (_rating_key_expr, plain cast(Utf8) branch for non-Float dtypes)
numerical.title: Decimal factor columns canonicalise with their declared scale, so a money/Decimal factor only matches string entries written to that exact scale (e.g. '25.50', not '25.5' or '25')
numerical.description: Decimal is neither Float32 nor Float64, so _rating_key_expr falls to the plain `cast(Utf8)`, which renders a Decimal preserving its scale (e.g. Decimal(scale=2) 25.50 -> '25.50'). A table authored with the human label '25.5' or '25' will not match, and the failure mode is again a miss (loud error or neutral-fill wrong premium). Lower severity than the Float32 case because Decimal factor columns are uncommon and the rendering is at least deterministic, but it is the same class of dtype-dependent key formatting.
numerical.evidence: Decimal(scale=2) column value 25.50 -> engine key '25.50'; matches entry '25.50' (f=[2.0]) but misses '25.5' and '25' (both -> [null]).
numerical.recommended_fix: Document that Decimal factor levels must be authored at the column's scale, or normalise Decimal keys to a scale-independent canonical form (e.g. cast to Float64 then through the same float key path, or strip trailing zeros) so '25.5'/'25.50' converge. Add a Decimal-column case to the engine key tests.

numerical.location: src/haute/routes/_optimiser_service.py:1585-1652 (_estimate_scenario_frontier_ranges) + 4537-4605 (_validate_and_project_auto_range) feeding 1366-1406 (_auto_frontier_ranges_from_config) and consumed by solver.frontier threshold_ranges
numerical.title: Frontier auto-range emits ABSOLUTE constraint-sum ranges for min_pct/max_pct constraints, which the solver then interprets as fraction-of-baseline thresholds (6+ orders-of-magnitude wrong swept range)
numerical.description: price_contour constraint specs support four threshold keys: `min`/`max` (ABSOLUTE thresholds on the constraint column SUM) and `min_pct`/`max_pct` (FRACTION of baseline). solver.frontier()'s `threshold_ranges` are documented as user-units: absolute for min/max, FRACTIONAL for min_pct/max_pct (price_contour/solver.py:223-226, frontier.py compose_row writes threshold_{name} in user units). The haute auto-range estimator is unit-blind: `_estimate_scenario_frontier_ranges` sums each quote's achievable per-quote min/max of the raw constraint COLUMN (Float32) across the portfolio, producing an ABSOLUTE envelope (e.g. loss_ratio total in [4.2e6, 5.1e6]). `_validate_and_project_auto_range` / `_auto_range_input_required_columns` treat every constraint key uniformly as a summable column name and never inspect whether the spec is `_pct`. The resulting absolute range is returned as OptimiserFrontierRange and (a) written verbatim into `frontier_ranges` (frontend OptimiserConfig handleAutoRange) and (b) passed straight to `solver.frontier(threshold_ranges=...)` by `_finalize_solve_result`/run_frontier. For a `min_pct`/`max_pct` constraint the solver then sweeps thresholds of ~4e6 as a FRACTION of baseline — a meaningless grid ~6 orders of magnitude off the intended ~[0.9,1.1]. The whole frontier for that constraint is numerically garbage with no error. NOTE: the canvas UI only exposes min/max (CONSTRAINT_TYPES at OptimiserConfig.tsx:74-77), so this requires a hand-authored config dict (config is free-form dict[str,Any] and _validate_config does not restrict spec keys); price_contour and `_frontier_point_constraints_override` (_CONSTRAINT_THRESHOLD_KEYS includes min_pct/max_pct) both fully support _pct, so the path is live. Distinct from catalog #44 (legacy frontier_min/max broadcast).
numerical.evidence: Config constraints={'loss_ratio': {'max_pct': 1.1}} with per-quote loss_ratio scenario values summing to a baseline-total ~4.5e6. Auto-range returns ranges['loss_ratio']=(min~4.2e6, max~5.1e6) (absolute sum envelope). run_frontier/_finalize_solve_result calls solver.frontier(threshold_ranges={'loss_ratio': (4.2e6, 5.1e6)}). Inside price_contour the max_pct axis is swept at L = threshold*baseline_LR, i.e. thresholds of 4.2e6..5.1e6 are multiplied by baseline loss-ratio (~0.7) -> the constraint is effectively never binding / absurd. Expected swept fractional range for max_pct is ~[0.9,1.1]. The reported total_loss_ratio and lambda_loss_ratio on every frontier point are therefore wrong, silently.
numerical.recommended_fix: Make the auto-range estimator and `_auto_frontier_ranges_from_config` constraint-spec aware. Detect each constraint's direction key: for `min_pct`/`max_pct`, the achievable range must be expressed as a FRACTION of the baseline constraint total (i.e. divide the absolute per-quote envelope by the baseline total, mirroring price_contour's L = pct*baseline_LR), or refuse auto-range for `_pct`/ratio constraints with a loud 400 naming the constraint and instructing the user to supply explicit fractional `frontier_ranges`. Ratio constraints (numerator/denominator, no column of their own) already fail loud via _missing_columns_detail; _pct sum constraints are the silent gap. Add a regression test: a max_pct constraint through auto-range -> assert the returned range is fractional (close to baseline ratio), not the absolute column-sum envelope.

numerical.title: scenario_value_stats std (and median/percentiles) differ for the SAME optimum depending on whether they come from the initial solve summary (Polars sample-std, nearest-interp) or a frontier-point selection (library population-std, linear-interp)
numerical.description: Two independent code paths compute `scenario_value_stats` for the identical `optimal_scenario_value` distribution and feed the SAME response schema field (OptimiserScenarioValueStats). (1) The solve summary path `_compute_scenario_value_stats` uses Polars: `std = col.std()` which defaults to ddof=1 (SAMPLE std), and percentiles via `col.quantile(p)` which default to interpolation='nearest'. (2) The frontier-point path `_scenario_stats_from_frontier_point` surfaces the library-emitted `sv_*` values, where price_contour `_compute_sv_stats_from_dataframe` computes `std = sqrt(sum((v-mean)^2)/n)` (ddof=0, POPULATION std) and percentiles via linear interpolation (`_percentile`). So for the same job, OptimiserStatusResponse.result.scenario_value_stats.std (initial solve, online mode with frontier_enabled) and OptimiserFrontierSelectResponse.scenario_value_stats.std (selecting that same optimum) report different numbers, and likewise p5/p25/p50/p75/p95 diverge under nearest-vs-linear interpolation. This is a silent inconsistency in a user-facing distribution panel; no crash.
numerical.evidence: For optimal_scenario_value = [0.8, 1.0, 1.2, 1.5] (n=4): population std (library sv_std) = sqrt(((0.8-1.125)^2+(1.0-1.125)^2+(1.2-1.125)^2+(1.5-1.125)^2)/4) ≈ 0.2550; Polars col.std() (sample, ddof=1) ≈ 0.2944 — a ~15% difference reported as 'std' for the same data. p50: Polars nearest gives 1.0 or 1.2 (a member); library linear gives 1.1. The initial-solve panel and the frontier-select panel for the identical selected point therefore display different spread/percentiles.
numerical.recommended_fix: Pick one convention as the single source of truth. Preferred: make `_compute_scenario_value_stats` match the library emitter (population std via ddof=0 and linear-interpolation percentiles, e.g. col.std(ddof=0) and col.quantile(p, interpolation='linear')) so the solve-summary stats agree bit-for-bit with the frontier-point sv_* stats the library produces. Add a test asserting `_compute_scenario_value_stats(df)` equals price_contour `_compute_sv_stats_from_dataframe(df)` for the shared keys on a small fixture.

numerical.location: src/haute/routes/optimiser.py:468-477 (_frontier_point_constraint_value) + 380-392 (_as_finite_float); produced NaN at price_contour/solver.py:434 (compose_row total_{name}=float(totals.get(name, nan)))
numerical.title: A frontier point whose total_{constraint} is NaN (library convention for a missing/degenerate constraint total) turns frontier select/apply/save into a hard 500 instead of a usable point
numerical.description: The Python-orchestrated frontier sweep emits `total_{name} = float(totals.get(name, float('nan')))` (price_contour/solver.py:434) and `lambda_{name} = float(lambdas.get(name, 0.0))`. So a frontier point can legitimately carry a NaN constraint total (e.g. a ratio constraint whose denominator sum is zero on the optimum, or a constraint absent from `total_constraints` for that point). `_frontier_point_constraint_value` reads `total_{name}` through `_as_finite_float`, which raises HTTPException(500, 'field not finite') for NaN/inf. This path is hit by `_frontier_point_result_dict` -> select_frontier_point, apply_lambdas (frontier branch), save_result and mlflow_log. The consequence is that selecting/saving an otherwise-valid frontier point whose constraint total is NaN fails with an opaque 500 ('Frontier point data is malformed') rather than surfacing the point with a NaN/None constraint or a targeted explanation. It is fail-loud (not a wrong number) but conflates an expected library output with internal corruption.
numerical.evidence: Frontier point dict = {'total_objective': 1.0e6, 'total_loss_ratio': nan, 'lambda_loss_ratio': 0.0, 'converged': True, ...}. _frontier_point_constraint_value(point, 'loss_ratio') -> _as_finite_float(nan, field='total_loss_ratio') -> raises 500 'Frontier point data is malformed: field total_loss_ratio is not finite'. The point is real (the sweep produced it); only the constraint total is undefined.
numerical.recommended_fix: Distinguish 'undefined-by-design' from 'corrupt'. For constraint totals (and sv_* stats), allow NaN to pass through as a null/None in the response (the schema field is float; consider Optional, or emit a documented sentinel) instead of a 500, OR raise a 422 with a message that names the constraint and explains the degenerate (e.g. zero-denominator ratio) cause. Keep the strict 500 only for genuinely missing/typed-wrong fields. Add a test feeding a NaN total_{name} frontier point and asserting a graceful response rather than a 500.

numerical.category: domain-correctness (saved artifact omits selected frontier-point constraint thresholds)
numerical.title: Saving/MLflow-logging a SELECTED online frontier point persists the point's lambdas and totals but NOT the swept threshold values, so the saved artifact's `constraints` block still shows the original (pre-sweep) thresholds
numerical.description: When a user selects an online frontier point and saves it, `_solve_result_for_selected_frontier_point` returns a `_summary_solve_result` SimpleNamespace built from the point dict (lambdas, total_objective, total_constraints, converged) — that part is correct. But `_build_artifact_payload` writes `payload['constraints'] = job_config.get('constraints')`, i.e. the ORIGINAL constraint spec from the optimiser node config, which for a swept constraint contains the pre-frontier threshold (or a None frontier-marker). The selected point's actual swept threshold_{name} values (which the online frontier varied and which `_frontier_point_constraints_override` reconstructs for the ratebook re-solve) are NOT written into the online saved artifact. The artifact's `lambdas` are point-specific and correct, so apply via OPTIMISER_APPLY (which uses lambdas) is fine; but the persisted `constraints` thresholds misrepresent what the saved point actually enforces, and any downstream re-solve from the artifact's constraints would target the wrong thresholds. For ratebook the materialised result re-solves with the override so its factor tables reflect the point; the online artifact has no equivalent threshold capture.
numerical.evidence: Config constraint {'premium_total': {'max': None}} (frontier-marker) swept over [4e6,5e6]; user selects point with threshold_premium_total=4.5e6, lambda_premium_total=0.3. Saved payload: lambdas={'premium_total':0.3} (correct), but constraints={'premium_total':{'max':None}} — the 4.5e6 threshold the point represents is absent. A reader of the artifact (or a re-solve from it) sees a None/original threshold, not 4.5e6.
numerical.recommended_fix: In `_build_artifact_payload`, when `selected_frontier_point is not None`, overlay the selected point's threshold_{name} values onto the persisted `constraints` block (reusing `_frontier_point_constraints_override(job, point_index)` which already maps threshold_{name} onto the correct min/max/min_pct/max_pct key), so the saved constraints reflect the swept point. Add a regression test asserting a saved online frontier-point artifact's constraints carry the point's swept thresholds, not the node config's originals.

numerical.title: Empty-input batch scoring hardcodes prediction column to Float64, diverging from the Int64 dtype the same model emits on non-empty input (classification hard labels / integer-valued regression)
numerical.description: In the zero-row branch of _batch_score_to_parquet, the output prediction column is created as pl.Series(output_col, [], dtype=pl.Float64) unconditionally (line 1401), and the proba column likewise as Float64 (line 1403). But on the NON-empty path the prediction column dtype is whatever the model returns: a CatBoost classifier raw .predict() returns integer hard labels (Polars infers Int64), and an integer-valued regressor (e.g. a count model) likewise yields Int64. So the SAME ScoringModel produces output_col=Int64 for a non-empty shard but output_col=Float64 for an empty shard. The empty path also cannot know the true dtype because no predict() ran. This is a schema-instability defect: two scoring calls of the same model (one on a fully-filtered/empty frame, one on a non-empty frame) yield parquet files with different prediction-column dtypes. A strict vertical pl.concat, a typed sink append, or any cached/declared output-schema contract that happens to be seeded from an empty scoring sample will silently up/down-cast or break. The eager path does not have this divergence (it preserves the model's dtype because it always materialises a real predict()).
numerical.evidence: Verified with executed repro against the real _batch_score_to_parquet. Stub raw classifier returning np.ones(n, dtype=int64) hard labels + (n,2) proba. NON-EMPTY classification: pred dtype = Int64, pred_proba = Float64, pred values [1,1,1]. EMPTY classification (zero-row input parquet): pred dtype = Float64, pred_proba = Float64. Result: '>>> DTYPE DIVERGENCE pred (non-empty vs empty): Int64 vs Float64 MISMATCH'. Int-valued regressor repro: shard0 (2 rows) pred=Int64, shard1 (empty) pred=Float64. Eager classification pred=Int64 (matches non-empty batch). So the divergence is isolated to the empty-input branch's hardcoded Float64.
numerical.recommended_fix: Do not assume Float64 for the prediction column on the empty path. Derive the correct output dtype the same way the non-empty path does: either (a) run the model's predict on a synthetic 1-row frame built from the input schema and take prediction.dtype (then write a 0-row column of that dtype), or (b) carry the realised dtype from the first non-empty batch and, for the truly-zero-row case, infer the prediction dtype from task+flavor (classification CatBoost -> Int64 hard label; otherwise Float64) so the empty parquet matches the non-empty one. The proba column dtype (Float64) is already correct. Add a regression test asserting read_parquet(empty_out).schema[output_col] == read_parquet(nonempty_out).schema[output_col] for both classification and an integer-returning regressor.

numerical.title: CatBoost classification SHAP explanation reports headline prediction_value as the scored HARD LABEL (0/1) while contributions/base reconstruct the LOG-ODDS, producing a meaningless output_difference and a waterfall that cannot reconcile to the displayed prediction
numerical.description: For task='classification', explain_catboost_prediction computes contributions and base_value in raw-formula (log-odds) space (ShapValues are always raw-formula), with prediction_space='raw_formula_val'. The caller explain_model_score_from_config passes prediction_value = the scored 'prediction' column value, which for a CatBoost classifier is the HARD LABEL (0 or 1) per the known scored-output semantics. Because output_value=_as_float(prediction_value, strict=False) is non-None (=1.0), the function sets effective_prediction=1.0 and output_difference=output_value-response_prediction = 1.0 - logodds. The traced-output additivity check is REGRESSION-ONLY (line 223 'if task == "regression"'), so no error is raised. The returned dict therefore reports prediction_value=1.0 (hard label) alongside model_output_value=prediction_from_shap=log-odds and an output_difference that is (hard_label - log_odds) — a number with no meaning, surfaced to the trace UI. A user inspecting the SHAP waterfall sees per-feature contributions that sum (with base) to the log-odds, but a headline 'prediction' of 1.0 that they cannot reconcile. This is distinct from catalog #24 (which is about training metrics vs scored prediction); this is the explanation dict itself emitting an internally-inconsistent (prediction_value, output_difference) pair for classification.
numerical.evidence: Executed repro on a real CatBoostClassifier (iterations=30). scored prediction column (hard label)=1; scored proba=0.9625. explain_catboost_prediction(..., task='classification', prediction_value=1.0) returned: prediction_value(headline)=1.0; model_output_value(logodds)=3.2455; prediction_from_shap=3.2455; output_difference=-2.2455; base+sum_contributions=3.2455. So contributions reconstruct 3.2455 (log-odds) but the headline prediction_value is the hard label 1.0 and output_difference=-2.2455 is meaningless. By contrast the GLM path and Poisson-regression CatBoost path are internally consistent (output_difference=0.0, headline in response space). No exception is raised because the response/traced check is gated on task=='regression'.
numerical.recommended_fix: Make the classification explanation space-consistent. Options: (1) For classification, do NOT treat the scored hard label as a value comparable to log-odds: either set prediction_value to the positive-class probability (sigmoid of the raw-formula sum, matching what the *_proba column carries) and report prediction_space='probability', OR keep raw-formula and set prediction_value=model_output_value (log-odds) with output_difference computed against a log-odds-space traced value; (2) at minimum, when task='classification', set output_difference=None (do not subtract a hard label from log-odds) and document that prediction_value for classification is a class label not comparable to the raw-formula contributions. Add a test asserting the classification explanation never reports an output_difference equal to (hard_label - logodds).

numerical.title: Training-diagnostics CatBoost predict re-derives the categorical set from the diagnostic frame's DTYPE rather than the declared cat_features, so an integer-coded categorical that trained fine crashes the diagnostics predict (loud, but train/predict disagree)
numerical.description: CatBoostAlgorithm.predict builds cat_cols = {c for c in features if selected[c].dtype in (Utf8, Categorical, String)} (lines 598-599) and passes only those to _prepare_predict_frame. The call site _training_job.py:1136 invokes algo.predict(model, diag_df, features) WITHOUT cat_features. Training, however, declares categoricals positionally via _build_pool's cat_indices derived from the explicit cat_features list. When a feature is declared categorical (cat_features) but stored as an integer code (a common encoding for region/postcode-district), training succeeds (the Pool marks the index categorical), but the diagnostics predict treats it as numeric (Int dtype is not in the {Utf8,Categorical,String} set), casts it to Float32, and feeds CatBoost a fully-numeric array while the model expects a categorical at that index. CatBoost then raises. This is a train-vs-diagnostic-predict inconsistency: the model trains but its own residuals/AvE diagnostics crash. It does NOT silently mis-predict (CatBoost raises), so it is fail-loud, but the categorical contract should be sourced from cat_features, not re-inferred from dtype, to keep the two paths in agreement.
numerical.evidence: Executed repro: trained a CatBoostRegressor via the project's _build_pool with features=['x','region'], cat_features=['region'] where region is int-coded (rng.integers(0,4)). Training succeeded. algo.predict(model, df, ['x','region']) RAISED CatBoostError: "'data' is numpy array of floating point numerical type, it means no categorical features, but 'cat_features' parameter specifies nonzero number of categorical features". The same predict on df with region cast to Utf8 succeeded (preds [-0.229, -0.0796, -0.229]). So the dtype-based inference, not the declared contract, governs the diagnostics predict and disagrees with training for int-coded categoricals.
numerical.recommended_fix: Thread the declared cat_features through to CatBoostAlgorithm.predict (the call site _training_job.py:1136 already holds cat_features) and pass them as cat_feature_names to _prepare_predict_frame, instead of re-deriving from selected[c].dtype. This mirrors _build_pool and _score_eager_unified (which both use the declared categorical set) and guarantees the diagnostics predict uses the exact categorical contract the model was trained with. Add a regression test training an int-coded categorical and asserting algo.predict succeeds and matches the string-coded predict.

numerical.location: src/haute/_expression_parser.py:1616-1635 (_ExprEvaluator._binop op_map: Add/Sub/Mult/Pow/Mod/FloorDiv via Python operator)
numerical.title: Integer arithmetic computed in unbounded Python int, not Int64 — evaluator shows a wildly different number than Polars on overflow/wraparound
numerical.description: _binop dispatches integer +, -, *, ** through Python's operator module, which uses arbitrary-precision ints. Polars stores integer columns as Int64 (or narrower) and WRAPS on overflow (two's-complement). For any expression whose intermediate or final integer result exceeds 2**63-1 (or underflows), the trace evaluator prints the mathematically-exact bignum while the real pipeline produced a wrapped Int64. In a pricing context this is the textbook 'wrong number that does not crash': the explainability panel asserts the node computed e.g. 10**20 when the executor actually produced a negative wrapped value, so the waterfall the actuary inspects contradicts the real output. Affects +, *, ** and any composite integer expression; narrower integer dtypes (Int32/UInt) wrap even sooner but the evaluator is dtype-blind so it cannot replicate any of them.
numerical.evidence: Through the real entry point evaluate_expression: i64max + 1 -> evaluator result_value=9223372036854775808; Polars (pl.col('a')+1 on Int64 i64max) wraps to -9223372036854775808. 10 ** 20 -> evaluator=100000000000000000000; Polars=7766279631452241920. i64max * 2 -> Polars=-2; evaluator=18446744073709551614. Verified on Polars 1.39.2.
numerical.recommended_fix: The evaluator is fundamentally dtype-unaware, so faithful Int64 wraparound cannot be reproduced from row values alone. Two defensible options: (a) when an integer arithmetic result falls outside the signed-64-bit range, do NOT display the bignum — return an explicit 'uncomputable / overflow' sentinel (None plus an error marker on the calculation) so the trace shows it could not be reproduced rather than a number Polars never produced; or (b) wrap integer results into int64 via ((r + 2**63) % 2**64) - 2**63 to mirror the default Int64 wrap (still wrong for narrower dtypes, but matches the common case). Per CLAUDE.md fail-loud guidance, (a) is preferred. Add a regression test asserting i64max+1 is not displayed as 9223372036854775808.

numerical.location: src/haute/_expression_parser.py:1616-1635 (_binop None-guard at 1619-1620) handling ast.BitAnd/ast.BitOr for boolean expressions
numerical.title: Boolean & / | do not implement Kleene three-valued logic: `False & null` and `True | null` return None instead of False/True, mis-selecting when/then branches
numerical.description: Polars uses Kleene (SQL three-valued) logic for boolean & and |: `False & null == False` and `True | null == True` (the determined operand dominates a null). The evaluator routes & and | through _binop, whose first action is the blanket null guard `if left is None or right is None: return None`. So any boolean combinator with one null operand collapses to None regardless of the other operand's truth value. This is directly load-bearing for pricing: the dominant conditional pattern is `pl.when(cond_a & cond_b).then(...)`. When one sub-condition is null (e.g. a missing factor), Polars may still decisively take/skip the branch (False & null -> False -> branch NOT taken), but the evaluator returns None -> the _BranchTrackingEvaluator treats it as falsy and can mis-report taken_branch / dimmed_branches, and _ExprEvaluator can return the wrong then/otherwise value. The result is a wrong displayed branch and wrong displayed factor.
numerical.evidence: Polars 1.39.2: pl.col('a') & pl.col('b') with a=False,b=null -> False; a=True,b=null with | -> True. Evaluator _binop: left=False/True, right=None -> hits None guard at line 1619-1620 -> returns None for both. DIVERGE=True for both. (Integer bitand 6 & 3 -> 2 matches; arithmetic null*0 -> None matches Polars, so the bug is specific to boolean Kleene cases, not all null handling.)
numerical.recommended_fix: Before the generic None guard in _binop (or in a dedicated boolean path), special-case BitAnd/BitOr on boolean operands with Kleene semantics: for And, if either operand is False return False (even if the other is None); else if either is None return None; else left and right. For Or, if either operand is True return True; else if either is None return None; else left or right. Only fall through to the numeric None-propagation guard for genuinely numeric BitAnd/BitOr. Add tests for False&null, True|null, null&null, True&null, False|null.

numerical.title: Negative base raised to a fractional power yields a Python complex number where Polars yields NaN
numerical.description: _binop evaluates ** via operator.pow. For a negative base with a non-integer exponent (e.g. (-8.0) ** 0.5) Python returns a complex number, whereas Polars (float pow) returns NaN. The evaluator therefore stores a complex value as result_value and propagates it into substituted_text / the user-facing calculation. Besides being a value Polars never produces, a complex result can break downstream numeric formatting/serialisation of the trace payload (JSON does not encode complex), or display nonsense like '(1.7e-16+2.83j)' as a premium contribution. Negative bases with fractional exponents arise from power-law rating curves applied to signed factors.
numerical.evidence: evaluate_expression('... (pl.col(a)**pl.col(b)) ...', {a:-8.0, b:0.5}).result_value = (1.7319121124709868e-16+2.8284271247461903j), type=complex. Polars 1.39.2 (-8.0)**0.5 = nan. CONFIRMED via real entry point.
numerical.recommended_fix: In _binop's Pow branch, mirror Polars float semantics: if the result is complex (isinstance(result, complex)) or the base is negative with a non-integral exponent, return float('nan') instead of the complex value. Equivalently compute via math.pow and convert its ValueError (negative base, fractional exp) into nan. Add a test for (-8.0)**0.5 == nan and (-8.0)**2 == 64.0 (integer exponent still exact).

numerical.title: clip() applies lower-then-upper (min(max(val,lower),upper)); diverges from Polars whenever lower_bound > upper_bound
numerical.description: The evaluator implements clip as: if lower is not None: val = max(val, lower); if upper is not None: val = min(val, upper) — i.e. min(max(val,lower),upper), so the UPPER bound always wins on a contradictory pair. Polars' clip applies the bounds in the opposite effective order (the lower bound dominates for the lower>upper case), so for lower_bound=10, upper_bound=0 the evaluator and Polars disagree. While lower>upper is itself a misconfiguration, clip bounds in rating are frequently column-derived (per-row min/max relativity caps), so a row where the computed lower exceeds the computed upper is reachable, and the trace would show the clamped-to-upper value while the executor clamped differently.
numerical.evidence: Polars 1.39.2: pl.col('a').clip(10.0, 0.0) at val=5 -> 10.0, at val=50 -> 0.0. Evaluator clip(5,10,0): max(5,10)=10 then min(10,0)=0 -> 0.0 (DIVERGE: Polars 10.0). Confirmed through evaluate_expression: clip(5,10,0) result_value=0.0 vs Polars 10.0. (For the well-ordered case lower<=upper, and for single-sided clip(upper_bound=10) at 15 -> 10.0, evaluator and Polars agree.)
numerical.recommended_fix: Match Polars' bound-precedence for the contradictory case. Simplest robust form consistent with Polars observed behaviour: apply upper first then lower — val = min(val, upper) if upper is not None else val; val = max(val, lower) if lower is not None else val. Add a regression test with lower=10, upper=0 across val in {-3,5,50} asserting equality with a live Polars clip.

numerical.location: src/haute/_expression_parser.py:1887-1899 (_call .log returns None for val<=0; .sqrt returns None for val<0)
numerical.title: log()/sqrt() (and domain-guarded ops) return None where Polars returns NaN or -inf
numerical.description: For out-of-domain inputs the evaluator returns None: .log() guards `if val>0` (else None), .sqrt() guards `if val>=0` (else None). Polars instead returns float NaN for sqrt(negative) and log(negative), and -inf for log(0). None and NaN/-inf are different values with different downstream meaning (null vs not-a-number vs negative infinity); a trace that shows None for sqrt(-4) misrepresents the real pipeline value (NaN), which in turn flows into is_nan()/fill_nan() logic differently than null flows into is_null()/fill_null(). For a pricing engine this conflation of null and NaN is exactly the silent-wrongness class to avoid.
numerical.evidence: Polars 1.39.2: sqrt(-4)=nan, log(-1)=nan, log(0)=-inf. Evaluator via evaluate_expression: sqrt(-4) result_value=None; log(0) result_value=None. CONFIRMED.
numerical.recommended_fix: Return math.nan for log(val<0)/sqrt(val<0) and -math.inf for log(0.0) instead of None, matching Polars float semantics; keep None only when the input itself is null. (Note this distinct from log(0)->-inf which must not be None either.) Add tests for sqrt(-4)==nan, log(0)==-inf, log(-1)==nan, and that a true null input still yields None.

numerical.title: max_horizontal/min_horizontal use Python max()/min(), whose NaN handling is argument-order-dependent and diverges from Polars
numerical.description: _eval_horizontal computes max_horizontal/min_horizontal as Python builtin max(non_none)/min(non_none). Python's max/min with a NaN element are order-dependent and return whichever way the comparison short-circuits: max([nan,5])=nan but max([5,nan])=5; min([nan,5])=nan but min([5,nan])=5. So the evaluator's horizontal max/min result depends on the textual order of the arguments and is non-deterministic relative to Polars. Polars has a fixed rule (max_horizontal(nan,5)=nan, min_horizontal(nan,5)=5.0 — it treats NaN as larger for max but ignores it for min in this case). The displayed horizontal aggregate can therefore be wrong (e.g. evaluator shows 5 for a max that Polars makes NaN, or vice-versa) purely based on column ordering. This is a distinct issue from the known concat_str / all-null findings (#47), which concern null, not NaN.
numerical.evidence: Polars 1.39.2: max_horizontal(nan,5)=nan, min_horizontal(nan,5)=5.0. Python: max([nan,5.0])=nan, max([5.0,nan])=5.0; min([nan,5.0])=nan, min([5.0,nan])=5.0. The evaluator builds the list in arg order then calls max/min, so for arguments listed as (b=5, a=nan) it returns 5 for max (DIVERGE from Polars nan), and the opposite ordering returns nan.
numerical.recommended_fix: Stop using bare Python max/min for float horizontal reductions. Reproduce Polars NaN semantics explicitly: if any non-null value is NaN, return NaN for max_horizontal (Polars treats NaN as the max) and ignore NaN for min_horizontal (or whatever the audited Polars rule is per dtype), making the result independent of argument order. At minimum, detect NaN among the operands and short-circuit to a fixed value rather than relying on comparison order. Add order-swapped tests: max_horizontal(nan,5) and max_horizontal(5,nan) must return the same value, equal to Polars.

numerical.title: round() uses Python round which can differ from Polars at binary-non-representable midpoints (e.g. round(2.675, 2) -> 2.67 vs Polars 2.68)
numerical.description: The evaluator implements .round(n) as Python's builtin round(val, n). For values that are exactly representable in binary both agree (Polars round is half-to-even like Python: 0.125->0.12, 0.625->0.62, 2.5->2.0, 3.5->4.0 all match). But for decimals that are NOT exactly representable, Polars' scaling algorithm and Python's round disagree at the rounding boundary: round(2.675,2) gives Polars 2.68 but Python 2.67 (because 2.675 stores as 2.67499999...). Monetary rounding at output is precisely where a 1-cent display discrepancy is noticeable, though this is display-only and confined to narrow midpoint inputs, hence low.
numerical.evidence: Polars 1.39.2: round(2.675,2)=2.68. evaluate_expression round(2.675,2) result_value=2.67. (Clean-binary halves match: round(0.125,2): both 0.12; round(0.625,2): both 0.62.) CONFIRMED divergence at 2.675 only.
numerical.recommended_fix: Reproduce Polars' rounding by scaling the way Polars does (round(val * 10**n) / 10**n with the same half-to-even tie-break Polars uses) rather than delegating to Python round, or document that single-row round display may differ by one ULP-scaled unit from the executor. Because this is display-only and rare, prefer a regression test pinning the known-divergent inputs and a comment over a fragile reimplementation; if reimplemented, test a battery of non-representable decimals against live Polars.

numerical.title: Division/floor-div/mod by zero raises in Python and is masked to the observed value, but the correct Polars value is +inf (float div) or null (int floordiv) — concrete new instance of the catch-all mask
numerical.description: Polars float division by zero yields +inf/-inf (1.0/0.0 -> inf, including for integer columns since / promotes to Float64), and integer floor-division/modulo by zero yields null. The evaluator computes these via operator.truediv/floordiv/mod, which raise ZeroDivisionError; the exception is swallowed by _compute_result's `except Exception: return row_values.get(target_column)` (line 1538-1539), so the trace displays the ALREADY-OBSERVED row value as if computed. The catch-all masking is catalogued (#23), but the specific divergence values are documented here for the fix: the evaluator should reproduce Polars' inf/null, not silently echo the observed value. Division by a zero rate/exposure is a realistic pricing edge.
numerical.evidence: Polars 1.39.2: 1.0/0.0 -> inf; 1/0 with Int64 columns -> inf (Float64); 1//0 Int64 -> null. evaluate_expression('(a/b)', {a:1.0,b:0.0,out:-999.0}).result_value = -999.0 (the observed value), not inf. CONFIRMED.
numerical.recommended_fix: Handle zero divisors explicitly in _binop to mirror Polars: truediv by 0.0 -> math.copysign(inf, numerator) (and nan for 0/0); floordiv/mod by integer 0 -> None (Polars null). This also removes one reliance on the value-laundering catch-all. Add tests: 1.0/0.0==inf, -1.0/0.0==-inf, 0.0/0.0 is nan, 1//0 is None.

numerical.title: canonical_json digest is NOT order-independent for sets containing ==-equal members of distinct types/signs (bool vs int vs float, -0.0 vs 0.0) — distinct from the NaN case V034
numerical.description: The module docstring (lines 81-99) and _canonicalise docstring (lines 119-123) promise sets/frozensets 'whose elements are the same regardless of the order they were inserted' encode identically. This is violated for any set whose literal contains two objects that are == and hash-equal but textually distinct, because a Python set deduplicates by ==/hash and keeps whichever object was inserted FIRST; _canonicalise then faithfully encodes the surviving representative. This collapse happens BEFORE _sort_key runs, so it is a different defect from V034 (which is the NaN no-total-order problem inside sorted()). I reproduced three concrete divergences (executed via the repo's .venv against haute._cache.canonical_json): (a) {1, True} -> '[1]' but {True, 1} -> '[true]'; (b) {0.0, -0.0} -> '[0.0]' but {-0.0, 0.0} -> '[-0.0]'; (c) {2, 2.0} -> '[2]' but {2.0, 2} -> '[2.0]'. In every case the two sets are == to each other (Python: {1,True}=={True,1} is True) yet canonical_json returns different bytes, so two callers that build the same logical set in different insertion orders would get different digests (phantom invalidation) or, conversely, the SAME representative could mask a genuine difference. Scope check: this is currently LATENT — the only live callers of canonical_json are _graph_base_fingerprint (node.data.config, which is JSON-parsed and therefore contains no Python sets), dataframe_execution_policy_fingerprint (the policy built by execution.py:dataframe_lazy_execution_policy, which defensively converts every set to sorted(...) lists of strings before returning), and execution.py runtime_files (dicts of str/int). So no production path passes a set with colliding members today. But canonical_json is explicitly documented as THE single general-purpose canonical encoder and _dataframe_execution_cache.py:273-275 comments that it 'canonicalises the embedded policy (set ordering, mapping-key sorting)' — i.e. downstream code already relies on set-order-independence as a property. A future policy/config that places a raw set of numeric/bool factor codes into digest material would silently get an order-dependent key.
numerical.evidence: Executed with PYTHONPATH=src .venv python: canonical_json({1, True})=='[1]'; canonical_json({True, 1})=='[true]'; the two argument sets satisfy {1,True}=={True,1}. Likewise canonical_json({0.0,-0.0})=='[0.0]' vs canonical_json({-0.0,0.0})=='[-0.0]', and canonical_json({2,2.0})=='[2]' vs canonical_json({2.0,2})=='[2.0]'. Each pair: set-equality True, digest-equality False.
numerical.recommended_fix: In _canonicalise's set/frozenset branch, normalise each member to a canonical numeric form BEFORE the dedup is observable, OR reject ambiguous mixed sets loudly. Concretely: after canonicalising members, detect when two members would collapse under ==/hash but differ in encoded text (e.g. a bool and an int, or an int and a float, or +0.0 and -0.0) and either (a) raise TypeError('Cannot fingerprint set with members that compare equal but encode differently: ...') consistent with the fail-loud policy, or (b) define a single canonical representative per equivalence class (e.g. coerce bool->int, and collapse -0.0 to 0.0 ONLY inside sets) so the surviving member is deterministic irrespective of insertion order. Option (a) is safer for a pricing engine. Whatever is chosen, fix the property test (see separate finding) so it can actually exercise distinct-but-equal members.

numerical.title: The property test meant to prove set-order independence is structurally incapable of catching the ==-collapse divergence
numerical.description: test_set_insertion_order_is_irrelevant receives an already-realised set 'members' from Hypothesis (st.sets(_canonical_scalars)). By the time the test sees it, any pair of ==-equal-but-distinct objects (1 and True, 0.0 and -0.0, 2 and 2.0) has ALREADY been deduplicated to a single representative object inside that set. The test then builds 'forward' and 'backward' by .add()-ing the SAME ordered list of those survivors in two directions — but since the survivors are identical objects, forward and backward end up with the same members and the same canonical_json. The test therefore can never reproduce the {1,True} vs {True,1} class of divergence, which requires two DISTINCT objects inserted into the ORIGINAL set in different orders. This is why the order-dependence defect above is not caught despite an otherwise thorough property suite. The unit pins nearby (e.g. line 420 {None, False, True, 5, 'a'}, line 590 {'b','a'}) also deliberately avoid colliding members, so the gap is total. Note: _canonical_scalars explicitly excludes NaN (line 504-505 comment), confirming V034 is a known, separately-tracked hole.
numerical.evidence: Lines 549-556: ordered = list(members); forward built by adding ordered; backward by adding reversed(ordered). Because 'members' is already a deduped set, ordered contains one representative per equivalence class, so forward==backward as sets and the assertion is trivially satisfied. No Hypothesis example can contain both 1 and True (a set literal collapses them), so the colliding-representative path is unreachable from this test.
numerical.recommended_fix: Add a dedicated parametrised test that builds the ORIGINAL set in both orders from distinct objects and asserts canonical_json equality (currently failing): assert canonical_json({1, True}) == canonical_json({True, 1}); assert canonical_json({0.0, -0.0}) == canonical_json({-0.0, 0.0}); assert canonical_json({2, 2.0}) == canonical_json({2.0, 2}). Pair it with the _canonicalise fix above so these pass (or, if the chosen fix is fail-loud, assert pytest.raises(TypeError)).

numerical.title: _sort_key orders bool members before numerically-smaller numbers and segregates bool from int/float, producing a counter-intuitive (though deterministic) set order
numerical.description: _sort_key assigns bool the tag '1_bool' and all int/float the tag '2_num'. Because tuples compare lexicographically by the tag first, a True (numerically 1) sorts BEFORE 0 in a mixed set: canonical_json({True, 0}) == '[true,0]', even though 1 > 0. canonical_json({False, 5}) == '[false,5]'. This is internally consistent and deterministic (so not a stability bug), and it matches the pinned unit test at tests/test_caching_correctness.py:420 which expects null<bool<number<string. But it means the set ordering does not reflect numeric order when bools and numbers are mixed, and it compounds the collapse issue above (bool being a separate bucket is why {1,True} can keep either representative AND why the two would sort into different positions if both somehow appeared). For a pricing digest this is acceptable as long as it is intentional; flagging because the docstring (line 91-92) describes the order as 'numbers (numeric order)' which is only true WITHIN the number bucket, not across the bool boundary.
numerical.evidence: Executed: _sort_key(True)==('1_bool', True); _sort_key(1)==('2_num', 1); canonical_json({True, 0})=='[true,0]' (True sorts first despite being numerically greater). Consistent with the pinned expectation at test_caching_correctness.py:418-422.
numerical.recommended_fix: No change needed for determinism. If cross-type numeric ordering is desired, fold bool into the numeric bucket by tagging it ('2_num', int(value)) so True orders as 1 among numbers; but this interacts with the collapse fix above and would change the pinned line-420 expectation, so make it a deliberate, version-bumped decision (ALGO_VERSION) rather than an incidental tweak. At minimum, tighten the docstring wording so it does not imply global numeric ordering across the bool boundary.

numerical.title: No money/precision policy anywhere on the pricing path: raw IEEE-754 Float64 premium is served verbatim to the customer at /quote (and via NDJSON), with rounding applied exactly ZERO times
numerical.description: The entire pricing path produces and serves raw floating-point money with no defined rounding/quantization step. The live deploy endpoint returns `result.head(returned_rows).to_dicts()` (line 309) straight to JSONResponse, and the NDJSON path emits `batch.write_ndjson()` (line 337). `score_graph` (deploy/_scorer.py:844-883) returns the collected Polars frame untouched, and the rating engine (_rating.py) computes every premium/relativity as raw Float64 multiply/add (`_combine_rating_columns`, lines 661-678: `expr = expr * pl.col(c)...`) with no `.round()`/quantize. A grep of the whole pricing path (rating/scoring/optimiser-apply/projection/deploy) finds round() only in diagnostics (modelling/_metrics.py, _charts.py), timings (ms), and RAM estimates — never on a served price. There is no currency/decimal_places/min_premium config knob (grep confirms none). For an insurance pricing engine this is itself a correctness smell: the served number is whatever IEEE-754 binary multiplication produced, so the customer-facing premium can be a non-decimal artifact that two equivalent rating chains disagree on.
numerical.evidence: Reproduced with the project venv: a 5-factor multiplicative chain base=100.0 * [1.1,1.05,0.97,1.02,0.99] yields Float64 113.13294300000001, and json.dumps of the served row is exactly {"premium": 113.13294300000001} — i.e. the API returns 113.13294300000001, not 113.13. Order-dependence is real and observable: (1.1*1.05)*0.97 = 1.1203500000000002 but 1.1*(1.05*0.97) = 1.12035 (NOT equal), so the served price depends on the (Polars-chosen) association/partition order of the multiply chain. Because there is no single defined rounding step, any consumer that rounds downstream inherits whichever raw float Polars produced.
numerical.recommended_fix: Define one explicit money/precision policy and apply it exactly once at the output boundary (the only place a single rounding step is correct). Add an optional, declared per-output rounding spec (e.g. on the Output node / deploy manifest: column -> decimal places + ROUND_HALF_EVEN or insurance-standard ROUND_HALF_UP) and apply it in _quote_response_content / the NDJSON writer (and mirror it in score_graph so dev preview, golden tests, and live serving agree). Use Polars `.round(n)` (or Decimal quantize at the JSON boundary) on the designated money columns only, never on intermediate relativities. Pin with a golden test asserting the served value is the rounded value, and a property test that the rounding is idempotent and applied exactly once.

numerical.title: Golden-quote drift gate field is named `tolerance_pct` but is consumed as a raw FRACTION (0.01 == 1%), not a percentage — a literal-minded operator who writes `tolerance_pct: 1` ("one percent") silently gets a 100% tolerance that accepts almost any premium drift
numerical.description: `_expected_value_matches` computes `allowed = abs(expected_decimal) * Decimal(str(tolerance_pct))` with no /100. The docs (docs/DEPLOY_DESIGN.md:435, DEPLOY_STRATEGY.md:508) and all tests use 0.01 to mean 1%, so the math is internally CONSISTENT with documented usage (this is not a wrong-number bug for documented inputs). The defect is purely the misleading `_pct` suffix on a value that is a fraction: an operator reasonably reading the field as a percent and entering `1` (meaning 1%) gets allowed = expected * 1.0 = +/-100% band, so a deployed pricing change that doubled or halved every test-quote premium would still pass the golden drift gate. The validator accepts any non-negative finite number, so `1` is not rejected.
numerical.evidence: docs/DEPLOY_DESIGN.md:435 golden row uses {"expected": {"premium": 548.57}, "tolerance_pct": 0.01} and the gate treats 0.01 as 1% (allowed = 548.57*0.01 = 5.4857). Therefore tolerance_pct=1 -> allowed = 548.57 (a 100% band). The field name asserts 'percent' but the arithmetic treats it as a fraction; there is no upper-bound sanity check (e.g. reject >1.0 or warn) and no /100 conversion.
numerical.recommended_fix: Either rename the public key to `tolerance_fraction` (or `rel_tolerance`) to match the math, or divide by 100 inside _parse_tolerance_pct so the name is honest (`fraction = float(value)/100.0`) — pick one and document it. Cheapest safe guard without a schema change: reject or warn when tolerance_pct > 1.0 (a >100% drift gate is almost certainly a units mistake) and state the fraction semantics in the error text. Add a test asserting the chosen semantics and that an out-of-range value is rejected/warned.

numerical.location: src/haute/_optimiser_apply_explainability.py:600-612 (_values_match) used by the ratebook reconciliation guard at :347-351
numerical.title: Optimiser-apply explainability reconciliation guard uses an ABSOLUTE abs_tol=1e-6, which for relativities near 1.0 can mask a genuinely divergent optimised factor (weak guard, not a value producer)
numerical.description: `_values_match` loosens the strict (string-cast) comparator with `math.isclose(float(left), float(right), rel_tol=1e-6, abs_tol=1e-6)`. It guards line 347 — that the explainability factor reconciles with the actual `{factor}_optimised_factor` output column. Optimiser relativities cluster near 1.0, where the constant abs_tol=1e-6 dominates rel_tol*|value| (~1e-6 either way), so two values up to 1e-6 apart are accepted as 'reconciled'. This is a guard that could accept a slightly-wrong explanation rather than raising OptimiserApplyTraceError; it does NOT itself emit a wrong served price (both sides are re-derived from the same artifact+input, so real divergence beyond float noise is unlikely). Related to the known catalog.md:318 absolute-1e-6 lineage-relocation issue but a distinct call site (reconciliation guard, not row relocation).
numerical.evidence: Line 611: `return math.isclose(float(left), float(right), rel_tol=1e-6, abs_tol=1e-6)`. For factor values ~1.0, abs_tol=1e-6 sets the effective floor; a divergence of, say, 5e-7 between the explained factor and the output factor is swallowed instead of flagged. The waterfall path by contrast uses a magnitude-scaled rel_tol of 1e-9 (_trace_waterfall.py:37,269), showing the codebase already knows the scale-aware pattern.
numerical.recommended_fix: Make this guard match the waterfall's scale-aware discipline: drop abs_tol to ~0 (or a far smaller floor) and use a magnitude-scaled relative tolerance, e.g. `math.isclose(l, r, rel_tol=1e-9, abs_tol=0.0)` or `abs(l-r) <= 1e-9*max(1.0,|l|,|r|)`, so a reconciliation mismatch on a near-1.0 relativity is not masked. Add a regression test feeding an explained factor that differs from the output factor by ~1e-7 and asserting OptimiserApplyTraceError is raised.

numerical.category: numerical/domain-correctness (float dtype erasure at JSON boundary)
numerical.title: Continuous-banding trace re-match uses exact float `==` for the `=`/`==` operator, so a Float32 factor the engine banded shows status='no_match' (self-contradictory) in the trace
numerical.description: enrich_banding re-derives which continuous rule fired by calling _match_continuous_rule(input_value, rule), and for the `=`/`==`/`!=`/`<>` operators that helper compares the (already JSON-jsonified) cell against float(threshold) with EXACT Python `==` (lines 303-306, applied 317-321). The cell value read from the per-node eager output has been widened from Float32 to its f64 image by _jsonify_row -> to_json_safe (e.g. Float32 0.1 -> 0.10000000149011612), while the rule threshold is parsed as a clean f64 (0.1). They are unequal, so no rule matches even though the engine (which casts both sides consistently, like the rating twin) assigned a band. The result is a factor_detail with status='no_match', rule_index=-1, is_default=False, matched_rule=None — yet selected_band/matched_band hold the real engine band. This is the banding sibling of the catalogued rating-key Float32 divergence (catalog #145-147), but at a DISTINCT location (banding continuous path, not normalise_rating_key) and not enumerated in the known catalog. It misleads the actuary-facing banding explanation and feeds _attach_banding_lineage / _banding_calculation_payload with an empty match.
numerical.evidence: Ran the real enrich_banding: cfg factor {op1:'=', val1:'0.1', assignment:'LOW', default:'OTHER'}, input_row={'score': 0.10000000149011612} (the exact post-jsonify Float32 image), output_row={'band':'LOW'} (engine genuinely produced LOW). Output: status='no_match' rule_index=-1 is_default=False matched_rule=None; _match_continuous_rule(f32(0.1), =0.1)=False. Control with Float64 exact 0.1 -> status='matched'. The defect is specific to Float32 dtype erasure, not the value 0.1.
numerical.recommended_fix: Make the banding trace match dtype-faithful, mirroring the recommended rating fix (catalog #147 option 1): thread the source factor column's original Polars dtype into enrich_banding and canonicalise BOTH the observed cell and the rule threshold through that dtype before comparing (e.g. pl.Series([v], dtype=pl.Float32).cast(Utf8) round-trip, or compare with a relative tolerance consistent with the rest of the module, math.isclose(rel_tol=1e-9)). Add an enrichment-agreement test for a non-integer Float32 banding factor with a continuous `=` rule asserting the trace reports 'matched', not 'no_match'.

numerical.title: Same-row-count fast path accepts a positionally-aligned parent row whenever the CARRIED shared columns match, with no uniqueness guard — a reorder over rows that are duplicates on the carried key shows the wrong upstream input value
numerical.description: When len(parent_df)==child_len, the fast path takes parent_df.row(child_row_idx), keeps the columns shared with the child (match_row), and accepts the row if all(_trace_values_match(candidate[c], match_row[c])) over those shared columns. The shared columns are exactly the ones that survived downstream; the parent's OTHER columns (the upstream inputs the trace will DISPLAY) are not checked.
