If a node reorders rows (sort/group-stable reshuffle) AND two parent rows are identical on the carried/shared columns but differ on a consumed input column, the positional row at child_row_idx ties on the shared columns yet is the wrong physical row, so the displayed upstream input (and the waterfall's value_before for that branch) is taken from a different policy. This is adjacent to catalogue #27 (which is the NO-shared-column reorder case); the NEW element is that #27's repro and fix target the empty-shared branch, whereas this fires WITH shared columns present, so #27's positional-acceptance guard discussion does not cover it. The fast path trusts equal row count + matching carried keys as proof of positional identity.
numerical.evidence: Reproduced the fast-path predicate directly: parent=pl.DataFrame({'key':[1,1],'secret_input':[10.0,999.0]}); the user's clicked lineage is parent row1 (secret_input=999.0) but a downstream reorder makes child_row_idx=0; match_row={'key':1}; candidate=parent.row(0)={'key':1,'secret_input':10.0}; shared=['key']; all(_trace_values_match(1,1))=True -> fast path ACCEPTS row0, so the trace would display secret_input=10.0 instead of the correct 999.0. No len(matched)==1 / uniqueness check exists in the fast path.
numerical.recommended_fix: Before accepting the positional candidate, require that the carried shared columns uniquely identify the row among parent rows (or that no OTHER parent row also matches match_row on the shared columns); when the carried key is non-unique, fall through to the value-matching path (which already records ambiguity diagnostics) instead of trusting position. At minimum, when the shared columns do not pin a unique row, emit an ambiguous_row_match diagnostic so the wrong-row risk is visible rather than silent.

numerical.title: _trace_values_match compares floats with math.isclose(rel_tol=1e-9) and NO abs_tol, so any near-zero value fails to match exactly 0.0 (rel tol is meaningless at zero)
numerical.description: The float comparison uses math.isclose(actual, float(expected), rel_tol=1e-9) with no abs_tol. math.isclose's relative tolerance degenerates at zero: isclose(1e-13, 0.0, rel_tol=1e-9) is False, as is isclose(1e-300, 0.0). For trace row correlation this is only reached when actual != expected already (line 99 short-circuits exact equality), and because the trace is fully in-process (both sides flow from the same jsonified DataFrame values, floats pass through to_json_safe unchanged), a genuine pair that should be equal is usually bit-identical and short-circuits. The latent hazard is the inconsistency: the module documents 'floating-point tolerance' but provides none against zero, and a future caller that compares a re-parsed/re-formatted value (e.g. a frontend-supplied cell) against a column holding ~0 would mis-classify a near-zero match as a miss, then fall to value-matching that can pick a different row. It also diverges from the value-match expression _build_value_match_expr (line 189) which uses EXACT equality for non-NaN floats, so the fast path and the value-match join can disagree on borderline floats.
numerical.evidence: Verified: math.isclose(1e-13,0.0,rel_tol=1e-9)=False; math.isclose(0.0,1e-13,rel_tol=1e-9)=False; math.isclose(1e-300,0.0,rel_tol=1e-9)=False; math.isclose(0.0,0,rel_tol=1e-9)=True. By contrast _build_value_match_expr emits pl.col(column)==value (exact) for non-NaN floats, so the two comparison paths use different float semantics for the same column.
numerical.recommended_fix: Add an absolute floor consistent with the engine's premium/factor scale, e.g. math.isclose(actual, float(expected), rel_tol=1e-9, abs_tol=1e-12) (or a documented abs_tol), and align the value-match join (_build_value_match_expr) to the same tolerance so the fast path and the value-matching fallback agree on borderline floats near zero.

numerical.category: domain-correctness (waterfall display semantics for negative-magnitude steps)
numerical.title: Implied multiplicative factor is computed as value_after/value_before with no sign handling, so a step that changes the sign of the column renders a negative 'x' factor (e.g. 'x-0.5') even though the operation is conceptually additive
numerical.description: _classify_contribution returns ('multiply', value_after/value_before) whenever value_before != 0, the factor is finite, and the AST hint is not 'add'. When the traced column legitimately crosses or flips sign (e.g. a margin/adjustment column going 100 -> -50, or -100 -> 100 via an additive correction with no parseable arithmetic hint), the implied factor is negative (-0.5, -1.0). The waterfall then displays a negative multiplicative factor, which is not a meaningful 'relativity' to an actuary and can read as a data error. The number still reconciles (build_waterfall re-derives delta = observed - value_before from the observed chain and _check_display_consistency reapplies prev*(value_after/value_before) == observed to ~2e-16), so this is display-only, not a wrong total — but the displayed CONTRIBUTION label is misleading for sign-changing steps, and the additive hint only rescues it when the upstream expression text is parseable as Add/Sub.
numerical.evidence: classify(value_before=-100, value_after=100) -> ('multiply', -1.0); classify(100, -50) -> ('multiply', -0.5); classify(-100,-120) -> ('multiply', 1.2). Reconciliation: vb*(va/vb)==va holds to float precision, so no WaterfallReconciliationError fires and the negative factor is rendered. The fallback to additive display only triggers via _operation_hint when the expression AST top-level is Add/Sub, which is absent for many sign-flipping transforms (joins, model scores, conditional corrections).
numerical.recommended_fix: When value_before and value_after have opposite signs (or value_before < 0), prefer additive (delta-only) display rather than emitting a negative implied factor, and log a 'waterfall_sign_change' note — mirroring the existing value_before==0 fallback at lines 403-412 which already chooses delta-only and logs. Keep the arithmetic value-derived so the total is unaffected.

numerical.location: src/haute/_trace_waterfall.py:245-275 (_check_display_consistency) as used by build_waterfall_from_steps at 484-495
numerical.title: In the production trace path the C8 display-consistency guard is a structural no-op for additive steps and can essentially never fire for multiplicative steps, so the only enforced invariant is the single final-reconciliation check
numerical.description: build_waterfall_from_steps always sets each step's 'cumulative' to the observed value and derives 'value' (the display amount) from the SAME observed values: display = observed - value_before (add) or observed / value_before (multiply). _check_display_consistency then re-applies prev_cumulative (op) display and compares to observed. Because the prior step snapped cumulative to its own observed value (== this step's value_before), the additive reapply prev + (observed - value_before) == observed is an algebraic identity that holds for ANY inputs (it can never fail), and the multiplicative reapply value_before * (observed / value_before) == observed holds to ~2e-16. Thus, on the production path, the per-step C8 guard cannot catch a corrupted intermediate — it only protects the hand-authored build_waterfall(steps) public API. The real enforced invariant for traced waterfalls is the single end-of-chain reconciliation (lines 501-511). This is not a wrong number, but it means the per-step guard advertised in the module docstring as the in-builder C8 protection provides no defense-in-depth for the actual trace pipeline; a future change that lets value_before drift from the prior cumulative (e.g. if observed-snapping were ever relaxed) would silently defeat it.
numerical.evidence: Trace of the data flow: value (display) is computed by _classify_contribution from (value_before, observed); cumulative is set to observed; the prior iteration set value_before = its observed (snapped). Reapply: add -> prev + (observed - prev) = observed (identity, independent of display); multiply -> prev * (observed/prev) = observed (float-exact, worst relative reapply error over 200k random multiply steps measured at 2.13e-16 << rel_tol 1e-9). So the per-step inequality |reapplied - observed| > tolerance is unreachable on the production path for any well-formed value_before == prior cumulative.
numerical.recommended_fix: Either (a) document explicitly that the per-step guard is purely for the hand-authored build_waterfall API and that traced-path correctness rests on the final reconciliation, or (b) strengthen the production guard to validate against an INDEPENDENT signal (e.g. the expression-evaluated factor/delta where available, or the parsed operation magnitude) rather than the observed-derived display value, so a corrupted intermediate observed value can be caught before the final-sum check rather than only when it happens to break the end total.

numerical.title: Whitelist row-locality proofs exercise each construct only in isolation on a fixed 3-column frame; compositional and dtype-specific divergences are not proven (defensive gap, not a live bug)
numerical.description: The §A3 proof (test_whitelisted_construct_chunked_equals_full) and meta-test (test_every_whitelist_entry_has_a_proof_case) guarantee each whitelisted method NAME has ONE chunked==full proof, but each proof runs the construct alone on the same (i:Int64, f:Float64, s:String) frame with literal/simple args. The admission logic (_row_local_call_is_supported) admits arbitrary COMPOSITIONS and arbitrary dtypes for these methods. I independently verified (polars 1.39.2) the realistic composition/dtype variants I could construct (clip(col,col), is_between(col,col), nested when/then on columns, cast(pl.Categorical), pl.lit(list), multi-statement local frames, concat_str ignore_nulls) are all genuinely row-local, so this is NOT a live divergence. The gap is the harness would not, by construction, catch a future Polars version where one of these gains an order-dependent path, nor a dtype-specific divergence (Categorical physical encoding) because the proof frame's String column always has its distinct values appear in chunk 0.
numerical.evidence: Proof generator _expr_case builds exactly 'df = source.with_columns(<fragment>)' on _frame_strategy() (only 3 columns, distinct strings 'a','b','x','' appear early). cast(pl.Categorical) is admitted (is_chunk_local_polars_code==True) but has NO Categorical proof case (expr_cast proves only cast(pl.Float64)). It is chunk-safe today ONLY because pl.using_string_cache() is True in 1.39.2 (verified: full physical codes [0,0,1,1,2,2]==chunked even when first-appearance is z|y|x across chunks).
numerical.recommended_fix: Strengthen the §A3 harness so proofs cover (1) at least one Categorical/temporal/Decimal dtype per cast-bearing entry and (2) two-construct compositions, and add an explicit proof for cast(pl.Categorical) that places a value's first appearance in a non-first chunk plus a downstream sort/join on it. This pins the global-string-cache assumption so a Polars upgrade that changes Categorical encoding fails CI rather than silently mispricing a categorical-keyed rate lookup.

numerical.title: cast(pl.Categorical) is admitted to the chunked path; its chunk-safety depends on the ambient global-string-cache setting, which is never asserted on the chunked path
numerical.description: A POLARS node with code df = source.with_columns(pl.col('s').cast(pl.Categorical)) is admitted as MAP_ONLY. Whether per-chunk Categorical casting yields identical physical encodings (hence identical downstream behaviour for any op keying on category identity/order) depends on Polars running with a global string cache. In polars 1.39.2 pl.using_string_cache() is True by default, so it is currently safe (verified adversarially). But iter_chunked_frames never enables or asserts a string cache; it relies on the library default. If a future Polars release reverts Categorical default ordering to per-frame physical (as older Polars did) or a caller disables the cache, two chunks would assign different u32 codes to the same string and a downstream sort/group/join keyed on the categorical (or any to_physical() consumer) would silently diverge between chunked and full — a wrong number with no crash.
numerical.evidence: Adversarial REPL (s=[z,z,y,y,x,x], chunk 2): values equal and physical codes [0,0,1,1,2,2] match full ONLY because pl.using_string_cache()==True. iter_chunked_frames sets no string-cache context. Downstream RATING_STEP neutralises this for join keys (casts to String via _rating_key_expr at _rating.py:583/596), but a user POLARS sort/group_by on a categorical, or any to_physical() consumer, is not neutralised.
numerical.recommended_fix: Either (a) reject cast to pl.Categorical/pl.Enum in the chunk whitelist (treat like a sort-dependent op) since its physical layout is not provably chunk-local in the abstract, or (b) have the chunk runner enter pl.StringCache() for the duration of all chunk collects AND add a proof pinning categorical physical encoding across chunk boundaries. Option (a) is most conservative and matches the module's fail-loud philosophy.

performance.location: src/haute/_code_extraction.py:919-981 (extract_user_code) + 700-735 (_finalise_polars) + 146-182 (_rewrite_outer_returns_as_assignment) + 185-226 (_strip_outer_trailing_return) + 335-386 (_strip_generated_passthrough_from_code); driven by src/haute/_config_builder.py:74-233 (_build_node_config) which calls one _extract_*_user_code per node on the healthy parse path (src/haute/parser.py:144,153-154)
performance.title: Each node body is re-parsed with ast.parse 3-4 times per GUI load, discarding the module AST that was already built once
performance.description: The healthy parser parses the whole file exactly once (parser.py:144 `tree = ast.parse(source)`) and _extract_function_bodies (parser.py:153) walks that tree to slice each function body out as TEXT. That body text is then handed to _build_node_config -> extract_user_code, which throws away the already-parsed AST subtree and re-runs ast.parse on the same body several times. For the common polars/transform path the body is parsed: (1) in _strip_trailing_return -> _strip_outer_trailing_return -> _outermost_returns -> _parse_user_code; then inside _finalise_polars: (2) _strip_generated_passthrough_from_code -> _is_exact_passthrough_return -> _parse_user_code (unconditional when params present), (3) _df_alias_target -> ast.parse(lines[0]) (unconditional), and (4) _rewrite_outer_returns_as_assignment -> _outermost_returns -> _parse_user_code. _unwrap_chain_assignment adds up to 2 more ast.parse calls for `df = (...)` bodies. modelScore/ratingStep add further _rewrite_identifier_tokens -> _parse_user_code passes. Nothing is memoised; the same source string is tokenised and parsed into a fresh ast.Module 3-6x per node. This is pure repeated work: every parse rebuilds the identical tree.
performance.evidence: Per-node parse count for a typical transform body (non-passthrough, not starting with `df = (`): _outermost_returns(parse #1, via _strip_trailing_return at line 974) + _is_exact_passthrough_return(parse #2, line 339) + _df_alias_target(parse #3, line 350) + _rewrite_outer_returns_as_assignment->_outermost_returns(parse #4, line 734). All four operate on the SAME body text. ast.parse is the dominant cost in each helper (tokeniser + parser allocate a full node tree). The information each helper needs (top-level Return nodes, first-statement shape, df-alias) is all derivable from ONE parse of the body, and in fact from the function subtree already present in the module `tree` that parser.py:144 produced.
performance.when_it_bites: Every GUI load / preview / save-reload of a healthy pipeline (parse_pipeline_file runs on each). Cost scales linearly with node count but with a 3-6x constant on the per-node ast.parse. Bites hardest on large ratebooks with many code-bearing nodes (transform/ratingStep/modelScore/scenarioExpander), each carrying a non-trivial body (tens of lines of Polars). At ~100-300 such nodes the redundant parses turn a single-digit-ms parse into tens of ms of avoidable CPU on the interactive load path; on very large pipelines (500+ nodes) it is the difference between a snappy and a visibly laggy canvas open.
performance.recommended_fix: Parse each node body at most once and thread the resulting ast.Module (or, better, reuse the FunctionDef subtree already available in the module `tree` from parser.py:144 rather than re-slicing text and re-parsing at all). Concretely: change _outermost_returns / _is_exact_passthrough_return / _df_alias_target / _rewrite_outer_returns_as_assignment / _strip_redundant_rhs_wrapper_once to accept a pre-parsed tree, and have extract_user_code parse the (dedented) body a single time, passing that tree to every consumer. The textual line/col rewriting can still run off the one tree. This removes 2-5 ast.parse calls per node with no behavioural change.

performance.title: Regex-fallback connect recovery rescans the whole source from index 0 once (often twice) per connect anchor → O(edges x source_length)
performance.description: For every `pipeline.connect(` anchor the fallback does multiple scans that each start at index 0 and run up to the anchor offset, making the pass O(A * n) where A = number of connect anchors (≈ number of edges) and n = source length. Specifically, _iter_connect_anchor_matches already calls _is_top_level_statement_anchor(source, m.start()) (line 270), which calls _parenthesized_wrapper_depth_before(source, idx) — a full character walk `while i < idx` from 0 (lines 116-139). Then _find_connect_calls, for the SAME anchor, computes the line number with source.count('\n', 0, m.start()) (line 337, scan 0->start) and calls _parenthesized_wrapper_depth_before(source, m.start()) AGAIN (line 338) — recomputing byte-for-byte the wrapper depth that _is_top_level_statement_anchor already computed for that exact index. So each anchor triggers ~3 left-to-right scans of the prefix, two of which are identical string-aware walks. Because connect calls in a generated ratebook scale with edges, and edges scale with nodes, and n scales with nodes, the real growth is roughly O(nodes^2).
performance.evidence: _parenthesized_wrapper_depth_before walks every prefix char with string/comment skipping (lines 116-139: `while i < idx: _skip_string_literal(...); ...`). It is invoked once per anchor inside _is_top_level_statement_anchor (line 180, reached from _iter_connect_anchor_matches:270) and a SECOND time on the same index in _find_connect_calls:338. Plus source.count('\n', 0, m.start()) at line 337 is a third 0->start scan. Net: ~3 * sum(anchor_offsets) char visits ≈ O(A*n), with the line-338 scan being provably redundant with the line-180 scan (same source, same index, deterministic result).
performance.when_it_bites: Only on the syntax-error fallback path (parser.py:145-147 triggers it solely when ast.parse raises). It bites when a user has a broken-but-large generated/ratebook file open in the editor — exactly when they are mid-edit and the canvas re-parses on every keystroke-debounce. A 2,000-line file with ~200 connect() calls performs on the order of 200 * (avg 1,000-char prefix) * 3 ≈ 600k extra char visits per parse, repeated on every edit while the file stays broken. For 5,000-line files with 500 edges this is multi-million-char-visit per parse and becomes perceptible interactive lag precisely while the user is trying to fix the error.
performance.recommended_fix: Two independent wins: (1) Eliminate the duplicate scan — have _iter_connect_anchor_matches yield (match, wrapper_depth) so _find_connect_calls reuses the wrapper depth instead of recomputing it at line 338. (2) Replace the repeated source.count('\n', 0, idx) line-number lookups with a single precomputed prefix newline-offset array (bisect over line-start offsets) so line numbers are O(log n) instead of O(n) each. Both keep behaviour identical and drop the connect pass from ~O(A*n) toward O(n + A log n).

performance.title: Fallback decorator/function discovery re-scans source from index 0 per decorator anchor via _position_is_code (O(decorators x source_length))
performance.description: _find_function_blocks iterates every `@pipeline.<type>` anchor from _RE_DECORATOR_ANCHOR.finditer and, for each, calls _position_is_code(source, m.start()) (line 517). _position_is_code walks from index 0 to the anchor with full string/comment skipping (lines 363-377: `i = 0; while i < idx`). With D decorator anchors this is O(D * n). On top of that, the per-block helpers compute line numbers with source.count('\n', 0, idx) at multiple sites (_recover_decorator_text:436, _find_decorated_def:498, and the connect/meta recovery), each an additional 0->idx scan. _recover_pipeline_meta:389 also calls _position_is_code per meta anchor. The same prefix is therefore walked once per decorator just to answer the boolean 'is this anchor inside a string/comment'.
performance.evidence: _position_is_code is a from-zero scan (line 363 `i = 0`). It is called once per decorator anchor in _find_function_blocks:517 and once per meta anchor in _recover_pipeline_meta:389. For D decorators at average offset n/2, total work ≈ D*n/2 char visits, on top of the connect-path scans (separate finding). Line-number computations via source.count('\n', 0, idx) recur at decorator/def/connect/meta sites, none sharing a precomputed index.
performance.when_it_bites: Fallback-only (broken file). Decorator count D equals node count, so on a broken large ratebook (e.g. 300 @pipeline nodes in a 3,000-line file) this is ~300 * ~1,500-char prefix ≈ 450k char visits per parse purely for the in-code checks, compounding with the connect-path quadratic on every re-parse while the file is broken. Negligible for small files; only material at large-pipeline scale during error-state editing.
performance.recommended_fix: Compute string/comment 'code regions' for the source ONCE (a single left-to-right pass producing a sorted list of (start,end) code spans, reusing _skip_string_literal), then make _position_is_code a bisect membership test (O(log n)) instead of a from-zero walk. Share the same precomputed newline-offset array used by the connect fix for all source.count('\n', 0, idx) line-number lookups. This makes decorator discovery O(n + D log n) with identical results.

performance.title: evaluate_expression re-parses the same code 2-3x per call and discards the AST + located target node it already computed
performance.description: A single evaluate_expression(code, col, ...) runs ast.parse on the identical code string 2 times for a plain column and 3 times for a conditional column, and each parse is followed by a fresh _build_safe_symbol_table, _resolve_reassignment_chains, _find_with_columns_calls, and _extract_expressions_from_with_columns over the WHOLE module. _parse_expression_impl already parses the tree, builds the symbol table, and locates the exact target best_match node; then _compute_result_impl throws all of that away and re-parses + re-builds + re-locates the same node, and for conditionals _evaluate_conditional_branches does it a THIRD time. The parsed tree, symbol table, and target node are pure functions of (code, target_column) yet nothing is shared or memoised.
performance.evidence: Instrumented the unmodified module (wrapped ast.parse + walk helpers) via .venv python. Per single call: CONDITIONAL column = {ast.parse:3, find_with_columns:3, build_symbol_table:3, resolve_reassignment_chains:3}; ARITHMETIC column = {ast.parse:2, find_wc:2, build_sym:2, resolve_chains:2}. Wall time (2000-iter timeit, 2-col node): conditional 367 us/call, arithmetic 247 us/call, vs parse_expression ALONE 117 us/call -- ~2-3x of the cost is pure re-parse overhead. _compute_result_impl:1549-1567 re-runs the same ast.parse + symbol-table + wc-extraction that _parse_expression_impl:1021-1086 already ran.
performance.when_it_bites: Every traced cell, for every step that created/passed the clicked column, for every element of the intra-node dependency chain. The 2-3x constant sits on top of the chain/step amplification. Worst on conditional pl.when/then/otherwise columns (the rating-logic columns actuaries trace most) which pay the 3x path.
performance.recommended_fix: Parse once per (code, target_column): have _parse_expression_impl return/cache the parsed tree, symbol_table, and located target node and pass them into _compute_result / _evaluate_conditional_branches instead of re-deriving. A functools.lru_cache keyed on the code string for the heavy invariant part (tree, symbol_table, wc_calls) is the lowest-risk behavior-preserving change and also fixes finding 2; node code strings are small/bounded. (review/03-simplification rejected the textual dedup of the four loops for bundling a behavior change -- caching the deterministic parse is different and is the real win.)

performance.title: Chain enrichment is O(N^2) in node width x chain depth: parse_expression_chain re-parses per chain element, then enrich_steps re-evaluates per chain element, each a full whole-node re-parse
performance.description: parse_expression_chain does its own ast.parse + symbol-table + _find_with_columns_calls, builds a converter for EVERY column in the node (2186-2196), then for each column in the dependency chain calls parse_expression(code_wrapped, col) AGAIN (line 2227), each re-parsing the whole node. enrich_steps then loops over that chain (1559-1568) calling evaluate_expression(raw_code, p.target_column, ...) per element, each of which triggers the 2-3 internal re-parses from finding 1. For a chain of length K from a with_columns block of width N, one traced cell pays O(K) outer iterations x O(N) per-parse extraction x the 2-3x internal factor ~ O(N*K) ast.parse passes and O(N*K*N) total walk/extract work. When K~N (each-column-derives-from-previous rating ladder) this is quadratic-to-cubic in node width.
performance.evidence: Measured exact enrich_steps per-column work (parse_expression + evaluate_expression + parse_expression_chain + evaluate_expression-per-chain-element) on a single with_columns node of width N with a full-depth chain, unmodified module, .venv python: N=5 -> 19 ast.parse calls, 2.68 ms for ONE traced cell; N=20 -> 64 ast.parse, 36.6 ms; N=50 -> 154 ast.parse, 190.3 ms. Wall time grows ~N^1.9 confirming quadratic total work though raw parse COUNT is ~3N+4. 154 ast.parse calls to explain one clicked cell on a 50-wide node is the headline.
performance.when_it_bites: Tracing a cell in a wide rating/banding node (one with_columns producing many derived columns where each builds on the last -- extremely common in insurance ratebooks). At ~50 derived columns one cell costs ~190 ms pure CPU in the parser; at ~100 columns ~0.7-1 s/cell. enrich_steps also walks every step, so a deep graph with several such nodes multiplies further. Trace/preview feels janky exactly on the large ratebooks the engine targets.
performance.recommended_fix: (1) Parse the node ONCE and reuse tree+symbol_table+wc_calls for all chain elements instead of calling parse_expression per element at 2227 (build each ParsedExpression from the col_defs already computed at 2199-2201). (2) In enrich_steps, since the chain is already parsed, expose a single chain-evaluate entry so the per-element evaluate_expression at 1563 does not re-parse -- or apply the lru_cache from finding 1, collapsing all duplicate ast.parse to one per distinct code string. Either fix removes the N factor; together a cell becomes O(N).

performance.title: Every parse pass re-walks the whole module and re-extracts/re-converts ALL columns to find ONE target, with no early-out
performance.description: _find_with_columns_calls does a full ast.walk(tree) of the entire module on every invocation. _parse_expression_impl additionally walks three more times (_has_control_flow_wrapping_target, _find_control_flow_assigned_vars, _build_safe_symbol_table) before it looks for the target. The last-match-wins search (1081-1086, mirrored at _compute_result_impl 1562-1566 and _evaluate_conditional_branches 1466-1471) calls _extract_expressions_from_with_columns for EVERY with_columns call, and parse_expression_chain builds a full _ExprConverter for EVERY column -- though only one target_column is wanted. No short-circuit on alias match, no reuse of walk results across passes within one parse. This O(node-width) factor is what findings 1 and 2 multiply against.
performance.evidence: Code trace: _find_with_columns_calls:917 for node in ast.walk(tree) (whole module). _parse_expression_impl:1044/1058/1055 invoke the two control-flow walkers (each ast.walk per top-level cf stmt, 854-863/878-891) + _build_safe_symbol_table. Search at 1081-1086 iterates all wc_calls x all exprs with no break on match. parse_expression_chain:2186-2196 builds _ExprConverter(...).convert(expr_node) for every (expr_node, alias) regardless of target. Instrumentation showed find_with_columns runs 2-3x PER evaluate_expression, each a full-module walk.
performance.when_it_bites: Scales with number of with_columns/statements in the blob and columns per block. The executor usually wraps one node's code, so wide nodes make each walk + extraction O(width); combined with per-call and per-chain-element re-parsing, this is the inner multiplier turning a 50-column node into 190 ms/cell. On its own (single parse_expression) it is a modest constant and only matters through the multiplication -- fix together with the caching above, not in isolation.
performance.recommended_fix: Short-circuit the target search (scan wc_calls in reverse, take first alias hit to preserve documented last-match-wins B005 semantics -- verify against that test before reordering). Build per-column converters in parse_expression_chain only for chain members. Most importantly cache _find_with_columns_calls + the symbol table on the parsed tree so the 2-3 passes within one evaluate_expression share a single walk. Bounded by small node blobs, so the absolute win is meaningful only at large node width; prioritise behind findings 1 and 2.

performance.title: Operator dispatch dicts rebuilt on every binop/compare evaluation (minor -- NOT worth fixing alone)
performance.description: _binop constructs a fresh 9-entry op_map mapping ast types to operator functions on every call, and _compare builds a 6-entry cmp_map on every comparison. These are module-constant tables (the module already hoists _OP_SYMBOLS/_CMP_SYMBOLS/_PREC at top level) but here are re-allocated per AST node during evaluation. Easy to flag but negligible vs the ast.parse cost dominating this module.
performance.evidence: Lines 1621-1631 define op_map = {ast.Add: operator.add, ...} inside _binop; 1657-1664 define cmp_map = {...} inside _compare, recreated per evaluated node. Measured impact is in the noise: evaluation is a tiny fraction of the 117-367 us/call dominated by parsing + symbol-table building, so eliminating these saves well under 1% of a trace cell.
performance.when_it_bites: Only at extreme expression-tree node counts during evaluation, which never dominates because per-call parse cost is 100-300x larger. Included for calibration: a premature micro-optimisation in isolation -- do NOT spend a dev/reviewer pair on it. If touched, hoist in the same diff as findings 1-3; otherwise leave it.
performance.recommended_fix: Hoist op_map and cmp_map to module-level frozen dicts (mirroring _OP_SYMBOLS/_CMP_SYMBOLS at 61-87) and reference them; zero behavior change. Bundle opportunistically with the real fixes.

performance.location: src/haute/executor.py:901-909 (execute_graph extra_keys + graph_fingerprint, runs unconditionally before the cache lookup)
performance.title: Per-preview cache-key build re-serialises and re-hashes runtime-input signatures via canonical_json on every click, including pure cache hits
performance.description: execute_graph computes extra_keys = [..., *runtime_input_extra_keys(graph)] and then fp = graph_fingerprint(graph, *extra_keys) BEFORE the _preview_cache.try_get(fp) lookup, so this work runs on every request including the common case where the user clicks a different node on an unchanged graph (a guaranteed cache hit). runtime_input_extra_keys -> _runtime_file_inputs_signature rebuilds a per-file-node entries list and calls content_hash_bytes(canonical_json(entries).encode()); _canonicalise recurses the whole entries structure and json.dumps(sort_keys=True) re-serialises it every call. cache_state_signature_for_graph similarly walks every apiInput node and stats two sidecar meta.json files per node. The stat-gating (one stat() per data file) correctly avoids re-hashing file BYTES, but the canonical_json serialisation + content hash of the assembled signature, and the apiInput sidecar double-stat, are redone from scratch each preview even when the inputs are byte-identical to the previous click.
performance.evidence: Cost per preview click is O(file_input_nodes) stats + one canonical_json+blake over the entries list, plus O(apiInput_nodes)*2 sidecar stats + _path_hash. For a graph with N file-backed dataSources and M apiInputs this is N+2M stat() syscalls + a JSON re-encode of an N-element nested mapping, on every click, even on a 100% cache hit. graph_fingerprint then does another content_hash_bytes over the joined extra_keys+base string. None of this is memoised across calls on the same (unchanged) graph instance the way _haute_base_fingerprint is.
performance.when_it_bites: Frequent previews on graphs with many file-backed inputs or many apiInput nodes (e.g. a 30-source ratebook pipeline the user is clicking through node-by-node). At ~50 file/apiInput nodes that is ~50-100 stat() syscalls + a JSON re-encode per click; on networked/Windows filesystems stat latency dominates and makes every otherwise-instant cache hit cost milliseconds of syscall time. Negligible for small graphs (<5 inputs).
performance.recommended_fix: Memoise the runtime-input signature on the PipelineGraph instance behind the same stat-gate the file fingerprints already use: cache (signature_string, per-file stat_gate tuple) on the graph and recompute only the entries whose (mtime_ns,size) sidecar/stat changed, rather than re-serialising the whole entries list. Equivalently, hoist runtime_input_extra_keys into a request-scoped memo keyed by graph identity + the cheap stat tuples so repeated clicks on the same unchanged graph reuse the assembled key. The stat() calls themselves are the irreducible freshness floor; the canonical_json re-encode and blake over unchanged entries are not.

performance.location: src/haute/_execute_lazy.py:120-122 and 704 (_resolve_graph_paths in _execute_lazy) + 1605 (_resolve_graph_paths in _execute_eager_core) -> execution.py:163-193 canonical_dataframe_execution_graph
performance.title: canonical_dataframe_execution_graph re-walks and re-resolves every node's file path on each eager/lazy execute, unmemoised
performance.description: Both _execute_eager_core (line 1605) and _execute_lazy (line 704) call _resolve_graph_paths(graph) = canonical_dataframe_execution_graph(graph) as their first step. That function iterates all graph.nodes, calls _graph_runtime_path_config_key(node) per node, and for file-bearing nodes calls resolve_runtime_file_path (filesystem path resolution). It returns the same graph unchanged when no path differs, but it still pays the full O(nodes) walk + per-file-node path resolution every call. On the preview path this runs once per cache miss/extend; on optimiser/training loops that call execute_lazy repeatedly on the same graph it runs every iteration. The result is also a fresh model_copy when any path changed, which discards the per-instance _haute_base_fingerprint cache on the copy (though the fingerprint used by execute_graph is computed on the original instance, so that particular cache is preserved upstream).
performance.evidence: canonical_dataframe_execution_graph (execution.py:168-193): `for node in graph.nodes: ... resolve_runtime_file_path(raw_path, source_file=..., prefer='project')`. resolve_runtime_file_path does Path resolution (and potentially project-root walking) per file node. No @cached_property or instance memo guards it, unlike node_map/parents_of/_haute_base_fingerprint which are memoised. Called at _execute_lazy.py:704 and _execute_lazy.py:1605.
performance.when_it_bites: Optimiser ratebook solves and training jobs that call _execute_lazy in a tight loop over the SAME graph (path resolution result is invariant across iterations) — the per-iteration node walk + path .resolve() is pure waste there. For interactive preview it is a single walk per cache miss, so low impact. Scales with node count and number of file-backed nodes.
performance.recommended_fix: Memoise the canonicalised graph on the PipelineGraph instance (a @cached_property or a module-level WeakKeyDictionary keyed by graph identity), invalidated by model_copy the same way _haute_base_fingerprint is. Since path resolution depends only on (node configs, source_file) — all immutable on a given instance — the resolved graph can be computed once per instance and reused by every execute call.

performance.location: src/haute/_execute_lazy.py:180-227 (_effective_contract) called at 1120 (_build_lazy_node) and 1767 (_execute_eager_core), per node per execute
performance.title: _effective_contract is rebuilt per node on every execute (and separately on eager and lazy paths) instead of being cached per (nodeType, config)
performance.description: When enforce_contracts is True (the production default), every node calls contract = _effective_contract(node) once per execution. _effective_contract calls Contract.from_tuple(get_column_contract(node.data.nodeType, node.data.config)) — which for rating/banding/modelScore nodes parses the node's config (tables, factors, columns) to derive the read/produce column sets — then overlays the user-declared contract via projection_planner.overlay_declared_contract. This derivation is a pure function of (nodeType, config) and the config is immutable for a given graph instance, yet it is recomputed: (a) once per node every preview cache miss/extend, and (b) again, independently, on the lazy path for sink/deploy. The column_cache in both functions caches the RESULT of collect_schema() but not the contract derivation itself.
performance.evidence: _execute_eager_core line 1767: `contract = _effective_contract(node) if enforce_contracts else None` inside `for nid in order:`. _build_lazy_node line 1120: identical call inside the per-node build. get_column_contract for a rating node walks config['tables'][*]['factors'] / ['entries']; for banding walks config['factors']; this O(config size) parse happens per node per execute. Two separate call sites (eager + lazy) means a graph previewed then sunk derives every contract twice.
performance.when_it_bites: Large ratebooks where rating/banding nodes carry big tables/factors lists in config: get_column_contract's per-node config walk is O(table_entries) and runs for every node on every cache miss. A 50-rating-step pipeline with large factor lists pays this whole derivation on each first-click of a new target (cache miss) and on each sink. Opaque-heavy graphs (user POLARS transforms) are cheaper because _should_check_contract skips the boundary check — but _effective_contract itself still runs to DECIDE that.
performance.recommended_fix: Cache the builder-derived Contract keyed by (nodeType, canonical-config-hash) — or memoise on the GraphNode/config object — so repeated executes and the eager/lazy split reuse one derivation. overlay_declared_contract is cheap; the get_column_contract config parse is the cost. Given configs are immutable per instance, a module-level cache keyed on id(config) (or the already-available canonical_json of the config used in the base fingerprint) eliminates the repeat.

performance.location: src/haute/_execute_lazy.py:1720-1723 (_schema_items_of) invoked at 1917, 1924, plus 1932 second build for MODEL_SCORE in _execute_eager_core
performance.title: Eager core computes each node's schema via collect_schema() two-to-three times per node (available, post-rename output, and a recomputed model-score available set)
performance.description: For every materialised node, _execute_eager_core calls _schema_items_of(result_lf) at line 1917 (available_columns, pre-select), then _schema_items_of(output_lf) at line 1924 (full_output_columns, post-select/rename). Each call does lazy_frame.collect_schema() and builds a list of (name, str(dtype)) tuples. collect_schema() walks the lazy plan to resolve the schema; doing it twice per node resolves the (largely overlapping) plan twice. For MODEL_SCORE nodes without code/renames/selected_columns, available_columns[nid] is then RE-ASSIGNED to full_output_columns at line 1932 — making the line-1917 schema computation for that node entirely wasted work. The lazy path's column_cache caches frozenset column sets across the producer/consumer boundary, but this eager-core schema duplication is within a single node's own processing and is not deduplicated.
performance.evidence: Line 1917 `available_columns[nid] = _schema_items_of(result_lf)`; line 1924 `full_output_columns = _schema_items_of(output_lf)`; line 1926-1932 for MODEL_SCORE re-sets `available_columns[nid] = full_output_columns`, discarding the 1917 result. When selected_columns/renames are absent, result_lf and output_lf have the SAME schema, so the two collect_schema() calls resolve identical plans.
performance.when_it_bites: Wide frames (hundreds of columns — common after joins in a rating pipeline) where collect_schema() and the list-comprehension over schema.names() are O(columns) each, run twice per node, once per preview cache miss across all materialised ancestors. At ~30 nodes x ~300 cols this is ~9000 redundant (name,dtype) tuple builds + a duplicate plan-schema walk per cache miss. Modest in absolute terms but pure waste on the interactive miss path.
performance.recommended_fix: When _apply_selected_columns and _apply_column_renames are both no-ops (the common case — detectable cheaply from config presence), reuse the result_lf schema for output_lf instead of recomputing. For MODEL_SCORE-without-transforms, skip the line-1917 available_columns computation entirely since it is immediately overwritten. Cache the collect_schema() result once per node and derive both available/output column lists from it.

performance.location: src/haute/executor.py:1259-1306 (_eager_execute) -> _compile_preamble with force_refresh=True default, run on every preview cache miss/extend
performance.title: Preview path recomputes the preamble execution fingerprint (AST walk + utility-file hashing pipeline) on every cache miss even when the preamble is unchanged
performance.description: _eager_execute (the preview executor body) calls _compile_preamble(graph.preamble or '', pipeline_dir=..., memo=fingerprint_memo) with the default force_refresh=True. That triggers preamble_execution_fingerprint, which: (1) calls preamble_imports_utility(preamble) (an AST parse/walk of the preamble text) to decide whether utility files are relevant, and (2) when utility is imported, hashes nearby utility.py/utility/**/*.py via _hash_utility_candidate, then canonical_json-serialises the parts and content-hashes them — all to produce the lru_cache key for _compile_preamble_cached. The actual compile is lru_cache-hit when unchanged, but the FINGERPRINT computation that gates it runs in full on every preview miss. The fingerprint_memo (GraphFingerprintMemo) deduplicates utility-file hashing within a single execute_graph call but NOT across clicks. Contrast the sink path (line 1497) which correctly passes force_refresh=False to skip this entirely.
performance.evidence: executor.py:1295 `preamble_ns = _compile_preamble(graph.preamble or '', pipeline_dir=_pipeline_dir(graph), memo=fingerprint_memo)` — no force_refresh, so default True. _compile_preamble (line 438) `if force_refresh: execution_fingerprint = preamble_execution_fingerprint(...)`. preamble_execution_fingerprint re-runs preamble_imports_utility (AST parse) + canonical_json over parts every call. The GraphFingerprintMemo is created fresh per execute_graph (executor.py:865 `fingerprint_memo = GraphFingerprintMemo()`), so cross-click reuse is zero.
performance.when_it_bites: Pipelines with a non-trivial preamble that imports a utility PACKAGE (utility/**/*.py): each preview cache miss re-stats and conditionally re-hashes every utility file (stat-gated, so usually just stats) AND re-parses the preamble AST + re-serialises the parts list. For a utility package with many modules, that is one stat() per module per cache miss plus an AST parse of the preamble. Correct for freshness (GUI utility edits must invalidate), but the AST re-parse and canonical_json re-encode are recomputable-once-per-instance. Empty/utility-free preambles are unaffected (short-circuited).
performance.recommended_fix: Memoise preamble_imports_utility(preamble) and the assembled fingerprint per (preamble text, pipeline_dir) behind the stat gate — only the utility-file stat tuples need re-checking each call; the AST walk and the canonical_json of parts are pure functions of unchanged inputs. Alternatively cache the preamble_execution_fingerprint on the graph instance keyed by the utility stat tuples, recomputing only when a stat gate moves.

performance.title: Preamble-error injection rebuilds node_map with a dict comprehension instead of using the cached graph.node_map property
performance.description: In executor._eager_execute, when a PreambleError occurred, the error-injection block builds `node_map = {n.id: n for n in graph.nodes}` (executor.py:1327) to look up node types for POLARS/LIVE_SWITCH nodes. PipelineGraph already exposes graph.node_map as a memoised @cached_property (built once per instance), so this comprehension re-materialises the same dict, allocating a fresh O(nodes) dict every time a preamble fails. Minor, and only on the error path, but it is a gratuitous re-build of an already-cached structure and slightly contradicts the codebase's own per-instance memoisation discipline.
performance.evidence: executor.py:1327 `node_map = {n.id: n for n in graph.nodes}` inside `if preamble_error:`. _types.py:697-700 defines `@cached_property def node_map(self): return {n.id: n for n in self.nodes}`. The local re-build duplicates it.
performance.when_it_bites: Only when a preamble fails to compile (error path), so frequency is low; cost is one redundant O(nodes) dict allocation per failed-preamble execute. Negligible at any scale but a free cleanup that aligns with the memoisation already in place. Flagged for completeness, not urgency.
performance.recommended_fix: Use `node_map = graph.node_map` (the cached property) instead of rebuilding the dict. The eager/lazy cores receive a re-canonicalised graph, but the cached property on that instance is equally valid; if the canonicalised copy's cache is cold this still computes once and memoises for any later use.

performance.location: src/haute/chunking.py:1011-1015 (_project_frame call per node per chunk) + 1514-1535 (_project_frame body, collect_schema at 1522); compounded by 1009-1010 (_apply_selected_columns/_apply_column_renames)
performance.title: Per-chunk collect_schema() storm: chunk-invariant node schemas are re-resolved O(nodes x chunks) times in the runner loop
performance.description: Inside iter_chunked_frames the per-chunk loop (lines 975-1016) re-derives every chunk node's output schema on every chunk. For each non-start chunk node, _project_frame (called at 1011) runs frame.collect_schema().names() UNCONDITIONALLY whenever the node has a concrete required-column set (line 1520-1522), and _apply_selected_columns (1009) / _apply_column_renames (1010) each run an additional frame.collect_schema() when the node config carries selected_columns/column_renames. Because the per-node builder fn and its config are fixed and only the row DATA varies between chunks (the source file schema is constant), the resolved schema is byte-identical on chunk 0 and chunk N. The work is therefore recomputed C times where C = number of source batches. On the projection-driven chunk path required_columns_by_node is ALWAYS populated (chunk_plan line 784-824 sets it from projection.needed_by_node for both the explicit-chunk_size and byte-budget policies), so the _project_frame collect_schema fires for every chunk node on every chunk regardless of sizing policy. collect_schema() resolves the LazyFrame logical plan (every with_columns/cast/select in the chunk suffix) each call; it is not a free metadata read.
performance.evidence: Cost = O(N_chunk_nodes x N_chunks) logical-plan schema resolutions, each walking that node's accumulated lazy subplan, for a result that is constant across chunks. A 50M-row source at source_chunk_size 500k yields 100 chunks; a 6-node chunk suffix where 2 nodes also carry selected_columns/renames => ~ (6 + 2) x 100 = ~800 collect_schema() resolutions, ~99% of them recomputing an identical schema. The only correctness use of the result is (a) the missing-column guard in _project_frame (1524-1533) and (b) the projection column ordering (1534) - both invariant across chunks. No memoization exists: _project_frame (1514) and the two apply helpers take a fresh frame each call and cache nothing.
performance.when_it_bites: Any chunked execution over a large source: the streaming frontier auto-range job (routes/_optimiser_service.py:3757-3770 iterates iter_chunked_frames over the full scenario-expanded dataset) on multi-million-row ratebooks with deep chunk suffixes. Scales linearly with (chunk count x suffix depth); negligible for a handful of chunks, material at hundreds-to-thousands of chunks. The deeper the row-local polars/banding/rating chain, the more expensive each redundant collect_schema().
performance.recommended_fix: Resolve each chunk node's output column ordering and run the missing-column contract check ONCE (e.g. on the first non-empty chunk, or precompute from the projection plan's known per-node output columns) and reuse the cached ordered projection list for subsequent chunks. Equivalently, hoist the selected_columns/column_renames/projection resolution into a per-node closure built before the loop (alongside _build_funcs at 920-931) so the loop body only applies a precomputed select. Keep a one-time schema validation to preserve the fail-loud contract; drop the per-chunk re-resolution.

performance.location: src/haute/chunking.py:716 (chunk_plan prepare_graph) + 784 (plan_execution_strategy -> projection.plan -> prepare_graph at projection.py:2491) + 869 (iter_chunked_frames prepare_graph)
performance.title: prepare_graph runs three times per chunked execution (twice in chunk_plan, once in the runner) on identical inputs
performance.description: chunk_plan calls prepare_graph(request.graph, request.target_node_id, source=request.source) directly at line 716, then calls plan_execution_strategy at 784 which routes to projection.plan (projection.py:2489-2505) and calls prepare_graph again with the SAME (graph, target_node_id, source) arguments. iter_chunked_frames then calls prepare_graph a third time at line 869 (after _resolve_graph_paths). prepare_graph (projection.py:2109-2135) is O(V+E): ancestors() reverse-reachability, topo_sort_ids(), build_parents_of(), plus a _sanitize_func_name(label) per node. The three computations produce equivalent order/parents/id_to_name structures (the runner re-prepares on the canonicalised graph, but the topology is the same as planning). The plan already carries node_ids, pre_chunk_node_ids, chunk_node_ids, required_columns_by_node and edge_demands, so the runner's re-derivation of order/parents largely duplicates information the plan already proved.
performance.evidence: Three full graph preparations (two within a single chunk_plan call, one per iter_chunked_frames call) for one logical execution. Each is a topo sort + ancestor walk + per-node name sanitisation over the prepared subgraph. The duplication inside chunk_plan (716 vs 784) is pure waste - same args, same result - and is invisible to callers. The runner's prepare at 869 is partly justified (it operates on the path-resolved graph and must re-establish node_map/parents for execution) but still recomputes order/id_to_name that the plan could have carried.
performance.when_it_bites: Deep/wide graphs (hundreds of nodes, dense edges) and/or frequent planning. The optimiser auto-range planner builds a chunk_plan during job setup (_optimiser_service.py:922) and the runner re-prepares at job start (3757); a solve that re-plans per constraint sweep multiplies the O(V+E) prep. Setup-time only (not per chunk), so impact is bounded - real on large graphs, immaterial on small ones.
performance.recommended_fix: Inside chunk_plan, prepare the graph once and pass the prepared order/parents/node_map into the projection step via the already-existing prepared entry points (e.g. compute_prepared_plan / plan_prepared_execution_strategy at execution.py:213) instead of calling the graph-re-preparing plan_execution_strategy. For the runner, consider trusting the plan's node_ids/parents (already validated by _assert_plan_matches_prepared_graph and _assert_runner_shape) and only re-resolve what genuinely changes after _resolve_graph_paths, avoiding a third full topo sort.

performance.location: src/haute/chunking.py:1514-1535 (_project_frame allocations per node per chunk)
performance.title: _project_frame allocates two sets + a filtered list per node per chunk for an invariant projection ordering
performance.description: Independently of the collect_schema cost (finding 1), _project_frame rebuilds schema_set = set(schema_cols) (1523), missing = set(columns) - schema_set (1524), and ordered = [c for c in schema_cols if c in columns] (1534) on every node on every chunk. Since columns and the node's output schema are constant across chunks, both the membership-diff and the ordered projection list are identical each time. This is short-lived allocation churn layered on top of the redundant schema resolution.
performance.evidence: Two set constructions + one list comprehension per chunk node per chunk, all producing chunk-invariant results. At ~800 node-chunk iterations (the 100-chunk/8-node example) this is ~1600 transient sets + 800 lists with no caching, plus GC pressure - small per item but pure waste that vanishes once the projection ordering is memoised.
performance.when_it_bites: Same envelope as finding 1 (high chunk counts x suffix depth). On its own this is minor and would be a premature micro-optimisation; it is worth fixing only as a side effect of caching the projection ordering for finding 1, not as a standalone change.
performance.recommended_fix: Fold into finding 1: when the per-node ordered projection list is computed once and cached, these set/list allocations disappear automatically. Do not optimise in isolation.

performance.title: Rating-step applies N tables without threading input schema: collect_schema() re-resolved per table on a growing lazy plan (O(N^2))
performance.description: _apply_rating_step_outputs loops over tables (lf = _apply_rating_table(lf, table)) and never passes input_schema, so line 588 (frame_schema = input_schema if not None else _frame_schema(lf)) calls lf.collect_schema() every iteration. Each table appends ~5-7 lazy ops (key casts, left join, map_batches miss-guard, dtype reverts, rename/fill, drop), so the Nth collect_schema() walks a plan of size O(N); summed = O(N^2) plan traversal in Polars' schema resolver (no data read). The executor ratebook path (_builders.py:1644-1683) already fixed this: resolve schema ONCE into schema_by_name, thread via input_schema=schema_by_name, update incrementally (schema_by_name[out_col]=pl.Float64). deploy/_config.py:593 also threads input_schema. The shared rating-step path did not, so the asymmetry is an unintended miss, not a deliberate trade-off.
performance.evidence: sum_{k=1..N} O(k) = O(N^2) logical-plan node visits, pure overhead vs resolving the source schema once and tracking added Float64 columns. _combine_rating_output (line 772) adds one more collect_schema() per legacy combined output.
performance.when_it_bites: Insurance rating steps carry one factor table per factor (age, vehicle group, postcode, NCD, cover, occupation...); 10-50 tables is normal, complex ratebooks reach 100+. Paid per node execution: every preview, trace, batch row-group, AND every standalone pipeline.run() (apply_rating_step_from_config routes here -- the deploy/production path). Independent of row count: a 100-table step does ~100 schema resolutions over a plan up to ~700 nodes even on a 1-row quote.
performance.recommended_fix: Mirror the executor ratebook pattern: resolve the frame schema once in _apply_rating_step_outputs, pass it as input_schema to each _apply_rating_table call, and update a local schema map with each table's Float64 output (and combined-output) columns. _apply_rating_table already accepts input_schema. Factor columns are always pre-existing input columns, so a once-resolved schema stays correct for the revert-dtype/existing-column logic.

performance.title: JSON apiInput cache build fully materialises the file as Python objects with ~3-4x peak-memory copies, defeating the streaming iterator; bounded only by a wall-clock timeout
performance.description: build_per_port_cache does records = list(_iter_records(dp, ...)). _iter_records is a generator built to stream (used elsewhere with islice(sample_size)), but the build collapses it to a full in-memory list of dicts. shred_to_buffers makes a SECOND full copy (per-port lists of per-row dicts); _buffer_to_frame makes a THIRD per-column pass (values = [row.get(c) for row in rows]) before pl.Series. So the process simultaneously holds the decoded JSON object graph + per-port row-dict buffers + (transiently) per-column value lists, all boxed Python objects far larger than Arrow. No row/byte cap; only a coarse _BUILD_TIMEOUT in routes/json_cache.py. Arbitrary-nesting multi-port shred has no native Polars equivalent so some Python work is unavoidable, but holding three full copies and materialising the streaming JSONL iterator are avoidable.
performance.evidence: Peak RSS ~= all-records object graph + all per-port row dicts + one column value list, held at once, single-threaded. Python boxing ~3-10x on-disk bytes, so a few-hundred-MB JSONL can push multi-GB transient RSS. The list() at 825 discards the bounded-memory property the JSONL generator already provides (line-by-line at :342-353).
performance.when_it_bites: Clicking 'Cache as Parquet' on a large nested-JSON/JSONL apiInput dataset (hundreds of MB to low-GB). Single-process engine with no _ram_estimate admission on this path, so a large ingest can OOM the whole server where a chunked build stays bounded; only ceiling is the minutes-scale timeout. Small datasets unaffected.
performance.recommended_fix: For JSONL, shred in bounded record chunks: read a batch from _iter_records, shred_to_buffers on that batch, append each port's rows to a per-port pyarrow ParquetWriter (same pattern as _databricks_io.fetch_and_cache), release, repeat -- peak O(chunk) not O(file). At minimum drop list(...) so shred consumes the generator lazily, and build each Series from an iterator. Keep whole-file .json eager but gate it by a documented size threshold like the other bounded-memory profiles.

performance.title: Coverage note: Polars usage is otherwise well-optimised (no action)
performance.description: Reviewed in full: _polars_utils, _rating, _edge_join, _io, _json_flatten, _optimiser_apply_explainability, deploy/_impact; plus hot regions of _execute_lazy (eager core + lazy schema caching), projection, _json_shred, routes/_optimiser_service (auto-range + solve), _databricks_io, _model_scorer, modelling/_metrics, routes/_explore_service, deploy/_scorer, _builders, chunking. Cross-checked all 89 entries in review/02-findings/findings.json and the perf hot-paths map; the two findings above are NEW.
performance.evidence: collect_schema() is treated as data-free and cached in the executor (column_cache keyed by (node,port); schema_by_parent in join-key checks). Collects are streaming-first via streaming_collect with explicit allow_broad opt-in. Scans use projection/predicate pushdown (_io.read_source; _match_ratebook_input_row pushes equality filter into Polars and materialises only the matching row). Databricks ingest streams Arrow batches straight to parquet. Optimiser auto-range uses a bounded hash-partitioned external merge. Explore computes all per-column stats in ONE aggregation pass. Every iter_rows site operates on a bounded frame (preview row_limit, one quote's candidates, or head(top_n) after group_by). The rating miss-guard stays lazy/streaming via map_batches. No map_elements/apply-where-native-expr-exists and no to_pandas on a hot path found.
performance.when_it_bites: N/A -- informational.
performance.recommended_fix: No change required for the rest of the Polars surface.

performance.location: src/haute/_dataframe_execution_cache.py:235-301 (dataframe_execution_cache_key), 215-232 (_upstream_subgraph), 270-271; called per-node at src/haute/execution.py:653-666 and again at src/haute/_execute_lazy.py:806-845
performance.title: Per-node cache-key build rebuilds a full PipelineGraph and recomputes the base fingerprint from cold — O(N_target x (V+E)) graph reconstruction + hashing, done twice per run
performance.description: Every dataframe-execution cache key is derived by calling _upstream_subgraph(graph, node_id), which materialises a brand-new PipelineGraph via two full list comprehensions over graph.nodes and graph.edges (lines 220-232), then graph_fingerprint(lineage_graph). Because the lineage graph is a freshly constructed instance each time, its @cached_property _haute_base_fingerprint is always cold, so _graph_base_fingerprint runs in full: sorted(nodes by id) + canonical_json(config) per node + canonical_json([source,sourceHandle,target,targetHandle]) per edge + a sort of the serialized edge lines + an xxh64 over the joined parts. This entire pipeline runs once per node in the request-build loop (execution.py:653) and is then repeated verbatim in the _execute_lazy validation loop (_execute_lazy.py:829, 'expected_key = dataframe_execution_cache_key(...)') to assert the caller-supplied key matches. The GraphFingerprintMemo threaded through (execution.py:651, _execute_lazy.py:805) only memoises utility-file content hashes — it does NOT memoise the dominant base-fingerprint or subgraph work, so it provides no relief for the hot part.
performance.evidence: For a run materialising M cache nodes on a graph of V nodes / E edges, total cost is roughly 2 * sum_over_M( O(V) subgraph node filter + O(E) subgraph edge filter + O(V log V) node sort + O(V) canonical_json(config) + O(E) canonical_json(edge) + O(E log E) edge-line sort ). With M proportional to V this is O(V^2 + V*E) of pure-Python serialization+hashing per execution, paid twice (build + validate). canonical_json itself is a double pass: _canonicalise recursively rebuilds the structure, then _canonical_dumps calls json.dumps with sort_keys=True (a second key-sort of every mapping).
performance.when_it_bites: Large ratebooks / deep pipelines: a 200-node graph with several hundred edges where the lazy backend caches per-node outputs. The cost is paid on every lazy execution (every trace, every cached batch run, every preview that routes through the dataframe-exec cache) regardless of cache hit/miss, because key construction precedes the cache lookup. At 100+ nodes this is the hundreds-of-microseconds-per-node figure noted in _types.py:714 multiplied by node count and by 2, i.e. tens of milliseconds of CPU before any data is touched, growing quadratically with graph size.
performance.recommended_fix: Cache the per-(graph-instance, node_id) lineage fingerprint instead of rebuilding+rehashing. Two complementary options: (1) Compute each node's upstream-id set once for the whole graph (single reverse-topo pass) and reuse it across all target nodes rather than calling upstream_node_ids per node. (2) Memoise the lineage base fingerprint on GraphFingerprintMemo keyed by (id(graph), node_id) or by the frozenset of included node ids, so the request-build pass and the _execute_lazy validation pass share one computation instead of two. Even simpler for the validation pass: pass the already-built keys_by_node down and compare identity/fields without recomputing dataframe_execution_cache_key a second time. None of this changes digest bytes.

performance.title: upstream_node_ids uses a Python list as a FIFO with stack.pop(0) and stack[0:0]=... — both O(n) shifts, making the traversal O(V*E) on wide/deep lineages
performance.description: The BFS over parents uses stack.pop(0) (line 41) and stack[0:0] = parents_of.get(current, []) (line 45). list.pop(0) is O(len(stack)) because it shifts every remaining element left, and slice-assignment at index 0 (stack[0:0]=...) is O(len(stack)+len(inserted)) for the same reason. The frontier can hold O(V) ids for a wide graph, so the traversal degrades from the expected O(V+E) to O(V*E) in the worst case. This function is invoked inside _upstream_subgraph for every cache-key build (see finding above), so the slowdown compounds the per-node rebuild cost.
performance.evidence: Each of up to V dequeues costs O(frontier size); inserting parents at the head re-shifts the frontier. For a diamond/fan-in lineage with a wide parent layer the frontier is O(V) and the loop runs O(V) times => O(V^2) list shuffling per call, and this call itself is made per target node.
performance.when_it_bites: Deep or fan-in-heavy lineages (hundreds of upstream nodes feeding a target) on large ratebooks, multiplied by the number of cache nodes per run. Negligible on small graphs; clearly measurable once a single node's upstream set is in the hundreds and there are many such nodes.
performance.recommended_fix: Use collections.deque (popleft() is O(1)) and extend()/extendleft() instead of list.pop(0) and slice assignment. The result list is order-significant ('nearest parents first') but a deque preserves the same visitation order with O(1) ends. This is a drop-in change with no behavioural difference.

performance.title: Every cache get()/scan() re-validates the parquet artifact (filesystem exists() + scan_parquet().collect_schema()) under the global cache lock, on each hit
performance.description: Both get() (line 361) and scan() (line 370) open 'with self._lock:' and immediately call _evict_if_invalid(entry), which calls _validate_entry: entry.path.exists() (a stat syscall, line 543) followed by pl.scan_parquet(entry.path).collect_schema() (reads the parquet footer/metadata from disk, line 550) — all while still holding self._lock. The lock is the single mutex serialising every operation on the cache (get, scan, put, eviction, store-window bookkeeping, release_scan). So each cache lookup performs blocking filesystem + parquet-footer I/O inside the critical section, serialising all other threads' cache access behind disk latency, and re-reads the same footer on every hit even when the artifact has not changed since the last validation.
performance.evidence: _evict_if_invalid -> _validate_entry does 1 stat + 1 parquet metadata read per lookup; on a hot trace the same entry is scanned repeatedly (e.g. preview then trace reuse the same DataFrames) so the same footer is read each time. The work runs under self._lock (the with-block at lines 361 and 370 spans the _evict_if_invalid call), turning a pure in-memory LRU hit into a disk-bound, globally-serialised operation. materialize_lazy_frame_with_cache compounds this: on a miss it calls scan() twice (line 595 pre-store and line 615 post-store), so a single materialisation triggers two full validations.
performance.when_it_bites: Concurrent previews/traces against the same cache (multiple browser sessions or the trace layer reusing preview frames) on a busy server, especially on Windows/networked filesystems where parquet footer reads and stat() have higher latency. Also any workload with many small cache hits per second — each pays a parquet open under the global lock. Single-threaded local use barely notices.
performance.recommended_fix: Do not re-read the parquet footer on every hit. Validate lazily/cheaply: gate the expensive collect_schema() check behind a fast stat (size+mtime) comparison against the stored metadata, and skip re-validation entirely for an entry validated within the same operation. At minimum, drop self._lock before the collect_schema() I/O (hold it only to read/remove the entry record), so disk latency does not serialise unrelated cache operations. Keep the post-store validation (it guards a real corruption case) but avoid running it a second time in materialize_lazy_frame_with_cache when the entry was just written and validated.

performance.title: Eviction capacity check is O(n) per put and re-scans all entries on every loop iteration, with DataFrameExecutionCache adding a second full dict scan per candidacy test
performance.description: _evict_if_over_capacity (_lru_cache.py:295) recomputes _capacity_entry_count() — a full scan of self._data filtering by _is_pinned — on every iteration of the while loop and again after each eviction. DataFrameExecutionCache overrides _capacity_entry_count (line 517) to call super()._is_pinned per key, i.e. another O(n) scan, and its _is_pinned (line 515) consults _store_pins on top. So a single put that must evict k entries is O(k * n) capacity recomputation, and each candidate-selection inner loop (_lru_cache.py:302) re-materialises list(self._data.keys()) (O(n) allocation) per eviction.
performance.evidence: For default max_entries=16 the counts are tiny so this is invisible, but the structure is O(n) per put with an O(n) re-scan per evicted entry and a fresh O(n) key-list allocation per eviction step. The cost scales with cache size, not data size.
performance.when_it_bites: Only if max_entries is raised to a large value (hundreds+) AND the cache is churned heavily (many puts each forcing eviction), e.g. a long-lived server with a big dataframe-exec cache under constant invalidation. At the shipped default of 16 entries it does not matter.
performance.recommended_fix: Maintain a running unpinned-count and current_bytes incrementally (already tracked for bytes) rather than rescanning, and break the eviction victim search using the OrderedDict iteration order without re-listing all keys each pass. Low priority — note it only as a scalability ceiling on max_entries, not a present bottleneck.

performance.title: canonical_json double-sorts mapping keys: _canonicalise builds the dict then json.dumps(sort_keys=True) re-sorts every mapping
performance.description: _canonicalise already walks the whole value and produces canonical dicts/sorted sets; _canonical_dumps then calls json.dumps with sort_keys=True, which sorts the keys of every mapping a second time during serialization. The recursive _canonicalise pass also allocates a parallel copy of the entire structure (new lists for every list/tuple, new dict for every mapping) before serialization. For the fingerprint path this canonical_json runs once per node config and once per edge on every (cold) base-fingerprint computation.
performance.evidence: Two traversals + two sorts of each mapping per canonical_json call, plus a full structural copy. Combined with the per-node, twice-per-run base-fingerprint computation (finding 1), the constant factor is multiplied across V configs + E edges.
performance.when_it_bites: Large node configs (rating tables embedded as config, deep nested mappings) on big graphs, amplified by the per-node recompute in finding 1. On small configs it is in the noise.
performance.recommended_fix: Since _canonicalise already canonicalises ordering (sets sorted; mappings can be emitted in sorted-key order), drop sort_keys=True from _canonical_dumps and have _canonicalise emit mapping keys pre-sorted, eliminating the second sort. Verify byte-identical output against the existing fixtures (the canonicalisation contract is pinned by tests). Strictly an allocation/constant-factor win; do not pursue unless finding 1 is addressed and profiling still shows canonical_json hot.

performance.title: prepare_graph builds the reverse-adjacency (parents_of) twice per plan: once inside ancestors(), once directly
performance.description: prepare_graph() calls ancestors(target_node_id, edges, all_ids) (line 2121) to compute the target's ancestor set. ancestors() internally calls build_parents_of(edges, all_ids) over the FULL pruned edge list (every edge in the graph). prepare_graph() then immediately calls build_parents_of(relevant_edges, set(order)) AGAIN at line 2127 to build the parents_of it returns. Both are full linear scans over (almost) the same edge list, allocating a dict-of-lists keyed by every node. The first parents_of (built by ancestors) is discarded.
performance.evidence: ancestors() at _topo.py:107 does `parents = build_parents_of(edges, all_ids)` then BFS-walks it; the dict is thrown away on return (only `visited` survives). prepare_graph then does `parents_of = build_parents_of(relevant_edges, set(order))` at projection.py:2127. For a graph with E edges and N nodes both calls are O(E + N). When target_node_id is None, ancestors() is skipped (needed = all_ids), so this only bites the targeted-preview path — but that is the most frequent path (single-node preview, trace). The two scans differ only in edge filtering (full vs ancestor-filtered), so the first result is a strict superset and could be reused/filtered.
performance.when_it_bites: Every targeted preview/trace/single-node execution on a large graph. Concrete scale: a ratebook pipeline with ~500-2000 rating-step/banding nodes and a comparable edge count pays two full O(E+N) adjacency builds (plus a third in build_parents_of-via-children downstream) on each of the many previews an actuary triggers while iterating. At a few thousand edges the duplicate build is sub-millisecond per call, so this is a low-to-medium constant-factor win, not an algorithmic fix — worth folding in opportunistically, not a standalone hot fix.
performance.recommended_fix: Have ancestors() optionally return (or accept) the parents_of map it builds, or inline an ancestor walk in prepare_graph that reuses the single build_parents_of(relevant_edges,...) result by computing ancestors against the already-built reverse adjacency. One adjacency build per prepare_graph instead of two.

performance.title: plan() converts parents_of -> children_of, then compute_prepared_plan immediately rebuilds parents_by_child from children_of
performance.description: prepare_graph already produces parents_of (node -> parents). plan() throws it away and calls _children_of(order, parents_of) to invert it into children_of (line 2498, building a fresh dict-of-lists over all edges). compute_prepared_plan then re-inverts children_of back into parents_by_child (lines 2152-2156, another full dict-of-sets over all edges) because the reverse-topo sweep needs BOTH directions. So the planner does parents->children->parents, performing two extra full adjacency inversions when it already held parents_of upstream.
performance.evidence: plan(): `_children_of(prepared.order, prepared.parents_of)` (2498). _children_of iterates every (parent, child) pair to build children_of (2067-2070). compute_prepared_plan: `parents_by_child = {nid: set() ...}` then double loop over children_of re-adding every (parent,child) into parents_by_child (2152-2156). compute_prepared_plan's signature only accepts children_of, so the parents_of it could have reused is structurally inaccessible. Each inversion is O(E + N) and allocates N lists/sets.
performance.when_it_bites: Every plan() call (preview, trace, batch, deploy projection) on every graph. Two redundant O(E+N) inversions plus N set allocations. On a 2000-node ratebook with ~3000 edges this is a few-thousand-element rebuild done twice unnecessarily per plan; constant-factor, sub-ms at typical sizes. Matters mainly because plan() is on the per-preview path and the work is pure overhead — the data already exists.
performance.recommended_fix: Pass parents_of (or both maps) through to compute_prepared_plan instead of only children_of, and have it consume the existing parents_of directly rather than re-inverting children_of. children_of itself can be derived once if needed. Avoids one or both inversions.

performance.title: projection_contract(node) recomputed per node multiple times (own-node + once per child as 'parent_produced'), with no memoisation
performance.description: projection_contract(node) is the per-node contract resolver: it calls get_column_contract (registry lookup + contract callable), overlay_declared_contract (which may Contract.from_user_declared-parse the node's declared 'contract' config), and to_tuple(). compute_prepared_plan invokes it for the current node at line 2281. Separately, for any opaque-contract child it builds parent_produced = {pid: _parent_produced_columns(node_map[pid])} at lines 2283-2285, and _parent_produced_columns calls projection_contract(parent) AGAIN for each parent. Because every non-leaf node is a parent of >=1 child, a node's contract is frequently resolved 2+ times across the sweep (once as itself, once per opaque-contract child that lists it as a parent). The single-parent Polars rule (line 1286) adds yet another projection_contract(node) call for the SAME node before line 2281 is even reached.
performance.evidence: No @lru_cache / memo on projection_contract; it recomputes from node.data.config every call. Confirmed extra calls: (a) line 2281 `produced, referenced = projection_contract(node).to_tuple()`; (b) line 2284 `_parent_produced_columns(node_map[parent_id])` -> projection_contract(parent) for every parent, recomputed for that parent again when the parent is later visited as the current node; (c) SingleParentPolarsExpressionRule.parent_demands at 1286 calls projection_contract(node) and, when the node has a concrete contract, returns None at 1287 — so line 2281 then recomputes the identical contract. overlay_declared_contract re-parses node.data.config['contract'] via Contract.from_user_declared on each call when a contract annotation is present (declared_inputs_by_parent at 1789-1801 parses the same annotation a THIRD time for fan-in nodes).
performance.when_it_bites: Scales with (nodes that are parents of opaque-contract children) x (contract-resolution cost). Bites hardest on large ratebooks where many rating-step/banding nodes feed edge-join/optimiser/modelScore opaque nodes: each opaque child triggers a fresh contract build for ALL its parents, so a parent with K opaque children is resolved ~K+1 times. With user-declared 'contract' annotations the cost includes repeated Contract.from_user_declared validation/parsing of the same dict. At hundreds-to-thousands of nodes per plan, and plan() on every preview, this is the most defensible real redundant-recompute on the surface.
performance.recommended_fix: Memoise contract resolution per (node_id) for the duration of one compute_prepared_plan sweep — e.g. a local `contract_cache: dict[str, tuple[frozenset|None, frozenset|None]]` populated lazily and shared by the own-node path (2281), _parent_produced_columns (2284), the single-parent rule (1286), and declared_inputs_by_parent.
