tests.recommended_fix: Add a failing route test (TDD for V096): seed a completed frontier job with >=2 points and live heavy state (solver/quote_grid), POST /api/optimiser/apply {point_index:0} expecting 200, then POST /api/optimiser/apply {point_index:1} on the same job and assert 200 (not 400). Pin the fix that apply_lambdas must preserve quote_grid/solver while the job still has frontier points (use the frontier-aware clear), mirroring the other session exits.

tests.title: Concurrency test for atomic_update only asserts 'no exception + >=1 field present', codifying the documented lost-update behaviour as acceptable
tests.description: test_atomic_update_thread_safety runs 20 threads each writing a distinct field_{idx} but asserts only that no exception is raised, status is unchanged, and at least one field_N survived (len(field_keys) >= 1). Its own docstring states the read-modify-write `old = d[k]; d[k] = {**old, **fields}` is NOT linearisable and concurrent writers to different keys can lose each other's updates, declaring that acceptable for the real single-writer workload. This is honest but it pins a lossy behaviour as intended: a future change that made atomic_update genuinely merge all concurrent distinct-key writes would not be rewarded, and a regression that LOST MORE updates would not be caught (the assertion passes as long as one of 20 writes survives). The stronger linearisability properties are only covered for the same-status compare-and-swap (test_atomic_update_with_expected_status_is_optimistic_lock:657) and the heavy-present path (553), not for plain distinct-key concurrent merges.
tests.evidence: Lines 938-942: `assert result['status'] == 'running'; field_keys = [k for k in result if k.startswith('field_')]; assert len(field_keys) >= 1`. With 20 distinct keys submitted, this passes even if 19 updates are lost. The docstring (lines 909-919) explicitly accepts non-linearisable lost updates.
tests.recommended_fix: Either strengthen to assert all 20 distinct-key writes survive (if the store is intended to be safe for distinct-key concurrent writers — which would also pin a real correctness property), or, if the single-writer contract is deliberate, replace the multi-distinct-key scenario with one that asserts the actual invariant the production code relies on (single background writer + reader sees no torn state, as test_atomic_update_vs_reader_no_partial_state already does) so the test stops implying distinct-key merge safety that the code does not provide.

tests.title: Categorical 'unsupported dtype' negative test covers only List, leaving the supported-but-strict-cast Binary path (V099) and other text bases unverified
tests.description: The single negative-path categorical test uses a List column, which _has_categorical_value_counts correctly classifies as unsupported (expandable=False, values=[]). This gives false confidence that non-text categorical dtypes are handled safely. But the dtypes that actually exercise the strict cast in _categorical_value_counts_expr are the _TEXT_DTYPE_BASES = (String, Categorical, Enum, Binary). Of these, only String/Categorical are tested with value-count assertions; Enum and Binary are never tested. Binary is the load-bearing gap (V099), and Enum (a frequently-used compact categorical) has no value-count test at all, so a future regression in Enum handling would also go unnoticed.
tests.evidence: _TEXT_DTYPE_BASES at src/haute/routes/_explore_service.py:78 includes Binary and Enum; the explore tests assert value counts for String (e.g. region at :813), Boolean (:819), Date (:823), and a count-named String column (:911), plus List as unsupported (:895). No Enum or Binary fixtures exist in the file.
tests.recommended_fix: Extend the categorical-summary tests to cover each member of _TEXT_DTYPE_BASES: add an Enum column (assert value counts render with the category labels) and a Binary column (UTF-8 and non-UTF-8 bytes; assert no crash and a sensible Text profile). This both closes the V099 gap and locks the contract that the categorical branch handles every dtype it admits.

tests.location: tests/test_deploy.py:304-323 (test_model_score_skipped_without_run_id) and tests/test_deploy.py:485-508 (test_registered_model_skipped_without_model_name); paired with serve-side src/haute/deploy/_scorer.py:677-733
tests.title: Bundler tests codify the silent-skip of misconfigured modelScore nodes; no serve-side test pins the resulting null-prediction passthrough (verified bug V044)
tests.description: VERIFIED-BUGS V044 (high): a modelScore node misconfigured so the bundler skips it entirely (no model AND no contract bundled) is served as a SILENT passthrough at deploy time — _scorer.py:_intercept's MODEL_SCORE branch finds remapped_path=None and bundled_contract_path=None, skips both guard branches, and hits `return None` (line 733), falling through to _build_model_score which passes the input through with no prediction. The fail-loud guard (model_score_missing_artifact, lines 681-704) only fires `if bundled_contract_path is not None`. The test suite codifies the bundler half of this bug as intended behaviour: test_model_score_skipped_without_run_id asserts a modelScore with `{'sourceType':'run'}` and no run_id yields `len(artifacts)==0`, and test_registered_model_skipped_without_model_name asserts the same for an empty registered_model. Because the bundler emits neither a model nor a contract for these nodes, they are exactly the precondition for V044's passthrough. test_deploy_scorer_artifact_cache.py:234-261 covers ONLY the contract-bundled-without-model branch (which correctly raises). There is NO test asserting that the neither-model-nor-contract case raises at serve time — and the bundler tests affirmatively pin the silent skip, so a reviewer reading the suite would conclude this is intended.
tests.evidence: test_deploy.py:322-323 `artifacts = collect_artifacts(graph, [], Path('.')); assert len(artifacts) == 0` for `config={'sourceType':'run'}` (no run_id). _scorer.py:677 `if bundled_contract_path is not None:` gates the only RuntimeError; with both None the code reaches `return None` at line 733 → passthrough. The only fail-loud test (test_deploy_scorer_artifact_cache.py:255 `pytest.raises(RuntimeError, match='model artifact')`) supplies `{f'ms__{CONTRACT_FILENAME}': str(contract_path)}` — a bundled contract, i.e. the OTHER branch.
tests.recommended_fix: When V044 is fixed (raise in _intercept when a configured-looking modelScore has neither remapped_path nor bundled_contract_path), add a serve-side regression test: build the _model_score_graph() with a real run_id/artifact_path config but pass artifact_paths={} (nothing bundled), call score_graph(...), and assert it raises RuntimeError naming the node rather than returning the input unchanged. Until then, the two bundler tests should be annotated (or paired with the serve-side assertion) to make clear that an unbundled modelScore must NOT be served as a passthrough — the current assertions silently bless the dangerous precondition.

tests.title: find_config_by_func_name traversal tests are vacuous: the only assertion is gated behind `if result is not None`, which never executes given the real guard
tests.description: The class TestFindConfigByFuncNameTraversal claims to verify that func_name path traversal is blocked. But src/haute/_config_io.py:297 rejects any func_name containing '..', '/' or '\\' by returning None. Both tests therefore ALWAYS take the `result is None` path and assert NOTHING. The body `if result is not None: ... assert config_data.get('leaked') is True` is dead code under current behaviour. These tests pass today, but they would also pass if the security guard were deleted entirely (the traversal would still resolve to a non-existent path under a different layout and return None), AND — far worse — they provide zero protection against a regression: if a future change made find_config_by_func_name return a non-None config for `../../secret`, the test would actively ASSERT that the leaked content is returned (asserting the vulnerability is 'working') rather than failing. A security test whose sole assertion fires only when the code is vulnerable is worse than no test: it inverts the intended contract.
tests.evidence: _config_io.py:297 `if '..' in func_name or '/' in func_name or '\\' in func_name: ... return None`. Test: `result = find_config_by_func_name('../../secret', base_dir=tmp_path); if result is not None: config_data, _ = result; assert config_data.get('leaked') is True` — the assertion is unreachable for the blocked input, so the test is a no-op.
tests.recommended_fix: Make the assertion unconditional and aligned with the contract: `assert find_config_by_func_name('../../secret', base_dir=tmp_path) is None` and `assert find_config_by_func_name('../model_scoring/victim', base_dir=tmp_path) is None`. Optionally also assert the warning log 'config_recovery_rejected' is emitted (via capture_logs) to pin that rejection — not mere absence — is the reason for None.

tests.title: Test named 'PathURLSchemeRejection' asserts that validate_safe_path does NOT reject URL schemes — the assertion contradicts the class/contract name
tests.description: The class docstring states 'validate_safe_path or read_source must reject paths starting with URL schemes.' The test test_url_scheme_in_validate_safe_path then asserts the OPPOSITE for validate_safe_path: for inputs like 'http://evil.com/data.csv' and 'file:///etc/shadow' it asserts `result.is_relative_to(tmp_path)` — i.e. that validate_safe_path silently TREATS the URL as a relative child path and returns it without rejection. I verified src/haute/routes/_helpers.py:78-102: validate_safe_path has no scheme check; it only blocks null bytes, absolute escapes and post-resolve escapes, so 'http://evil.com/...' becomes `(base / 'http:/evil.com/...').resolve()` inside base. The companion read_source test (lines 714-727) does enforce rejection, so the suite is not vacuous overall — but this specific assertion codifies a surprising behaviour (a URL-looking string passing the path validator) under a class name that promises rejection. A reader scanning for 'is URL-scheme rejection covered?' is actively misled, and if a future hardening adds scheme rejection to validate_safe_path, this test will fail spuriously and be 'fixed' by re-deleting the protection.
tests.evidence: _helpers.py:78-102 contains no URL-scheme handling. Test asserts `result.is_relative_to(tmp_path.resolve())` for scheme_path in {'http://evil.com/data.csv','https://...','ftp://...','file:///etc/shadow'} with the message 'URL-scheme path should resolve within base, not trigger external access'.
tests.recommended_fix: Rename/retarget the assertion to reflect the real defence boundary: the protection against SSRF lives in read_source (extension/scheme guard), not validate_safe_path. Either (a) split this into a clearly-named test 'validate_safe_path treats URL-looking strings as in-tree filenames (no fetch)' and keep the SSRF contract solely on the read_source test, or (b) if URL schemes SHOULD be rejected by validate_safe_path, change the assertion to `pytest.raises(HTTPException)` and fix the helper. As written, the class name overpromises while the body under-delivers.

tests.title: Dev-mode --port propagation to the Vite proxy is untested (verified bug V004): the test asserts only that npm is invoked
tests.description: VERIFIED-BUGS V004: in dev mode --port is silently broken — the backend port is never propagated to the Vite dev server, whose proxy targets a hardcoded 127.0.0.1:8000 (frontend/vite.config.ts). The dev-mode test asserts ONLY that subprocess.Popen is called once with npm as argv[0]; it never inspects the child env (the `env=` kwarg) for any backend host/port, nor the displayed banner URLs. So a user running `haute serve --port 9000` in dev mode gets a frontend that proxies to the wrong backend, with zero test coverage of the regression. The non-dev test (lines 220-254) correctly checks uvicorn gets port 9000, which creates a false sense that --port is fully covered.
tests.evidence: test_cli_serve.py:279-290 asserts `mock_popen.assert_called_once()` and that the command basename starts with 'npm'; no assertion on `mock_popen.call_args.kwargs.get('env')`. VERIFIED-BUGS V004 fix note: 'propagate the backend bind to the Vite child via env (env["HAUTE_BACKEND_HOST"]=..., env["HAUTE_BACKEND_PORT"]=...)'.
tests.recommended_fix: Add a test that invokes `serve --no-browser --host 127.0.0.1 --port 9000` in dev mode and asserts the Vite child env carries the backend bind (e.g. `mock_popen.call_args.kwargs['env']['HAUTE_BACKEND_PORT'] == '9000'`) once V004 is fixed; as a RED test it currently demonstrates the missing propagation. Also assert the dev banner reflects the chosen port.

tests.title: In-flight admission: the first/single reservation exceeding (available_ram - os_reserve) is never tested (verified bug V029)
tests.description: VERIFIED-BUGS V029: _reserve_in_flight_budget (src/haute/_execution_admission.py:507-523) refuses the FIRST admission when a single profile's memory LIMIT exceeds (available_ram - os_reserve), because the guard `if reserved + reservation_bytes > limit_bytes` has no clamp for the empty-ledger case. The existing test sets available_ram to a generous 10 GiB so the FIRST OPTIMISER_SETUP job is admitted, and only the SECOND concurrent job is rejected with reason='in_flight_memory_budget_exceeded'. It thus exercises the cumulative-ledger path but never the pathological single-job-too-big case (reserved==0 and reservation_bytes > limit_bytes), which is the actual defect: on a modest machine the very first/only heavy job is refused even with nothing else running. No test pins that a single reservation must always be admitted.
tests.evidence: _execution_admission.py:513 `if reserved + reservation_bytes > limit_bytes:` with reserved==0 reduces to `reservation_bytes > limit_bytes` and raises. Test monkeypatches available_ram to 10*gib (line 269-270) so the first job fits; assertion at line 284 only covers the second job rejection.
tests.recommended_fix: Add a test that patches available_ram_bytes low enough (and/or sets a large per-profile memory limit via env) so a SINGLE heavy admission has reservation_bytes > (available - os_reserve) on an empty ledger, and assert it is still admitted (the per-context rss_limit_bytes is the real bound for one job). This becomes the RED test for V029; once fixed (`if reserved > 0 and reserved + reservation_bytes > limit_bytes:` or a clamp), it stays green.

tests.title: No test for the no-haute.toml deploy path where the raw --pipeline arg clobbers the resolved/discovered path (verified bug V005)
tests.description: VERIFIED-BUGS V005: in handle_deploy's no-haute.toml branch (src/haute/cli/_deploy.py:118-124), the code first resolves the user-supplied pipeline argument via resolve_pipeline_file (which accepts a DIRECTORY and discovers the project pipeline inside, returning an absolute file path), then unconditionally overwrites it with the RAW unresolved CLI arg: `if config.pipeline_file: overrides['pipeline_file'] = Path(config.pipeline_file)`. So passing a directory as the pipeline argument breaks directory-discovery. The deploy CLI test file only exercises the haute.toml-present path (every test calls _make_toml(tmp_path)); there is no test for the no-toml branch at all, and no test passes a directory as the pipeline argument. The override-clobber regression is therefore entirely uncovered.
tests.evidence: Every TestDeploy method in test_cli_deploy.py calls `_make_toml(tmp_path)` (which writes haute.toml), so the `bounds/no-toml` branch at _deploy.py:118-124 is never entered. No test passes a directory to `haute deploy <dir>`.
tests.recommended_fix: Add a test with NO haute.toml present that runs `haute deploy <project_dir>` (a directory containing a discoverable pipeline) and asserts the DeployConfig/resolve receives the discovered absolute file path, not the raw directory. As a RED test it reproduces V005 (resolution discarded); after the fix (make the override branch-aware) it passes.

tests.title: Windows RAM path test over-mocks and asserts only that GlobalMemoryStatusEx was called, never the value it returns
tests.description: available_ram_bytes is pricing-adjacent (it gates downsampling and in-flight admission). The Windows test fully mocks ctypes so the struct field ullAvailPhys is never populated, and the test explicitly notes 'we can't easily intercept field values'. Its only assertion is `mock_windll.kernel32.GlobalMemoryStatusEx.assert_called_once()`. It never asserts the returned byte count, the unit, or that the value is propagated — so a regression that called the API but returned a wrong/zero value (or ignored ullAvailPhys) would pass. This is a structure/'no exception + API called' assertion rather than a value assertion. The Linux/sysconf paths ARE value-checked (e.g. the 4 GiB fallback at lines 157-184), so this is a localized gap rather than a systemic one.
tests.evidence: test_ram_estimate.py:151-153 comment '...we can't easily intercept field values. Verify the API was called.' and line 155 `mock_windll.kernel32.GlobalMemoryStatusEx.assert_called_once()` is the sole assertion.
tests.recommended_fix: Drive the value through a fake: have the mocked GlobalMemoryStatusEx side_effect write a known ullAvailPhys into the passed struct (or refactor available_ram_bytes to read the field via an injectable seam) and assert available_ram_bytes() returns that exact byte count. That converts the test from 'API was called' to 'correct RAM value is returned', catching unit/field-mapping regressions.

tests.title: Disjunctive `== correct_value OR is None` assertions codify the evaluator's silent value-laundering as acceptable
tests.description: These trace-expression-evaluator tests assert the result with an OR-None escape hatch: `assert math.isnan(result.result_value) or result.result_value is None` (1194), `assert result.result_value == float('inf') or result.result_value is None` (1202), `assert result.result_value == float('-inf') or result.result_value is None` (1207). The correct single-row Polars value for `x*2` with x=inf is +inf, for `x+1` with x=-inf is -inf, and for `x+1` with x=NaN is NaN. The `or ... is None` clause makes the test PASS even when the evaluator silently returns None. None is exactly the laundered value produced by `evaluate_expression`'s top-level `except Exception` (src/haute/_expression_parser.py:1302-1304), which on ANY internal failure returns `row_values.get(target_column)` (None when the key is absent). So these assertions bless the precise silent-failure path that VERIFIED-BUGS catalog #23 (`except Exception` masks wrong numbers) and CLAUDE.md ("fail loudly ... a fallback which is incorrect and hard to notice") forbid. A genuine regression that broke inf/NaN handling inside the evaluator would not be caught.
tests.evidence: src/haute/_expression_parser.py:1302-1304: `try: return _evaluate_expression_impl(...) except Exception: parsed = parse_expression(...)` then EvaluatedExpression(..., result_value=row_values.get(target_column), ...) at line 1323. Catalog #23 repro `parser__expr-evaluator-catchall-masks-bugs.py` ran green proving a real ZeroDivisionError on `pl.col('a')/pl.col('b')` is laundered into the observed value with no log. The disjunctive asserts here accept that None outcome.
tests.recommended_fix: Pin the exact correct value: `assert result.result_value == float('inf')` (and `-inf`, and `math.isnan(result.result_value)`). If the evaluator legitimately cannot represent a single-row inf/NaN, that is a design decision that should be asserted as an explicit error/marker, not silently permitted via `or is None`. Add a companion test that injects a real internal evaluator failure (e.g. division by zero) and asserts the trace surfaces an error/None-with-marker rather than echoing the observed value, per the catalog #23 fix.

tests.location: tests/test_trace.py (TestRowCorrelation* classes, ~145-374) and tests/test_trace_integration.py:1434-1572 (TestRowCorrelation* classes) — no test anywhere exercises a numeric trace value against a string parent column; `_build_value_match_expr` has zero direct coverage (grep across tests/ = no files)
tests.title: No test covers the dtype-asymmetric correlation crash (V027): a numeric value vs a string parent column aborts the entire trace
tests.description: VERIFIED-BUGS V027 is a confirmed, still-live HIGH-area crash: `_build_value_match_expr` (src/haute/_trace_correlation.py:186-189) casts the COLUMN to Utf8 only when the match VALUE is a str; when the value is numeric and the parent column is Utf8 it emits bare `pl.col(column) == value`, which Polars rejects with ComputeError('cannot compare string with numeric type'). Symmetrically a NaN/inf value against a Utf8 column emits `is_nan()`/`is_infinite()`, raising InvalidOperationError. This runs inside `indexed.select(...)` on the trace.py post-hoc correlation path with NO try/except, so a perfectly ordinary graph (parent has a string code column; a child casts it to Int and filters rows so the same-row-count fast path is bypassed) makes the whole 'click a price to trace it' request hard-fail instead of degrading to the documented (None,-1). The entire row-correlation test surface only ever matches values whose dtype already agrees with the column (or shares the column name so casting is symmetric), so this critical crash is invisible to CI.
tests.evidence: I executed review/04-exhaustive/repro/V027.py against the current tree: '[A] numeric value vs string column RAISED ComputeError: cannot compare string with numeric type (i32)'; '[C] NaN value vs string column RAISED InvalidOperationError: is_nan operation not supported for dtype str'; '[D] _correlate_rows_posthoc RAISED ComputeError ... [(col("code")) == (dyn int: 20)].fill_null([false])'. Source still has the asymmetric guard at _trace_correlation.py:186-189. Grep for `_build_value_match_expr` in tests/ returns no files.
tests.recommended_fix: Add failing tests first (per CLAUDE.md TDD-for-bugs): (1) unit `_build_value_match_expr('x', 2)` against a Utf8 column and `_build_value_match_expr('s', float('nan'))` against a Utf8 column must NOT raise (assert a False/non-matching predicate); (2) end-to-end via execute_trace with a parent string column, a child that casts it to Int and filters rows (so the positional fast path is bypassed), asserting the trace returns with a no-match/ambiguity diagnostic rather than raising. Then make the comparison dtype-robust (compare stringwise, or wrap so an incompatible compare yields False) preserving the (None,-1) fail-soft.

tests.title: Reorder-correlation tests give false confidence: the dangerous rename+sort-with-no-shared-column case (V027/#27 positional fast-path misroute) is untested
tests.description: VERIFIED-BUGS catalog #27 confirms (executed repro, exit 1) that `_correlate_rows_posthoc` attaches the WRONG parent row when a same-row-count transform reorders rows and leaves NO column name shared between parent and child output (e.g. `df.select(pl.col('a').alias('b')).sort('b', descending=True)`): the `if not shared:` fast-path at _trace_correlation.py:637-643 accepts the positionally-aligned parent row, so the actuary sees a different policy's input as the contribution to the clicked price, silently. The test suite's `TestRowCorrelationSortChangesOrder` docstring explicitly claims 'Sort reorders rows; positional matching would give wrong results', but its body uses `df.sort('id')` where `id` is SHARED, so value-matching rescues it — it never exercises the no-shared-column path that actually triggers the bug. `test_positional_match_with_columns` likewise keeps the `x` column shared. The suite therefore advertises reorder-robustness it does not have.
tests.evidence: test_trace_integration.py:1551-1570 builds `_transform_node('sorted', "df = df.sort('id')")` with `id` present in both parent and child; the assertion `sorted_step.output_values['id'] == 1` passes via value-match. Catalog #27 repro `projection-trace__posthoc-positional-fastpath-reorder.py` (REPRODUCED, exit 1): parent a=[10,20,30], child b=[30,20,10] via `parent.select(pl.col('a').alias('b')).sort('b', descending=True)`; clicking child b==30 correlates to parent a==10 (positional row 0) instead of a==30. Control without the sort returns correct, isolating reorder as trigger.
tests.recommended_fix: Add a failing test mirroring the repro: source a=[10,20,30] -> transform `df.select(pl.col('a').alias('b')).sort('b', descending=True)`; trace child row 0 (b==30) and assert the correlated parent row is a==30 (true lineage) OR that the trace surfaces an 'unresolved/ambiguous' diagnostic — never the positional a==10. Then gate the `if not shared:` positional acceptance behind a proven row-order-preservation invariant (or a stable row-identity token).

tests.location: tests/test_trace_fail_loudly.py:195-489 (every test in TestItem3SilentEnrichmentExcepts and the parametrised smoke test) and :665-712
tests.title: Fail-loudly tests pass on ANY exception via `if exc is not None: return`, and only exercise injected raises — never the real silent value-laundering they were written to prevent
tests.description: Each test uses `_run_trace_loudly`, which catches ExecutionError and returns it; the test body then short-circuits with `if exc is not None: return` (lines 213-215, 251-252, 302-303, 383-384, 410-411, 471-472; and 695-698 for the waterfall test). This means the test passes if the trace raises ANY ExecutionError for ANY reason — including reasons unrelated to the injected failure — without ever checking the failure is the specific one under test. Worse, the suite proves fail-loudly only by monkeypatching helper functions (`parse_expression`, `evaluate_expression`, `build_waterfall`, ...) to raise `_BoomError` from OUTSIDE. The actual catalogued bugs (#23/#29/#47) are NOT raises: the real `evaluate_expression` swallows internal failures in its own `except Exception` (src/haute/_expression_parser.py:1302-1304) and returns the observed value, so it never raises and never sets a visible-failure field. These tests structurally cannot exercise that path because they force the raise externally; they validate the outer wrapper while the inner laundering remains uncaught. The file's own docstring asserts coverage of '15+ silent except Exception sites' but the real silent site (the inner catch-all) is untested.
tests.evidence: test_trace_fail_loudly.py:145-146 `_run_trace_loudly` returns `(None, exc, captured)` on ExecutionError; bodies then `if exc is not None: return` (e.g. 213-215). The injected failures all come via `monkeypatch.setattr('haute.trace.<fn>', _explodes)` (205, 243, 294, 375, 402, 463, 678). Catalog #23 repro shows the real inner `except Exception` at _expression_parser.py:1536-1539/1302-1325 launders ZeroDivisionError/TypeError into the observed value with NO raise and NO log — a path these tests never enter.
tests.recommended_fix: (1) On the `exc is not None` branch, assert the exception is the injected one (e.g. `isinstance(exc.__cause__, _BoomError)` or message contains the sentinel) instead of returning unconditionally. (2) Add tests that drive a REAL internal evaluator failure without monkeypatching the outer function — e.g. a construct that raises inside `_evaluate_expression_impl` (division by zero, `round` on a str) — and assert the trace surfaces an error/marker rather than `result_value == observed`. This is the regression the catalog #23 fix requires and that the current suite misses.

tests.location: tests/test_projection_planner.py (entire TestSingleParentPolars* family ~783-1755; no test references pl.sum/pl.mean/pl.min/pl.max/pl.first/pl.std/pl.n_unique with a string column argument)
tests.title: Projection planner has no test for string-argument Polars aggregation shortcuts that silently under-demand the parent (V007)
tests.description: VERIFIED-BUGS V007 (executed repro) confirms `_referenced_polars_columns` (src/haute/projection.py:789-802) returns an empty column set for top-level aggregation shortcuts that name a column by string argument — `pl.sum('a')`, `pl.mean('a')`, `pl.min/max/first/last/std/var/median/count/n_unique('a')` — instead of bailing to full width as the module's stated invariant requires (the dynamic `pl.col(...)` branch correctly returns None). Several of these are row-preserving inside `with_columns`, so the planner emits a NARROWED edge demand that omits the referenced column, under-demanding the parent. The projection planner suite is otherwise extremely thorough about `pl.col('a')` references, select/rename/filter, and derived columns, but contains zero coverage of the string-argument aggregation shortcuts, so this silent under-demand (which surfaces as ColumnNotFoundError, or a wrong narrowed scan at deploy if a same-named column exists) is untested on a pricing-critical strict-profile path.
tests.evidence: Grep of test_projection_planner.py for `pl.sum(`/`pl.mean(`/`pl.min(`/`pl.max(`/`pl.first(`/`pl.std(`/`pl.n_unique(` and 'under-demand' returns only union-walk commentary at lines 1658/1705-1706, none exercising the shortcuts. V007 repro is listed REPRODUCED in VERIFIED-BUGS (executed-repro). Source `_referenced_polars_columns` only special-cases `pl.col(...)` (projection.py:796-801).
tests.recommended_fix: Add planner tests for a single-parent polars node whose code is e.g. `df = df.with_columns(total=pl.sum('a'))` (and the other shortcuts) under LAZY_SINK, asserting the parent edge demand INCLUDES 'a' (or bails to full width / None), never an empty/narrowed set that drops it. Pair with the V007 production fix (return None for any `pl.<func>(...)` with a non-`pl.col` argument that cannot be proven column-free).

tests.location: tests/test_trace_waterfall.py:458-517 (TestPassthroughSteps) and tests/test_trace_coverage.py build_waterfall section (~644+); src/haute/_trace_waterfall.py:483 gate
tests.title: No test for the identity-for-this-row rating step silently dropped from the waterfall (catalog #56)
tests.description: build_waterfall_from_steps gates membership on `column in diff.columns_modified` (src/haute/_trace_waterfall.py:483), and `_compute_schema_diff` marks a column modified only if in_val != out_val on the single traced row (src/haute/_trace_correlation.py:155). A genuine multiplicative rating step that evaluates to factor 1.0 FOR THIS ROW (e.g. `when(region=='X').then(1.2).otherwise(1.0)` for a non-X row) leaves the cell unchanged, lands in columns_passed, and is silently omitted from the explanation — yet the cumulative still reconciles so no WaterfallReconciliationError fires (catalog #56, executed repro EXIT=0). The waterfall tests do cover TRUE passthrough exclusion (`test_passthrough_between_rating_steps_adds_no_entry` asserts an unrelated node is absent), but they never assert that a step which STRUCTURALLY targets the traced column but is identity-for-this-row is still represented (or deliberately excluded with a documented reason). The completeness gap is untested, so a fix or regression here would be unguarded.
tests.evidence: src/haute/_trace_waterfall.py:483 `elif column in diff.columns_modified:` — identity rows go to columns_passed (correlation.py:151-158), bypassing this branch. Catalog #56 repro `projection-trace__waterfall-modified-gate-omits-identity-contributor.py` EXIT=0: 'region_relativity present in steps: True, present in waterfall: False; final cumulative 300.0 == traced output 300.0; result is a list (no error payload)'. test_trace_waterfall.py TestPassthroughSteps only covers unrelated-node exclusion.
tests.recommended_fix: Add a test driving a real multiply node that resolves to factor 1.0 for the traced row (via a when/otherwise relativity), asserting it appears as an explicit x1.0 / delta-0 entry while a genuinely carried (unassigned) column does NOT, leaving reconciliation untouched. This pins the intended completeness behavior before changing the modified-gate.

tests.title: replace_strict and concat_str are tested only at parse level (referenced_columns); the evaluator value divergences (catalog #29/#47) are uncovered
tests.description: `test_replace_strict_dict` and the concat_str tests assert only `expr.referenced_columns` / `expression_type` from parse_expression — they never call evaluate_expression and never assert result_value. Catalog #29 (executed repro) shows the evaluator treats replace_strict identically to replace, returning the base value for an unmapped key with no default where real Polars raises InvalidOperationError('incomplete mapping'); catalog #47 (executed repro) shows `pl.concat_str([...], separator=...)` returns None from the evaluator where real Polars returns the joined string. These wrong/None values are surfaced as the actuary-facing 'calculation'. The parse-only assertions are correctly scoped to parsing but leave the value path — the one that misleads users — with no coverage, so the divergence cannot be caught here.
tests.evidence: test_expression_parser_advanced.py:493-494 asserts only `expr.referenced_columns == ['grade']`; :582-583 asserts only `set(expr.referenced_columns) == {'city','state'}`. Catalog #29 repro: evaluate_expression(replace_strict {'A':1.0}, value 'B') -> result_value='B' while Polars raises. Catalog #47 repro: concat_str(pl.col,pl.col,separator='-') -> evaluator None vs Polars 'x-y'.
tests.recommended_fix: Add evaluate_expression value tests: replace_strict with value-in-mapping (returns mapped), value-absent+no-default (must NOT fabricate the base value — assert error/None-with-marker), value-absent+default (returns default); and concat_str returning the joined string for present values. These pin the catalog #29/#47 fixes.

tests.title: Ctrl+Shift+Z redo test fires a physically-impossible {key:"z", shiftKey:true} event, making the permanently-broken redo shortcut (V079) pass
tests.description: The test `it("Ctrl+Shift+Z calls redo")` dispatches `new KeyboardEvent("keydown", { key: "z", ctrlKey: true, shiftKey: true })` and asserts `redo` is called. In a real browser, when Shift is physically held the `KeyboardEvent.key` for the Z key is the UPPERCASE "Z" (key reflects the produced character), never lowercase "z". The production handler at useKeyboardShortcuts.ts:54 checks `mod && e.key === "z" && e.shiftKey` — a condition that can NEVER be true with a real Shift press (it would need key==="z" AND shift simultaneously). This is verified bug V079 ("Ctrl+Shift+Z / Cmd+Shift+Z redo is unreachable"). jsdom does not derive `key` from `shiftKey`; it uses the literal value passed, so the synthetic event satisfies the broken guard and the test goes green while the only macOS redo shortcut is dead. The test codifies the bug as intended behaviour and is exactly why CI did not catch V079.
tests.evidence: Test: `fireKey("z", { ctrlKey: true, shiftKey: true }); expect(params.redo).toHaveBeenCalledOnce()` with `fireKey = (key, opts) => window.dispatchEvent(new KeyboardEvent("keydown", { key, bubbles: true, ...opts }))`. Production: useKeyboardShortcuts.ts:54 `if (mod && e.key === "z" && e.shiftKey && !isTyping) { ...; redo() }`. Catalog: V079 high-confidence executed-repro.
tests.recommended_fix: When the fix lands, the test must dispatch the realistic event `fireKey("Z", { ctrlKey: true, shiftKey: true })` (uppercase key) — which fails against today's code and passes only once the handler normalises case (e.g. `e.key.toLowerCase() === "z"`). Add a sibling negative test asserting that `{ key: "z", shiftKey: true }` (the impossible combo) does NOT need handling, plus a Cmd+Shift+Z (metaKey) variant for macOS. The same uppercase-key realism must be applied to the TEXTAREA-ignore test at line 85-92 which has the identical defect.

tests.title: Every keyboard-shortcut test uses lowercase e.key, so CapsLock-breaks-all-letter-shortcuts (V080) is completely uncovered
tests.description: Verified bug V080: all letter-key shortcuts (undo z, copy c, paste v, select-all a, group g, search k) silently break when CapsLock is on, because the handler compares `e.key` against lowercase literals with no case normalisation. With CapsLock on (and Shift off), the browser delivers `key: "Z"/"C"/"V"/...`. The entire 490-line test file only ever fires lowercase keys (`fireKey("z"...)`, `fireKey("c"...)`, etc.), so there is zero coverage of the uppercase code path. A user with CapsLock on loses every Ctrl shortcut and no test would notice.
tests.evidence: Handler: useKeyboardShortcuts.ts:42,49,54,60,67 all use `e.key === "s"/"z"/"c"/"y"` literals; no `.toLowerCase()` anywhere. Tests only ever pass lowercase: e.g. lines 58,63,131,140,151,239,290. Catalog: V080 high-confidence code-trace.
tests.recommended_fix: After the handler normalises case, add a parametrised test that fires each shortcut with the uppercase key (CapsLock simulation: `{ key: "Z", ctrlKey: true }` with shiftKey false) and asserts the same action fires as the lowercase form. This pins V080 against regression.

tests.title: sanitizeName tests claim backend parity but never test a Python keyword, masking the missing keyword-prefix divergence (V091)
tests.description: Verified bug V091: the frontend `sanitizeName` omits the keyword-prefix step that the backend `_sanitize_func_name` performs, so a node labelled "class" (or def/return/import/lambda/etc.) sanitises to "class" on the frontend but "node_class" on the backend — a silent identifier divergence that breaks generated-code/round-trip parity. The test file explicitly documents itself as enforcing parity with the backend `_sanitize_func_name` (comment block at lines 65-70, and the non-ASCII `café -> caf_xe9_` cases) yet contains NO test for any Python keyword. It thoroughly tests spaces, hyphens, punctuation, leading digits, non-ASCII, CJK, emoji, and idempotency — giving the false impression of complete parity — but the one rule the implementation is actually missing is untested. Confirmed by source: sanitizeName.ts only prefixes when the result starts with a digit (line 36); there is no keyword check, and the docstring's 6-rule list omits keyword handling entirely.
tests.evidence: sanitizeName.ts:36 `if (name && /^[0-9]/.test(name)) name = ...` is the ONLY prefix step; no keyword set. Tests assert e.g. `sanitizeName("abc123")==="abc123"` but never `sanitizeName("class")`. Catalog: V091 high-confidence code-trace, backend ref `src/haute/_graph_utils.py _sanitize_func_name`.
tests.recommended_fix: Add failing tests `expect(sanitizeName("class")).toBe("node_class")`, `expect(sanitizeName("return")).toBe("node_return")`, and a non-keyword control `expect(sanitizeName("klass")).toBe("klass")`, mirroring the backend keyword set. Fix sanitizeName.ts to prefix Python keywords with `node_` (sharing the keyword list with, or kept in sync with, the backend), and update the docstring rule list. This is a high-value codifies-the-gap finding because the test's self-description asserts a parity it does not verify.

tests.title: detectGaps tests never exercise overlapping/nested rules, so the predecessor-upper (not running-max) bug (V073) is uncovered
tests.description: Verified bug V073: `detectGaps` compares each sorted interval's upper bound against only its immediate predecessor's upper (`intervals[i].interval.upper`), not the running maximum upper seen so far. When rules overlap or nest (e.g. a wide rule [0,100] followed by a narrow nested rule [10,20] and then a far rule (>50)), the algorithm reports spurious or wrong gaps because a contained interval's small upper bound resets the comparison baseline. Every test in the detectGaps block uses cleanly ordered, non-overlapping intervals (simple gap, point gap, multiple gaps, open-ended). None feeds an overlapping or nested pair, which is precisely the input class that triggers the bug. detectOverlaps is separately tested for containment (line 122-129), so the data shapes were available — they were just never routed through detectGaps.
tests.evidence: bandingUtils.ts:146-157 loop uses `const curr = intervals[i].interval` (predecessor), not a running max. Tests at lines 163-209 only use disjoint sorted ranges. Catalog: V073 high-confidence code-trace.
tests.recommended_fix: Add a test with a nested/overlapping set, e.g. rules [>=0,<=100], [>=10,<=20], [>50] and assert detectGaps returns [] (fully covered, no spurious gap). Add a second case where a genuine gap exists beyond an overlapping pair and assert only the real gap is reported. After fixing detectGaps to track running-max upper, these pin V073.

tests.title: OptimiserDataPreview's 600-line suite never feeds a non-finite series value, so the Chart-silently-coerces vs Statistics-throws divergence (V051) is untested
tests.description: Verified bug V051: the Chart tab silently coerces/drops non-finite (NaN/Infinity) series values (emitting e.g. an SVG path containing literal 'NaN' or dropping points), while the Statistics tab throws on the identical rows and trips the ErrorBoundary. This is an inconsistent failure mode across two tabs over the same data. The test suite is large and exercises chart rendering, series checkboxes, statistics means, navigation, and capping — but every `margin`/`volume` value in every fixture is a clean finite number. There is no test that places NaN or Infinity in a series and asserts how Chart and Statistics each behave. Because the two tabs diverge precisely on this input, the absence of any non-finite fixture means the bug is invisible to CI and the intended (consistent) behaviour is unspecified.
tests.evidence: All fixtures use finite values (e.g. margin: 100..240, volume: 0.86..1.0); the only 'extreme' value used is 1_000_000 (finite) at line 363. No NaN/Infinity anywhere in the file. Catalog: V051 high-confidence code-trace, `frontend/src/panels/OptimiserDataPreview.tsx:42-57`.
tests.recommended_fix: Add a fixture with `margin: Number.NaN` / `volume: Number.POSITIVE_INFINITY` and assert the decided contract on BOTH tabs: e.g. Chart path `d` strings contain no 'NaN'/'Infinity' (skip non-finite points like LossTab does) AND the Statistics tab renders without throwing (non-finite excluded from aggregates or shown as an explicit marker). Mirror the LossTab pattern (LossTab.test.tsx:18-53) which already does this for loss curves.

tests.title: LossChart has no non-finite path-coordinate test, unlike its sibling LossTab, leaving V089 (makePath emits 'NaN' coordinates) uncovered
tests.description: Verified bug V089: `LossChart.makePath` filters points only with `e[key] != null` (LossChart.tsx:42), so a NaN/Infinity loss value yields an invalid SVG path segment like `L12.3,NaN`. The sibling component LossTab guards with a finite check and is explicitly tested for it (LossTab.test.tsx:18 "renders a valid loss curve without NaN or Infinity path coordinates" and the empty-state test at line 38). LossChart shares the identical logic (its own header comment says so) but its test file only ever uses clean finite data and never asserts the absence of 'NaN'/'Infinity' in path output. This is asymmetric coverage: the fix/guard was applied and pinned in LossTab but LossChart remains unguarded and untested. Note: catalog records that the related y-range-poisoning premise was refuted because backend `_assert_json_finite` guards loss_history, which lowers real-world reachability — hence medium/medium rather than high — but the per-point makePath defect (V089) was still verified by code-trace and the coverage gap versus the sibling is genuine.
tests.evidence: LossChart.tsx:42 `.map((e,i) => e[key] != null ? ... : null)` (null-only filter). LossTab.tsx guards with isFiniteNumber (per catalog V089) and is tested. LossChart.test.tsx uses only finite fixtures (lines 22-25, 37-41, 49-53). Catalog: V089 verified TS bug.
tests.recommended_fix: Port LossTab's non-finite test to LossChart: render with a loss_history containing `eval_rmse: Number.NaN` and `train_rmse: Number.POSITIVE_INFINITY` and assert no path `d` attribute matches /NaN|Infinity/. Fix LossChart.makePath to skip non-finite points (`isFiniteNumber(e[key])`) consistent with LossTab.

tests.title: FeatureImportance bar-width tests never use a negative or zero first importance, so the maxVal = items[0].importance bug (V090) is uncovered
tests.description: Verified bug V090: `maxVal = items[0]?.importance || 1` (FeatureImportance.tsx:28) assumes the first item holds the maximum importance and is positive. Bar width is `(Math.abs(fi.importance)/Math.abs(maxVal))*100%`. For SHAP/permutation importances that can be negative or zero, or any list not sorted descending by magnitude, this denominator is wrong: bars overflow past 100% (when a later |importance| exceeds |items[0]|) or divide by an effectively wrong base. The test 'shows max 10 features' constructs importances `15 - i` (strictly positive, descending), so items[0] always equals the true max — the one arrangement that hides the bug. No test uses a negative importance, a zero first importance, or an unsorted list. The tests assert feature names render but never assert any computed bar width, so the value logic is entirely unverified.
tests.evidence: FeatureImportance.tsx:28 `const maxVal = items[0]?.importance || 1`; width at line 60. Test fixture line 78-81 uses `importance: 15 - i` (always positive descending). No assertion on the rendered `width` style anywhere. Catalog: V090 verified code-trace.
tests.recommended_fix: Add a test with importances like `[{feature:'a',importance:2},{feature:'b',importance:-9}]` and assert that the rendered bar widths are clamped to <=100% / scaled by the max magnitude (b should be the full-width bar, a ~22%). After fixing maxVal to `Math.max(...items.map(i=>Math.abs(i.importance)))`, this pins V090. Also add a zero-first-value case to exercise the `|| 1` fallback path intentionally.

tests.title: removeFactor test only asserts terms is updated, never that orphaned interaction references are cleaned, hiding V064
tests.description: Verified bug V064: `removeFactor()` (GLMFactorConfig.tsx:134-137) deletes a column from `terms` only, never from `interactions`. Any interaction row referencing the removed factor is left dangling, the dropdown then shows a value not in its option list, and the stale name is persisted and sent to the backend where it flips `include_main` semantics. The test 'clicking remove on a factor removes it from terms' asserts only the `terms` onUpdate payload. There is no test that adds an interaction referencing a factor and then removes that factor while asserting the interaction is pruned (or the stale reference cleared). The incomplete assertion makes the buggy partial-removal behaviour look correct.
tests.evidence: Test asserts `expect(baseProps.onUpdate).toHaveBeenCalledWith("terms", {...})` only (lines 313-316); no interactions assertion. GLMFactorConfig.tsx:134-137 removeFactor mutates terms only. Catalog: V064 high-confidence executed-repro.
tests.recommended_fix: Add a test: render with `terms: {age, region}` and `interactions: [{factors:['age','region'], include_main:true}]`, click 'Remove age', and assert onUpdate is called for BOTH `terms` (age gone) AND `interactions` (the orphaned row removed or 'age' cleared). After fixing removeFactor to also prune interactions, this pins V064.

tests.title: Paired-key tests never clear a key to empty, so the independent left/right normalisation producing unequal-length arrays (V060) is uncovered
tests.description: Verified bug V060: `updatePairedKey` (EdgeJoinEditor.tsx:113-117) normalises `leftOn` and `rightOn` INDEPENDENTLY via `normalizeKeyRows`, which trims trailing empty entries. If a user clears one side of the only pair to '' while the other side is non-empty, `normalizeKeyRows(["a"]) === ["a"]` but `normalizeKeyRows([""]) === []`, persisting leftOn length 1 / rightOn length 0 — unequal-length arrays the backend rejects. The test 'updates paired key rows and can add another pair' only ever sets a key to a non-empty value ('region') and adds a pair; it never clears a key to empty, which is the exact trigger. The asymmetric-normalisation path is therefore untested.
tests.evidence: EdgeJoinEditor.tsx:116 `onUpdate({ on: [], leftOn: normalizeKeyRows(nextLeft), rightOn: normalizeKeyRows(nextRight) })` (independent trims); normalizeKeyRows trims trailing '' (lines 534+). Test only sets value 'region' (line 218) and adds a pair (line 225). Catalog: V060 high-confidence executed-repro.
tests.recommended_fix: Add a test: render with `leftOn:['policy_id'], rightOn:['lookup_policy_id']`, change 'Join key 1' (right side) to '' and assert the persisted onUpdate keeps leftOn and rightOn the SAME length (either both length 1 with '' preserved, or both trimmed together). After fixing updatePairedKey to normalise the pair atomically (trim a row only when BOTH sides are empty), this pins V060.

tests.title: useMlflowBrowser tests never simulate out-of-order async resolution, so the stale-response race (V082) is uncovered
tests.description: Verified bug V082: out-of-order getRuns/getModelVersions resolutions can overwrite current data (refreshRuns/refreshVersions have no request-sequence/staleness guard). The hook tests mock the API with `mockResolvedValue` (resolves immediately, in call order) and only assert call counts and final arrays for sequential, in-order resolutions. None of the tests make an earlier call resolve AFTER a later call (e.g. a slow exp-1 fetch resolving after a fast exp-2 fetch) to prove the newer result is not clobbered. So the race condition is not pinned.
tests.evidence: Tests use `mockGetRuns.mockResolvedValue(fakeRuns)` and assert `runs` equals the single fixture; no deferred-promise ordering test. Catalog: V082 high-confidence code-trace, `useMlflowBrowser.ts:112-121,133-144`.
tests.recommended_fix: Add a test using deferred promises: trigger refreshRuns('exp-1') (slow), then refreshRuns('exp-2') (fast), resolve exp-2 then exp-1, and assert `runs` reflects exp-2 (the latest request) — failing today, passing after a request-id/AbortController guard. Same shape for refreshVersions.

types.severity: high - removes the entire class of typo/drift bugs between the lifecycle layer and the wire contract, and lets the type checker prove every terminal_reason on the wire is a member of the closed set the UI branches on
types.title: terminal_reason is a free `str | None` on the wire although a canonical `TerminalReason` Literal already exists internally
types.description: `terminal_reason: str | None` appears on five status/metrics response models. The codebase ALREADY defines the closed vocabulary as `TerminalReason = Literal['completed','superseded','timed_out','cancelled','memory_limited','contract_error','error']` in src/haute/routes/_job_lifecycle.py:24-32, with a `TERMINAL_REASON_TO_STATUS` mapping (line 34) and a precedence table (line 48) keyed on exactly those literals. Producers set these values from that closed set (e.g. _optimiser_service.py:329 `terminal_reason='memory_limited'`, :2855 `'contract_error'`; _worker_isolation.py:107/131/142). Because the wire field is `str`, the contract does not express the invariant `terminal_reason in TERMINAL_REASON_TO_STATUS`; a producer or test that emits a misspelled reason (e.g. 'memory_limit' vs 'memory_limited') type-checks and serialises fine, and the frontend silently falls through its switch. The `JobStatus` field on these same models IS a Literal, so the asymmetry is striking: status is closed but the reason that DERIVES the status is open.
types.recommended_design: Move `TerminalReason` (the Literal) into schemas.py (or import it there so it is the single source of truth shared with _job_lifecycle.py), and change every `terminal_reason: str | None` to `terminal_reason: TerminalReason | None`. Then `JobStatus` can be derived as `JobStatus = Literal['running'] | TerminalReason`-equivalent (see separate finding) so the two sets can never drift. This makes the lifecycle layer's `TERMINAL_REASON_TO_STATUS` mapping total-by-construction over the wire type.

types.severity: high - eliminates a hand-maintained duplicate-literal-set that must be kept in sync across two modules; a divergence today is only caught (if at all) by runtime KeyError, not by the type system
types.title: JobStatus and TerminalReason are two independently-authored literal sets that must agree by hand
types.description: schemas.py defines `JobStatus = Literal['running','completed','error','cancelled','superseded','timed_out','memory_limited','contract_error']` (8 members). _job_lifecycle.py independently defines `TerminalReason` (7 members) and derives `JOB_STATUSES = frozenset({RUNNING_STATUS, *TERMINAL_STATUSES})` (line 45) plus a per-status string constant for each (lines 15-22). The intended invariant is exactly `JobStatus == {'running'} ∪ TerminalReason`, but nothing enforces it: the two literal lists are typed out by hand in different files. If someone adds a new terminal reason (say 'evicted') to TerminalReason and the mapping, `JobStatus` will not include it, so `ExploreStatusResponse(status='evicted')` raises a Pydantic validation error at the boundary that the type checker could not foresee — and conversely a value added only to JobStatus is unreachable. `_job_lifecycle.py:13` already imports `JobStatus` from schemas, so the dependency edge exists; the relationship is just not expressed structurally.
types.recommended_design: Express the union at the type level so it cannot drift: define `TerminalReason` once (the canonical 7-member Literal), then `JobStatus = Literal['running'] | TerminalReason` using `typing.Literal` composition (or `TerminalReason` plus an explicit `RunningStatus = Literal['running']` and `JobStatus = RunningStatus | TerminalReason`). Keep both in schemas.py and import into _job_lifecycle.py. Add a one-line static assertion test `set(get_args(JobStatus)) == {'running'} | set(get_args(TerminalReason))` so any future edit to one is forced to update the other.

types.severity: medium - NodeResult.status is consumed by `== 'error'` / `== 'ok'` comparisons in at least four modules; an enum/Literal makes those comparisons exhaustively checkable and prevents a producer from emitting an out-of-band status
types.title: NodeResult.status is a free `str` though it is a closed two-value set consumed by equality checks
types.description: `NodeResult.status: str` (a required field, no default). Every producer sets it to exactly 'ok' or 'error' (executor.py:1168/1190/1200/1228), and consumers branch on those exact strings: executor.py:1249 `r.status == 'error'`, cli/_run.py:63 `res.status == 'ok'`, _scaffold.py:1213 `res.status != 'ok'`, routes/pipeline.py:608 builds `node_statuses` from `r.status`. Because the field is `str`, a refactor that introduced a third state ('skipped', 'partial') or a typo ('erro') would compile and serialise, and the downstream `== 'error'` checks would silently treat it as success. This is the same closed-set pattern the file already models correctly elsewhere with Literal (e.g. ExploreRunResponse.status, TrainResponse.status).
types.recommended_design: Introduce `NodeStatus = Literal['ok', 'error']` and type `NodeResult.status: NodeStatus`. Update `PreviewNodeResponse.node_statuses: dict[str, str]` (line 284) to `dict[str, NodeStatus]` so the per-node status map is equally closed. The equality-check sites then become statically exhaustive (mypy can flag a missed branch via assert_never).

types.severity: medium - small closed set ('missing'|'stale') produced in exactly two places; a Literal makes the two-value contract explicit and lets the UI switch be checked
types.title: SchemaWarning.status is a free `str` for a two-value enum ('missing' | 'stale')
types.description: `SchemaWarning.status: str`. The only producers are executor.py:1124 `SchemaWarning(column=c, status='missing')` and executor.py:1160 `status='stale'`. The field name `status` overloaded as a *warning kind* is itself slightly misleading, but the concrete defect is that the closed set {'missing','stale'} is typed as open `str`. The frontend renders different affordances per kind; an unmodelled third value would render as nothing. Contrast `ExploreDataQualityIssue.severity: Literal['warning','danger']` (line 429) in the same file, which models its closed kind correctly.
types.recommended_design: Introduce `SchemaWarningKind = Literal['missing', 'stale']` and type `SchemaWarning.status: SchemaWarningKind` (consider renaming the field to `kind` in a coordinated frontend change, but the Literal is the load-bearing fix). NodeResult.schema_warnings and the three node_schema_warnings maps then carry the closed kind automatically.

types.severity: medium - three adjacent closed-set fields modelled as open str; makes the diagnostic contract self-describing and lets the UI exhaustively branch on code/severity
types.title: TraceCorrelationDiagnosticResponse.code / severity / match_strategy are free `str` for closed sets
types.description: Three fields on this diagnostic model are stringly-typed: `code: str`, `severity: str`, `match_strategy: str`. The producer (_trace_correlation.py:211-223) emits a single fixed `code='ambiguous_row_match'` and `severity='warning'`; `match_strategy` is sourced from _trace_correlation.py:308 `'relaxed'` / :363 `'exact'`. So in practice code∈{'ambiguous_row_match'}, severity∈{'warning','danger'} (the file's own ExploreDataQualityIssue uses exactly that severity pair), and match_strategy∈{'relaxed','exact'}. As written, the wire contract cannot tell a client which codes exist, and a typo'd severity would defeat any UI colour-coding silently. The sibling severity field elsewhere in the same file is already a Literal, so this is an internal inconsistency.
types.recommended_design: Add `TraceDiagnosticCode = Literal['ambiguous_row_match']` (extend as new diagnostics appear), reuse a shared `DiagnosticSeverity = Literal['warning','danger']` (factor it out of ExploreDataQualityIssue so both share one definition), and `MatchStrategy = Literal['exact','relaxed']`. Type the three fields accordingly. Also reuse `MatchStrategy` for any other match_strategy field.

types.severity: medium - 'online'|'ratebook' is a pervasively-branched closed set; a Literal prevents an unmodelled mode from flowing to the apply/score path
types.title: OptimiserSolveResult.mode is `str | None` for the closed 'online' | 'ratebook' set
types.description: `OptimiserSolveResult.mode: str | None`. Across the optimiser/builders code, `mode` is exhaustively branched as the two-value set 'online'|'ratebook': _builders.py:1383 `!= 'ratebook'`, projection.py:696 `== 'ratebook'`, _optimiser_service.py:552/2351('online')/2501('ratebook'), optimiser.py:1571 `== 'ratebook'`. The default is always 'online'. Modelling this as open `str | None` on the wire means a serialised result could carry an unmodelled mode and the consuming ratebook/online branches would silently take the else-path. The optional `None` additionally overlaps semantically with the 'online' default — two representations of effectively the same state (mild illegal-states smell).
types.recommended_design: Introduce `OptimiserMode = Literal['online', 'ratebook']` and type `mode: OptimiserMode | None` (or, if a mode is always known by the time a result exists, make it required `OptimiserMode` and drop the None to collapse the redundant null/'online' duplication). Reuse the same `OptimiserMode` alias anywhere the optimiser config mode is surfaced.

types.severity: medium - 8-value documented closed set typed as open str; additionally the channel is overloaded to carry error strings, mixing a value-enum with an error message
types.title: row_lineage_type is `str | None` for a documented 8-value closed set, and the same field doubles as an error-message carrier
types.description: `TraceStepResponse.row_lineage_type: str | None`. The producer `detect_row_lineage_type` (_trace_enrichment.py:870) documents and returns exactly one of {'created','selected','filtered','aggregated','joined','expanded','sorted','passthrough'} (return type annotated merely `str`). Two defects: (a) stringly-typed — the closed lineage vocabulary is not on the type; the trace UI keys colour/iconography on these strings and an unmodelled value renders blank. (b) illegal-states overloading — _trace_enrichment.py:1815 assigns `step.row_lineage_type = f'error: row lineage detection failed: {exc}'`, so the SAME field that is supposed to hold a member of the enum can instead hold a free-form error string. A consumer cannot distinguish 'a lineage value' from 'an error sentinel' except by string-prefix sniffing 'error:'.
types.recommended_design: Define `RowLineageType = Literal['created','selected','filtered','aggregated','joined','expanded','sorted','passthrough']`, annotate both `detect_row_lineage_type` -> RowLineageType and the field `row_lineage_type: RowLineageType | None`. Carry the detection failure in a separate optional field (e.g. `row_lineage_error: str | None`) rather than poisoning the enum field, so 'value' and 'error' become unrepresentable simultaneously in the wrong slot.

types.severity: medium - closed 3-value set documented in inline comments in 3+ files but never typed; consumers compare with `== 'holdout'`
types.title: diagnostics_set is a free `str` whose closed set ('train'|'validation'|'holdout') is only documented in comments
types.description: `TrainResponse.diagnostics_set: str = 'validation'` with an inline comment `# 'train' | 'validation' | 'holdout'`. The identical comment-documented-but-untyped pattern repeats at modelling/_result_types.py:30 and modelling/_training_job.py:181 & :249. Producers assign from a closed set (_training_job.py:1117 'holdout', :1120 'validation', :1123 'train') and consumers branch on it: _model_card.py:111 `diag.diagnostics_set != 'holdout'`. The three legal values are effectively an enum; encoding them as `str` lets a typo flow to the model card and silently change which header/metrics block renders.
types.recommended_design: Define `DiagnosticsSet = Literal['train', 'validation', 'holdout']` once and use it for the wire field and for the internal dataclasses in modelling/_result_types.py and _training_job.py (replacing the three duplicated explanatory comments with the type). The `!= 'holdout'` comparison then becomes statically meaningful.

types.severity: low - closed 4-value set produced by one module; a Literal documents the policy taxonomy and prevents drift
types.title: budget_policy is a free `str` for the closed set {'fixed_default','explicit_env','adaptive_local'}
types.description: `ExecutionAdmissionPayload.budget_policy: str = 'fixed_default'` and `ExecutionMemoryPressureEventPayload.budget_policy: str | None = None`. The producer enumerates the closed taxonomy in _execution_admission.py: 'explicit_env' (line 310), 'adaptive_local' (line 324), 'fixed_default' (line 334), and the dataclass default 'fixed_default' (line 220). These are the only values that ever occur. Modelling as `str` means the policy vocabulary is invisible in the contract and a new policy could be emitted without the schema (or any dashboard parsing it) being updated.
types.recommended_design: Define `BudgetPolicy = Literal['fixed_default', 'explicit_env', 'adaptive_local']` and use it for both payload fields and the internal _execution_admission dataclass field (budget_policy at lines 220/229). The two wire models then share one source of truth with the producer.

types.severity: medium - a 0..1 fraction with no bound permits NaN/inf/negative/>1 values to cross the wire and reach progress bars; a constrained float makes the invariant unrepresentable-if-violated and is consistent with the file's own bounded-int fields
types.title: progress is an unconstrained `float` despite being a 0.0..1.0 fraction
types.description: Four status models declare `progress: float = 0.0`. Producers feed it fractional values (e.g. _explore_service.py:773 `progress=0.1`, :792 `progress=0.85`) and the UI renders it as a 0..100% bar. There is no `ge=0, le=1` constraint, so a buggy producer (or a job-store dict that was never coerced — values come via `job.get('progress', 0.0)` at modelling.py:111, optimiser.py:1230, etc.) can emit a negative, >1, NaN, or inf progress and Pydantic will happily serialise it, overflowing or NaN-poisoning the progress bar. The file already constrains other bounded numerics (PreviewNodeRequest.row_limit `ge=1, le=10000`, StreamingChunkSize `ge=1`, OptimiserFrontierRequest.n_points_per_dim `ge=1, le=100`), so leaving the progress fraction unbounded is an inconsistency.
types.recommended_design: Define a shared `Progress = Annotated[float, Field(ge=0.0, le=1.0, allow_inf_nan=False)]` and use it for all four progress fields (and `OptimiserHistoryEntry`/other 0..1 ratio fields where applicable). This makes an out-of-range progress unrepresentable on the wire and forces producers to clamp at the source.

types.severity: medium - the response-side range model permits min>max and NaN/inf bounds even though the request side rigorously rejects them via the shared _normalise_frontier_range_pair; the invariant is enforced on input but not on the value's own type
types.title: OptimiserFrontierRange allows min > max and non-finite bounds (the request path validates this, the response model does not)
types.description: `OptimiserFrontierRange` is `{min: float, max: float}` with no validator. The request side enforces the full invariant (finite, min<=max) via `_normalise_frontier_range_pair` (schemas.py:45-69) wired into `OptimiserFrontierRequest._validate_threshold_ranges`. But the response/auto-range model `OptimiserFrontierRange` re-declares the same min/max pair WITHOUT any guard, and is constructed directly from a producer dict (_optimiser_service.py:3542 `OptimiserFrontierRange(min=value['min'], max=value['max'])`, :3833 likewise) that is not routed through the canonical validator. So a degenerate or inverted range (min>max, or NaN bounds) is representable in the response and flows to the frontier UI, which assumes a well-ordered finite interval. The ordering invariant is a property of the *value*, so it belongs on the type, not only on one entry path.
types.recommended_design: Attach a `@model_validator(mode='after')` to OptimiserFrontierRange that calls the existing `_normalise_frontier_range_pair((min,max), field='range')` (reusing the single source of truth) to assert finiteness and min<=max — making an ill-formed range unconstructable regardless of which path builds it. Optionally encode bounds as `Annotated[float, Field(allow_inf_nan=False)]` to cover the finiteness half at the field level.

types.severity: low - small closed set ('parquet'|'csv') the codegen already hardcodes; a Literal documents the supported sink formats
types.title: SinkResponse.format is a free `str` defaulting to 'parquet' for a known closed set
types.description: `SinkResponse.format: str = 'parquet'`. The sink codegen only ever emits two formats — _codegen_builders.py:372 `format='parquet'` and :382 `format='csv'` — and executor.py:1566/1589 logs/sets the format from that same closed choice. The wire field being open `str` hides the supported-format set from clients and would let an unsupported format value be reported without any type-level signal.
types.recommended_design: Define `SinkFormat = Literal['parquet', 'csv']` and type `SinkResponse.format: SinkFormat`. Reuse the alias at the codegen/executor sink sites so the supported-format list has one definition.

types.location: src/haute/schemas.py:86-94 (SavePipelineRequest.sources:93, active_source:94, source default at PreviewNodeRequest.source:256 etc.)
types.type_name: SavePipelineRequest (sources / active_source) and the pervasive `source` field
types.severity: low - the active_source ∈ sources invariant is left unchecked; an inconsistent pair (active_source not in sources) is representable and would later fail deep in execution rather than at the boundary
types.title: SavePipelineRequest.active_source is not constrained to be a member of sources (cross-field invariant unmodelled)
types.description: `SavePipelineRequest` has `sources: list[str] = ['live']` and `active_source: str = 'live'` as two independent fields. The implicit invariant is `active_source in sources`, but nothing enforces it, so a payload with `sources=['live','prod']` and `active_source='staging'` is accepted and only fails (if at all) later when execution tries to resolve the active source. More broadly, `source` is a free `str` defaulting to 'live' on ~10 request models (PreviewNodeRequest:256, TraceRequest:305, SinkRequest:371, ExploreRunRequest:468, TrainRequest:822, OptimiserEstimateRequest:1021, ...); the set of valid sources is dynamic so a Literal is not appropriate, but the cross-field membership invariant for the save request is checkable at the boundary.
types.recommended_design: Add a `@model_validator(mode='after')` on SavePipelineRequest asserting `active_source in sources` (and `sources` non-empty), turning an inconsistent source selection into a 422 at the contract boundary instead of a deferred runtime failure. Consider a `SourceName = NewType('SourceName', str)` alias to document the otherwise-bare `source` strings, even though their domain stays open.

types.location: src/haute/_api_input_schema.py:107-142 (ColumnV2, TableV2, ApiInputV2Config TypedDicts) consumed by validate_v2_schema at :263-403
types.severity: medium - the entire v2 schema contract is a `total=False` TypedDict whose every invariant (required label/path/name, allowed type, unique labels, levels-non-empty, row_id membership) is re-checked by hand in a 140-line imperative validator; required-ness and the ColumnType/ColumnStatus enums are declared on the TypedDict but the all-optional shape means the type system proves none of them
types.title: v2 schema is an all-optional TypedDict with every invariant enforced by a hand-written validator instead of the type
types.description: `ColumnV2`, `TableV2`, and `ApiInputV2Config` are `TypedDict(total=False)`, so EVERY field is optional at the type level — `name`, `path`, `label`, `type`, `status` all included. The real contract (validate_v2_schema, lines 263-403) requires `label` (non-empty str), `path` (parseable), each column's `name` (non-empty, unique) and `path` (under table path) and `type` ∈ allowed set, plus `levels` non-empty-if-present and `row_id_column` membership. None of these are expressed by the TypedDict: a `ColumnV2` literal missing `name`/`type`, or with `type='date'` mistyped, type-checks fine; the 140 lines of `isinstance(...)` / `not ... or ...` re-assert at runtime what a stricter model could guarantee. Note the field-level enums ARE declared (`type: ColumnType`, `status: ColumnStatus` at lines 110/111, with ColumnType/ColumnStatus Literals at 64-65) — good — but `total=False` makes them non-binding, and the `_ALLOWED_COLUMN_TYPES` frozenset (line 67) duplicates `ColumnType`'s members as a parallel runtime constant that must be kept in sync by hand.
types.recommended_design: Promote the v2 schema to a Pydantic model hierarchy (ColumnV2Model, TableV2Model, ApiInputV2ConfigModel) with required fields required (`name: str`, `path: str`, `label: str`, `type: ColumnType`, `status: ColumnStatus`), field validators for the path-shape checks (parse_table_path/parse_column_path), and model validators for the cross-field invariants (unique labels, sanitised-label collision/B2, unique column names, levels-non-empty, row_id_column ∈ column names). Derive `_ALLOWED_COLUMN_TYPES` from `get_args(ColumnType)` instead of duplicating the literal set. This collapses the imperative validator into declarative constraints and makes an invalid schema largely unconstructable; keep ApiInputSchemaError only for the genuinely cross-table checks Pydantic can't express, raised from a model_validator.

types.location: src/haute/schemas.py:680-695 (JsonCacheBuildResponse: row_count:683, column_count:684, size_bytes:686, skipped_records:694) and the many `*_bytes`/`*_count`/`row_count` ints across the file
types.type_name: JsonCacheBuildResponse and peer payloads (count/byte integer fields)
types.severity: low - dozens of non-negative quantities (row_count, column_count, *_bytes, *_count, skipped_records) are unconstrained ints; a negative value is representable and meaningless, though producers are unlikely to emit one
types.title: Non-negative count/byte integer fields are unconstrained `int` (negatives representable)
types.description: Quantity fields that are physically non-negative are typed as bare `int`, e.g. JsonCacheBuildResponse.row_count/column_count/size_bytes/cached_at and skipped_records (694), NodeResult.row_count/column_count/memory_bytes, FetchTableResponse.row_count/column_count/size_bytes, and the ExecutionMetricsPayload rss_*_bytes family. None carry `ge=0`. A negative row_count or size_bytes is a nonsense state that the contract nonetheless permits; it would silently propagate to UI summations and percentage math. This is the same omission class as the unbounded `progress` finding but lower severity because producers derive these from len()/os.stat and are unlikely to go negative — still, the type does not encode the invariant.
types.recommended_design: Introduce `NonNegativeInt = Annotated[int, Field(ge=0)]` (or use pydantic's `NonNegativeInt`) and apply it to the count/byte/row fields across the response models. This is a mechanical, low-risk tightening that makes negative quantities unrepresentable and documents the domain. Apply the same to the few non-negative floats (elapsed_ms, size in seconds) via `Field(ge=0)`.

types.severity: low - clustered booleans (is_main/is_read_only; is_yours/is_current/is_archived) admit contradictory combinations the domain forbids; modest bug-surface, mainly a clarity/illegal-state observation
types.title: Git status/branch boolean clusters permit contradictory flag combinations
types.description: GitStatusResponse carries `is_main: bool` and `is_read_only: bool` as independent flags; GitBranchItem carries `is_yours/is_current/is_archived` as three independent bools. Some combinations are domain-contradictions (e.g. a branch that is both `is_current=True` and `is_archived=True`, or main-detection flags that disagree with the branch name). Independent booleans make those illegal combinations representable. This is a milder instance of the boolean-blindness anti-pattern; the read-only/main relationship in particular is a derived fact, not two free inputs.
types.recommended_design: Where a cluster is mutually exclusive, model it as a single Literal/enum (e.g. branch lifecycle `Literal['active','archived']` instead of `is_archived`, and `is_current` derived against the response's `current` field rather than stored). For is_read_only as a function of is_main, consider computing it via a `@computed_field` so the relationship can't be set inconsistently. Lower priority than the status/enum findings but removes a representable-contradiction class.

types.severity: high
types.title: PipelineGraph permits a nodes list with duplicate ids; node_map silently collapses them (uniqueness is not a type invariant)
types.description: PipelineGraph.nodes is a plain `list[GraphNode]` with no model_validator enforcing id-uniqueness. The canonical `node_map` is built as `{n.id: n for n in self.nodes}` (line 700), which silently drops all but the last node sharing an id, and `parents_of`/topo/cache-key code all assume `node_map` is a total bijection over `nodes`. So a `PipelineGraph` where two GraphNodes share an id is a representable-but-illegal state: every id-keyed lookup (executor node_map, projection, fingerprint, deploy) operates on a different node-set than `len(graph.nodes)` implies. The existing finding `duplicate-func-name-node-collapse` (review/02-findings/findings.json:900) documents the PARSER symptom and proposes a parser-layer guard; this is the distinct TYPE-LEVEL root cause: the canonical graph type itself accepts the collision, so any producer (parser, submodel merge, route edits, programmatic construction) can reintroduce it. Promoting uniqueness to a constructor invariant makes node_map total-by-construction and closes the class, not one instance.
types.recommended_design: Add a Pydantic `@model_validator(mode="after")` on PipelineGraph that raises if `len({n.id for n in self.nodes}) != len(self.nodes)`, naming the duplicate ids. This makes the collapse unconstructable and lets node_map/parents_of/fingerprint code rely on `nodes` and `node_map` having identical cardinality. (Independently, the parser should be fixed per the existing behavioral finding; the type invariant is the backstop guaranteeing no other code path can recreate it.)
types.recommended_severity_rationale: Removes an entire class of silent node-loss across executor, codegen, projection and deploy — any path that mutates the node list is currently unguarded.

types.severity: high
types.title: active_source not constrained to be a member of sources on PipelineGraph, though the identical invariant IS enforced on SidecarModel
types.description: PipelineGraph declares `sources: list[str] = ["live"]` and `active_source: str = "live"` with no validator tying them together, so `PipelineGraph(sources=["live"], active_source="test")` is constructible. The SAME pair of fields on SidecarModel (routes/_helpers.py:62) carries a `@model_validator` `_active_source_must_be_in_sources` that raises when `active_source not in sources`. The canonical graph type — which is what codegen (codegen.py:954/1090/1252), the dataframe cache (_dataframe_execution_cache.py:230-231) and the save path (_save_pipeline.py:866-867) actually read — has no such guard, and _save_pipeline assigns both fields by raw mutation (`graph.sources = ...; graph.active_source = ...`) with no re-validation. The invariant exists in the system but is encoded on the wrong (peripheral) type, leaving the source-of-truth type able to hold a selection that points at a non-existent source.
types.recommended_design: Lift the `active_source in sources` check onto PipelineGraph as a `@model_validator(mode="after")` (the SidecarModel one can then delegate or be deduplicated). Pair with `validate_assignment=True` (see encapsulation finding) so the `_save_pipeline` raw assignments are re-checked. Consider modelling `sources` as a value object guaranteeing `"live"` is always present and first, since multiple call sites special-case that (routes/_helpers.py:689-696).
types.recommended_severity_rationale: An out-of-range active_source silently routes execution/codegen down a non-existent branch; encoding it on the canonical type closes the gap the sidecar guard only half-covers.

types.severity: high
types.title: Graph models are mutable with no validate_assignment; in-place mutation silently desynchronises PipelineGraph's cached node_map/parents_of/fingerprint
types.description: None of NodeData, GraphNode, GraphEdge, or PipelineGraph set `frozen=True` or `validate_assignment=True` (the only model_config anywhere is `ignored_types=(cached_property,)` on PipelineGraph, line 645). PipelineGraph went to real trouble to invalidate `node_map`/`parents_of`/`_haute_base_fingerprint` on the COPY path by overriding `model_copy` (lines 673-695) — but that protection is defeated by ANY in-place mutation: `graph.nodes.append(node)`, `graph.edges.pop()`, or `graph.nodes[0].id = "x"` mutates structure while the three @cached_property memos keep serving stale values (the cache is only cleared on copy, never on mutate).
