Because the fields are public and mutable, the carefully-built immutable-copy idiom is advisory, not enforced — a caller who mutates instead of `model_copy(update=...)` gets a silently incoherent graph (wrong parents, stale fingerprint -> wrong cache hits). `_save_pipeline.py:866-867` already mutates `graph.sources`/`active_source` in place, demonstrating the pattern is used in production code.
types.recommended_design: Make the graph models immutable: `model_config = ConfigDict(frozen=True)` on GraphNode/NodeData/GraphEdge and add `frozen=True` to PipelineGraph (it already overrides model_copy as the evolution path, so frozen is the natural completion). If full immutability is too invasive for current callers, minimally set `validate_assignment=True` AND change the cached_property memos to be derived only through the copy path (or expose `nodes`/`edges` as read-only tuples). Convert the remaining in-place mutators (e.g. _save_pipeline source assignment) to `model_copy(update=...)`. This makes 'mutate without cache invalidation' unrepresentable.
types.recommended_severity_rationale: Stale node_map/parents_of/fingerprint produce wrong wiring and wrong cache hits with no error — exactly the silent-wrongness class the model_copy override was written to prevent, left open on the mutation path.

types.location: src/haute/_types.py:593-608 (NodeData.config) and the per-type *Config TypedDicts at 84-405
types.severity: medium
types.title: NodeData has an untyped `config: dict[str, Any]` even though a full discriminated union (nodeType -> per-type Config TypedDict) is defined in the same module
types.description: _types.py defines ~20 precise TypedDicts (ApiInputConfig, ModelScoreConfig, RatingStepConfig, OptimiserConfig, ...) AND a NodeType StrEnum, yet NodeData stores `config: dict[str, Any]` with zero linkage to nodeType. The relationship 'nodeType=MODEL_SCORE => config conforms to ModelScoreConfig' exists only as prose docstrings and is re-checked ad hoc at runtime via `config.get(...)` everywhere (_builders.py:88-89, 466-467, 514-518; projection, codegen). Consequences: (a) wrong-shaped config for a node type is fully representable and only fails deep in a builder, often as a KeyError/None on a `.get` default rather than at the graph boundary; (b) the *_CONFIG_KEYS tuples (lines 149-160, 487-570) are a hand-maintained second source of truth for the same key sets, which can (and the codebase notes elsewhere they do) drift from the TypedDicts. The discriminated union that would make illegal nodeType/config pairings unrepresentable is 90% written but never wired into NodeData.
types.recommended_design: Model NodeData as a discriminated union keyed on nodeType, e.g. a `Annotated[Union[ApiInputNodeData, ModelScoreNodeData, ...], Field(discriminator="nodeType")]` where each variant pins its concrete config (the TypedDicts become Pydantic models or `config: ModelScoreConfig`). Where full migration is too large, at minimum add a `@model_validator` on NodeData that validates `config` against the TypedDict selected by `nodeType` (TypedDicts are runtime-introspectable), and derive the *_CONFIG_KEYS tuples from the TypedDict `__annotations__` so the two representations cannot diverge.
types.recommended_severity_rationale: Collapses 'config doesn't match node type' from a deep latent failure into a boundary-time type error and eliminates the duplicated CONFIG_KEYS drift surface; medium because most shapes are caught eventually by builders.

types.severity: medium
types.title: Contract permits inputs_by_parent to be set while inputs/outputs are None — an explicitly 'malformed' combination handled only at runtime
types.description: Contract is `(inputs: frozenset|None, outputs: frozenset|None, inputs_by_parent: Mapping|None)`. Nothing in the dataclass or `from_user_declared` prevents `Contract(inputs=None, outputs=None, inputs_by_parent={'p': {...}})`. projection.py:1414-1417 documents this exact state as a 'malformed fan-in declaration' (a node declaring per-parent ownership without the concrete inputs/outputs needed to apportion it) and handles it defensively at projection time. So a known-invalid contract shape is constructible and is policed by scattered runtime logic rather than the type. Additionally `from_user_declared` is a 6-branch normaliser accepting Contract | dict | str-'opaque' | 2-tuple | duck-typed object | None (lines 63-108) — flexible at the edge, but it means the only guarantee that a Contract is internally consistent is whatever each branch happens to assert.
types.recommended_design: Encode the dependency: add `__post_init__` (frozen dataclasses support it via object.__setattr__-free validation) raising when `inputs_by_parent is not None and (inputs is None or outputs is None)`. Better, model the two legitimate shapes as distinct types — e.g. `OpaqueContract` (no fields) vs `ConcreteContract(inputs: frozenset, outputs: frozenset, inputs_by_parent: Mapping[...] = {})` — and make `Contract = OpaqueContract | ConcreteContract`. Then 'per-parent ownership without concrete sides' is unrepresentable and projection.py's malformed-fan-in branch becomes dead code that can be deleted.
types.recommended_severity_rationale: Removes one inconsistent-contract class and lets a runtime guard be deleted; medium because the malformed state mostly originates from user declarations already partially validated.

types.location: src/haute/_contracts.py:20-32 (ColumnContract tuple alias) coexisting with Contract dataclass:35; conversions at 49-60
types.severity: low
types.title: Two parallel representations of a column contract (anonymous (set|None, set|None) tuple vs Contract dataclass) with lossy round-trips and reversed field order
types.description: The same concept is modelled twice: `ColumnContract = tuple[set[str]|None, set[str]|None]` (produced, referenced) and the `Contract` dataclass (inputs, outputs, inputs_by_parent). They use OPPOSITE field order — the tuple is (produced/outputs, referenced/inputs) while Contract is (inputs, outputs) — and `from_tuple`/`to_tuple` (lines 49-60) hand-swap them, a classic site for silent transposition bugs. The tuple form also cannot carry `inputs_by_parent`, so `to_tuple()` is lossy and every `projection_contract(node).to_tuple()` call site (projection.py:1286, 1376, 1625, 2281) drops fan-in ownership. The registry stores `column_contract: Callable[..., Any]` (registry.py:65) returning the bare tuple, forcing the lift at every read.
types.recommended_design: Make Contract the single representation and retire the public ColumnContract tuple to an internal codec only (or delete it). Have the registry's contract function return `Contract` directly. If a positional form must remain for back-compat, give it a NamedTuple with explicit `produced`/`referenced` fields so the order is self-documenting and the transpose risk disappears. Remove `to_tuple()` from hot projection paths so fan-in ownership is never silently dropped.
types.recommended_severity_rationale: Low direct bug surface but removes a transpose-prone dual representation and a lossy conversion used in the projection hot path.

types.severity: low
types.title: GraphNode carries a second, stringly-typed `type` field that is effectively always 'pipelineNode' and duplicates/obscures the real discriminant nodeType
types.description: GraphNode has `type: str = "pipelineNode"` (the React Flow node-renderer key) sitting next to the semantically meaningful `data.nodeType: NodeType`. The `type` field is an unconstrained `str` with a constant default; a grep of src shows it is never read for dispatch (no `node.type ==` comparisons in the backend) — all logic dispatches on `data.nodeType`. So the field is dead-weight from the backend's perspective yet fully mutable/arbitrary: `GraphNode(id=..., type="anything")` validates. This invites confusion ('which type field do I switch on?') and lets a wrong renderer key be persisted with no check.
types.recommended_design: If the React Flow wrapper key must round-trip, constrain it: `type: Literal["pipelineNode"] = "pipelineNode"` (or a small Literal-union if other renderer keys are legitimate) so arbitrary strings are rejected and intent is explicit. Document that `data.nodeType` is the sole semantic discriminant. If the backend never needs `type`, consider dropping it from the canonical model and re-deriving it at the serialization boundary.
types.recommended_severity_rationale: Low — primarily clarity and a tiny stringly-typed surface; the field is currently inert in the backend but is an attractive nuisance and an unvalidated persisted value.

types.location: src/haute/_types.py:602-605 (GraphNode.id) — and pervasive `str` node-id parameters across _graph_utils.py, _topo.py, _contracts.py
types.severity: low
types.title: Node ids are bare `str` throughout, interchangeable with labels, ports, source names and func-names with no type distinction
types.description: GraphNode.id is `str`, and every helper threads ids as `str`: build_parents_of, upstream_node_ids, ancestors/topo_sort_ids, Contract.inputs_by_parent keys, node_map keys, edge.source/target. In this module's vocabulary there are at least five distinct string roles — node id, sanitized func-name, port/handle name, source name ("live"/...), and human label — and they are all the same type, so passing a label where an id is expected (or an unsanitized id where a func-name is expected) type-checks. _config_io.py:174 ('Translate GUI node ids in config to ids produced by parsing') and the func-name-vs-id round-trip notes in _codegen_builders.py:1072 show these conversions are real and error-prone. A NewType wall would catch the swaps statically.
types.recommended_design: Introduce `NodeId = NewType("NodeId", str)` (and optionally `PortName`, `SourceName`, `FuncName`) and thread them through GraphNode.id, GraphEdge.source/target/handles, node_map, parents_of, Contract.inputs_by_parent keys, and the topo/ancestors helpers. NewType is zero-runtime-cost and would make 'passed a label/port where an id belongs' a type error. Adopt incrementally starting at the PipelineGraph public surface.
types.recommended_severity_rationale: Low/medium: no runtime change and large mechanical scope, but it statically eliminates a recurring id/label/port/func-name confusion that several existing comments and the duplicate-func-name bug all touch.

types.severity: low
types.title: position modelled as open dict[str, float] permitting missing/extra keys; readers defensively `.get('x')` and tolerate None
types.description: `position: dict[str, float]` with a default factory of `{"x": 0.0, "y": 0.0}` does not require the x/y keys nor forbid extras. routes/_helpers.py:788-789 reads it as `position.get("x")`/`position.get("y")` — i.e. the consumer assumes the keys may be absent and accepts `None`. So `GraphNode(id=..., position={})` or `{"x": 1.0}` or `{"x":1,"y":2,"z":3}` are all representable, and a half-populated position flows to downstream code as `(None, y)`. The invariant 'a position is exactly an (x, y) pair of floats' is structurally unenforced.
types.recommended_design: Replace the open dict with a closed model: `class Position(BaseModel): x: float = 0.0; y: float = 0.0` (extras forbidden via `model_config = ConfigDict(extra="forbid")`), and type `position: Position`. This makes both fields always-present floats, eliminates the `.get(...)/None` defensive reads, and rejects stray keys at the boundary.
types.recommended_severity_rationale: Low — UI metadata, not pricing-critical, but trivially fixable and removes a None-leak into layout code.

types.location: src/haute/_types.py:654 (PipelineGraph.submodels) and the `graph.submodels or {}` pattern at codegen.py:904, routes/submodel.py:155, _graph_shape.py:93, _save_pipeline.py:671
types.severity: low
types.title: submodels is `dict[str, Any] | None` where None and {} are semantically identical, and its value type is fully untyped
types.description: `submodels: dict[str, Any] | None = None` makes 'no submodels' representable two ways (None and {}), and indeed every reader normalises with `graph.submodels or {}` (codegen.py:904; routes/submodel.py:155; _graph_shape.py:93; _save_pipeline.py:671) — a tell that the Optional buys nothing but a recurring defensive idiom and a latent `None.items()`/`None[...]` hazard if a caller forgets it (routes/submodel.py:164 indexes `submodels[sm_name]` after the `or {}`). The value type `Any` also means the submodel metadata shape (file/childNodeIds/inputPorts/outputPorts — already captured by SubmodelConfig at line 584) is unenforced.
types.recommended_design: Drop the Optional: `submodels: dict[str, SubmodelMeta] = Field(default_factory=dict)` so 'none' has one representation and readers can delete the `or {}` guard. Promote the value type from `Any` to a concrete model (turn the existing SubmodelConfig TypedDict into a Pydantic model `SubmodelMeta`). This removes the None/{} ambiguity and types the metadata that codegen and submodel routes depend on.
types.recommended_severity_rationale: Low — mostly ergonomic and a small None-deref hazard; collapsing the dual empty-representation and typing the value is a clean, low-risk tightening.

types.severity: high — removes the single largest bug-surface class in this subsystem: every node type can carry any other type's keys, and every consumer must defensively re-validate shape at the point of use
types.title: NodeData.config is dict[str, Any] with no discriminated union tying nodeType to its config shape — the 18 per-type TypedDicts are documentation-only and never the actual field type
types.description: NodeData declares `nodeType: NodeType` and `config: dict[str, Any]` as two independent fields. The pairing (apiInput→ApiInputConfig, ratingStep→RatingStepConfig, …) is the central invariant of the whole graph model, yet it exists only as a runtime convention: `_TYPED_DICT_BY_NODE_TYPE` in _config_validation.py maps the two for a *warn-only* key check (warn_unrecognized_config_keys never raises) and a *runtime* write-allowlist (_prepare_config_for_sidecar logs and drops off-spec keys). Nothing at the type level prevents constructing `NodeData(nodeType=NodeType.RATING_STEP, config={'baseInput': 'x', 'how': 'cross'})` — an edgeJoin config attached to a ratingStep node. Every consumer in the surface compensates with `config.get(...)` + isinstance ladders (e.g. _rating_step_config._validate_factors re-checks `isinstance(factors, list)` and re-checks each element is a str; _edge_join._required_role re-checks `isinstance(value, str)`; _banding_config repeatedly re-checks `isinstance(factor, dict)`). Because the TypedDicts are never used as the declared type, mypy verifies none of the ~200 `config.get('key')` call sites against the per-type schema, so a typo'd key, a key read on the wrong node type, or a shape drift between writer and reader is invisible statically and only surfaces (if at all) as a runtime KeyError/ValueError or a silent default.
types.recommended_design: Promote the existing TypedDicts into a Pydantic discriminated union and make it the type of the config field. Either (a) give each per-type config a Pydantic model with `model_config = ConfigDict(extra='forbid')` and a literal `node_type` tag, then `NodeConfig = Annotated[ApiInputConfig | DataSourceConfig | …, Field(discriminator='node_type')]` and replace NodeData with a tagged union of `(NodeType, NodeConfig)` pairs; or (b) keep NodeData but type config as the union and add a `@model_validator(mode='after')` that asserts `type(self.config) is _MODEL_BY_NODE_TYPE[self.nodeType]`. Pydantic then rejects cross-type configs and unknown keys at construction/deserialisation (the wire boundary), `_prepare_config_for_sidecar`'s drop-allowlist and `warn_unrecognized_config_keys` collapse into the parse step, and every `config.get(...)` becomes attribute access type-checked against the correct schema. This makes 'wrong key on wrong node type' unrepresentable rather than warn-logged.
types.recommended_design_note: Well-designed already: NodeType (StrEnum, single source of truth shared with frontend) and the GraphEdge handle validator (rejects '' rather than coercing to None) are exemplary — the fix is to extend that same rigor from the edges to the node config payload.

types.location: src/haute/_types.py:111 DataSourceConfig.sourceType / :166 ModelScoreConfig.sourceType / :386 OptimiserApplyConfig.sourceType; compared as bare string literals in ~15 files (deploy/_bundler.py:75,89; deploy/_scorer.py:170,172,531; execution.py:158,448,542; _builders.py:544; routes/pipeline.py:138; cli/_helpers.py:230; etc.)
types.severity: high — a single mistyped literal ('registerd', 'flatfile') silently routes to the wrong loader/else-branch with no error; an enum makes every such typo a compile-time failure across all ~15 comparison sites
types.title: sourceType is a free `str` with three incompatible per-node-type domains, hand-compared against bare string literals in 15+ files instead of an enum
types.description: Three different node types each have a `sourceType: str` field whose legal values are documented only in trailing comments and differ per type: dataSource = {flat_file, databricks}; modelScore = {run, registered}; optimiserApply = {file, run, registered}. The value is built stringly (_config_builder.py:97 hardcodes `config['sourceType']='databricks'`, :104 `'flat_file'`) and consumed by ~15 sites that compare against bare literals (`== 'databricks'`, `== 'run'`, `== 'registered'`, `== 'file'`). There is no enum, no Literal union enforced at the type level, and no exhaustiveness: every consumer is an `if ==…: … elif ==…: … else:` ladder where the `else` silently means 'treat as flat_file' / 'don't load MLflow'. A typo'd literal in any one site, or a new sourceType added without updating a branch, produces silent mis-routing (e.g. a 'registered' model treated as live 'run'), which is exactly the class behind existing behavioral finding #65-family deploy/validate divergences. The frontend already hardcodes the matching literals in DataSourceEditor/ModelScoreEditor/OptimiserApplyEditor JS, so the contract is duplicated across the language boundary with no shared source of truth.
types.recommended_design: Define per-type StrEnums next to NodeType (e.g. `class DataSourceKind(StrEnum): FLAT_FILE='flat_file'; DATABRICKS='databricks'`, `class ModelSource(StrEnum): RUN='run'; REGISTERED='registered'`, `class OptimiserApplySource(StrEnum): FILE='file'; RUN='run'; REGISTERED='registered'`) — mirroring the existing SourceFormat/ExecutionProfile StrEnums already in the codebase. Type the TypedDict/Pydantic field as the enum (StrEnum still serialises to the same JSON string, so the wire format is unchanged and the frontend literals keep working). Then `match source: case ModelSource.RUN: … case ModelSource.REGISTERED: …` gives mypy exhaustiveness; an unhandled/new variant is a type error, and a typo'd literal is rejected at deserialisation. Validation moves once, to the boundary, instead of being re-encoded as ad-hoc string equality in every branch.

types.location: src/haute/_types.py:227 RatingStepConfig.operation / :219 RatingTable.onMissing; validated by frozenset membership at src/haute/_rating.py:290-291,403-415,475-483
types.severity: medium-high — converts three scattered runtime frozenset re-validations (_SUPPORTED_COMBINE_OPERATIONS, _SUPPORTED_ON_MISSING) into one type-level guarantee, and removes the `str(operation or 'multiply')` silent-default trap
types.title: Rating `operation`/`onMissing` are `str` re-validated against module-private frozensets at materialisation time, not enums — the legal domain lives in three places and the value is silently coerced
types.description: RatingStepConfig.operation and RatingTable.onMissing are declared `str` (legal values only in comments: operation = multiply|add|min|max, onMissing = error|neutral). The actual domain is enforced at runtime by _rating.py via `_SUPPORTED_COMBINE_OPERATIONS = frozenset({'multiply','add','min','max'})` and `_SUPPORTED_ON_MISSING = frozenset({'error','neutral'})`, checked in `_normalise_combine_operation` (line 475) and `_normalise_on_missing` (line 403). These two frozensets are the real source of truth, but they are private to _rating.py and invisible to the TypedDict, the config builder (_config_builder.py:165-179 builds `operation`/`combinedOutputs` with no validation and `str(op)`), and the sidecar codec. The combine path additionally does `str(operation or 'multiply')` — an empty/falsy operation is silently coerced to 'multiply' rather than rejected, so a config that lost its operation key prices as a product silently. Because the field is `str`, the builder, the codec, and the executor cannot agree statically that only four operations exist; a fifth operation added to the engine without touching _config_builder, or a misspelled 'mutiply' in a hand-edited sidecar, is caught (if at all) only deep inside `_combine_rating_columns` at materialisation, far from where the config was constructed.
types.recommended_design: Replace with StrEnums owned by the type module: `class RatingOperation(StrEnum): MULTIPLY='multiply'; ADD='add'; MIN='min'; MAX='max'` and `class RatingMissPolicy(StrEnum): ERROR='error'; NEUTRAL='neutral'`. Type operation/onMissing/combinedOutputs[].operation as these enums; delete the private frozensets in _rating.py and switch `_combine_rating_columns` to `match RatingOperation(operation)` for compiler-checked exhaustiveness (the neutral-element table becomes a total mapping keyed by the enum). Keep an explicit required default at the model layer (`operation: RatingOperation = RatingOperation.MULTIPLY`) instead of the `or 'multiply'` coercion, so a present-but-empty value is a validation error rather than a silent product.

types.recommended_design: (1) `class JoinHow(StrEnum): INNER; LEFT; RIGHT; FULL; SEMI; ANTI; CROSS` and type `how` as JoinHow; delete _ALLOWED_HOW and the line-160 recheck; switch narrow_join_parent_demand's `{'inner','left','semi','anti'}` to a JoinHow membership set. types.recommended_design_note: Well-designed already in this file: JoinKey = str | list[str] as an alias, and resolve_edge_join_role_indices's exhaustive base/join distinctness + connectivity checks are good defensive runtime validation — the gap is that none of it is reflected in the static config type.

types.severity: medium — closes a documented-vs-actual domain mismatch (TypedDict comment lists values that do not exist) and removes the silent `or 'continuous'` coercion that lets an unknown banding type masquerade as continuous until late
types.title: BandingFactor.banding is `str` whose documented domain ('continuous'|'discrete') contradicts the engine's real domain ('categorical'|'breakpoints'|'continuous'); the value is silently coerced and the rules shape depends on it untyped
types.description: BandingFactor.banding is declared `str` with the comment `# "continuous" | "discrete"` (_types.py:189). That comment is wrong: the engine never recognises 'discrete'; _banding_config branches only on 'categorical' and 'breakpoints' (_expand_rule_map lines 36/44, _compact_rule_map lines 105/115) with 'continuous' as the implicit fall-through, and the compaction gate is `_COMPACT_RULE_TYPES = frozenset({'categorical','breakpoints'})` (line 9). types.recommended_design: `class BandingKind(StrEnum): CONTINUOUS='continuous'; CATEGORICAL='categorical'; BREAKPOINTS='breakpoints'` and type `banding: BandingKind = BandingKind.CONTINUOUS`. Then make BandingFactor a discriminated union on BandingKind so each variant carries its correct rules shape: ContinuousFactor (rules absent), CategoricalFactor(rules: list[{value,assignment}] | dict[str,scalar]), BreakpointFactor(rules: list[{boundary,label}] | dict[str,scalar]). Replace the `or 'continuous'` coercion with enum validation so an unknown banding type is rejected at parse time; delete _COMPACT_RULE_TYPES (membership becomes `kind in {BandingKind.CATEGORICAL, BandingKind.BREAKPOINTS}`) and fix the docstring. This makes 'discrete' (and any other typo) unrepresentable and ties the rules-shape branch to a typed discriminator.

types.severity: medium — the entry type is a no-op placeholder so every invariant (factor keys present, single scalar value, value/outputColumn agreement, dual list-or-map shape) is enforced only by hand-rolled runtime walks; making the row shape a real type removes a recurring source of write/read asymmetry bugs
types.title: RatingTableEntry is an empty TypedDict and RatingTable.entries is list[dict[str,Any]], so the canonical-row invariant (exactly the table's factor keys + one scalar `value`) is entirely runtime-asserted and the compact-map alternative shape is untyped
types.description: RatingTableEntry (_types.py:202-205) has an empty body with only a comment ('Keys are dynamic factor names'), so it contributes nothing — it is `dict` with documentation. RatingTable.entries is `list[dict[str, Any]]`, but the field is bimodal: on disk it is a nested factor→value MAP (compact sidecar), and in memory it is a row-ARRAY (`{factor: key, …, 'value': scalar}`). The whole of _rating_step_config.py exists to convert and re-validate between these untyped shapes: _entry_value re-derives the single value and rejects the 'both value and outputColumn disagree' illegal state (line 129-138); _normalise_entry_rows re-asserts every factor key is present and non-null (line 161-163); _validate_rating_value re-checks scalar-ness/finiteness/non-bool at line 82-101; _expand_entries_map re-walks depth to match factor count. None of these invariants are expressible because the row type is `dict[str, Any]`. This is precisely the surface where the existing behavioral findings cluster (04-#63/#68 write/read key-normalisation asymmetry, 05 float-key divergence): an untyped dual-shape dict is the substrate that makes those asymmetries possible, because there is no single typed definition of 'a canonical rating row' that both the writer and reader must satisfy.
types.recommended_design: Model the two shapes explicitly. (1) Canonical in-memory row: a Pydantic model `RatingRow` with the factor columns and a single `value: float` (or a NewType `RatingValue` carrying the finite-non-bool invariant validated once), replacing list[dict[str,Any]]. (2) The compact sidecar map as its own recursive type `CompactEntries = dict[str, 'CompactEntries | RatingValue]` so the nesting-depth-equals-factor-count invariant is at least shape-checkable. Then expand/compact become typed total functions `CompactEntries -> list[RatingRow]` and the value/outputColumn agreement + factor-presence checks move into RatingRow's validator (one place, runtime-once at the boundary) instead of being re-litigated in _entry_value/_normalise_entry_rows/_expand_entries_map. Delete the empty RatingTableEntry. This gives the writer and reader a shared typed contract, which is the structural fix for the write/read asymmetry class.
types.recommended_design_note: Well-designed already: the canonical-key helper normalise_rating_key being shared by engine + sidecar + trace is the right single-source-of-truth instinct; the gap is that the row/table that holds those keys is not itself typed.

types.title: Control-flow markers ('_load_error', 'instanceOf') are smuggled as magic string keys inside the untyped config dict rather than typed fields on NodeData
types.description: The save/collect path keys behaviour off magic strings stored inside config: collect_node_configs skips a node when `config.get('instanceOf')` is truthy (line 342) or `config.get('_load_error')` is set (line 344); config_load_errors keys off the same `_load_error` marker (line 369). types.recommended_design_note: Well-designed already: the path-traversal guards in config_path_for_node/load_node_config (reject '..'/separators, assert is_relative_to config root) and the duplicate-key rejection in _load_json_object are strong boundary invariants worth preserving as-is.

types.location: src/haute/_registry.py:47-65 (NodeRegistryEntry); cross-cut with src/haute/_builders.py:464-1295 (every @_register'd _build_*) and src/haute/_codegen_builders.py:337-1117 (every _gen_*/template)
types.severity: high — this is the type-level root cause of the entire codegen<->executor equivalence cluster (catalog items 1,2,3): nothing in the registry encodes whether a NodeType is a pure passthrough or applies stateful logic, so the exec builder and the codegen builder independently (re)decide and silently disagree.
types.title: Passthrough-vs-stateful-apply is unencoded in NodeRegistryEntry; the two sides can disagree by construction
types.description: NodeRegistryEntry bundles `exec` and `codegen` as two free function pointers with NO shared declaration of the node's execution semantics. For banding/ratingStep/modelScore the exec builder applies a real operation AND the codegen template emits a call to the SAME `apply_*_from_config`/`score_from_config` helper — they agree only because two humans kept two code paths in sync. For optimiser/optimiserApply/modelling/scenarioExpander the exec builder applies an operation (e.g. _build_optimiser_apply -> optimiser_apply_fn loads the artifact and adds __optimiser_version__) while the codegen template emits `return {first}` (a pure passthrough). The registry type cannot tell these classes apart, so `validate_registry_complete` (which only checks both fields are non-None) reports the broken pair as healthy. The illegal state is: `entry.exec` is stateful but `entry.codegen` is passthrough (or vice-versa). It is representable, constructible, and currently constructed in production.
types.recommended_design: Make the dispatch SEMANTICS a field, not an implication. Add a `kind: NodeSemantics` (StrEnum: PASSTHROUGH | STATEFUL | SOURCE) to NodeRegistryEntry and require it at registration (`register_exec(node_type, *, kind=...)`). For STATEFUL nodes, require an `apply: ApplyFn` helper on the entry that BOTH the exec builder and the codegen-emitted body call (see separate finding). Extend `validate_registry_complete` to assert: PASSTHROUGH entries' codegen emits only `return {first}` AND exec returns `_passthrough_fn`; STATEFUL entries carry a non-None `apply` and their codegen body references it. This converts 'codegen forgot to embed the apply call' from a silent pricing divergence into an import-time RuntimeError.

types.location: src/haute/_registry.py:48-65 (NodeRegistryEntry has no `apply` slot); src/haute/_builders.py:824-834 (_build_rating_step calls _apply_rating_step_outputs) vs src/haute/_codegen_builders.py:360-369 (_RATING_STEP emits apply_rating_step_from_config); src/haute/_builders.py:999-1038 (optimiser_apply_fn -> _dispatch_apply) with NO codegen counterpart
types.severity: high — promotes the 'one apply helper shared between executor and codegen' rule from an unwritten convention (kept by discipline for 3 node types, violated for 4) to a constructor-enforced invariant.
types.title: The 'single shared apply helper per stateful node' invariant exists only by convention; it should be a required field on the entry
types.description: The codebase already KNOWS the correct pattern: stateful nodes route through a single `apply_*_from_config`/`score_from_config` helper that the executor calls directly and the generated standalone file calls via its body. But this is enforced nowhere — it is replicated by hand in banding/ratingStep/modelScore and simply omitted for optimiser/optimiserApply/modelling/scenarioExpander, which is exactly the bug surface. Because there is no `apply` field on NodeRegistryEntry, the registry cannot require 'a STATEFUL node MUST share one apply callable across both sides', so the equivalence is a runtime property discovered only by executing the saved file (catalog items 2,3) rather than a type-level guarantee.
types.recommended_design: Add `apply: ApplyFn | None = None` to NodeRegistryEntry, where `ApplyFn = Callable[[_Frame, Mapping[str, Any]], _Frame]` is the config-driven transform. Refactor each stateful exec builder to call `entry.apply(lf, config)` and each stateful codegen template to emit a body that imports and calls the SAME helper (the banding/ratingStep mechanism, generalised). Make `register_exec(..., kind=STATEFUL)` reject a missing `apply`. Then a single registration site is the source of truth for the operation, and the executor and codegen are wired to the identical callable BY CONSTRUCTION — they cannot drift because there is only one function. This is the concrete realisation of 'could the registry enforce by construction that every stateful node shares one apply helper between executor and codegen?': yes — make the helper a mandatory field and dispatch both sides through it.

types.title: NodeRegistryEntry fields are mutable-public, so the 'complete after validate' invariant is not preserved post-construction
types.description: The module guarantees (docstring, validate_registry_complete) that after import every entry has both sides populated. types.recommended_design: After completion, freeze the registry into an immutable total mapping: build entries via a builder, then in `ensure_registry_ready` construct `NODE_REGISTRY_FINAL: Mapping[NodeType, FrozenNodeEntry]` where FrozenNodeEntry is `@dataclass(frozen=True, slots=True)` with NON-optional `exec: ExecFn`, `codegen: CodegenFn`, `column_contract: ColumnContractFn` (and the proposed `kind`/`apply`). get_exec/get_codegen then index a total map and never branch on None. types.title: Two independent, manually-synchronised job-status vocabularies bridged by a runtime cast
types.description: `_job_lifecycle.py` imports the authoritative 8-member `JobStatus = Literal[...]` from schemas (line 13) and then immediately re-declares the SAME vocabulary as a parallel set of bare string constants (`RUNNING_STATUS = "running"`, `COMPLETED_STATUS = "completed"`, ... lines 15-22) plus a `TERMINAL_REASON_TO_STATUS` map and a `JOB_STATUSES` frozenset (lines 34-45). These are two disconnected sources of truth for the same closed set of strings: nothing at type-check time forces `JOB_STATUSES` to equal the members of `JobStatus`, or `RUNNING_STATUS` to be a `JobStatus` member. The disconnect is then papered over at runtime: `require_job_status` (91-96) validates `status` against the `JOB_STATUSES` *frozenset* and then `cast(JobStatus, status)` — the cast asserts a relationship the compiler cannot verify. If `JobStatus` gains a member (e.g. a new terminal state) but `JOB_STATUSES`/the constants are not updated, `require_job_status` will *reject a legitimate status as corrupt*; if the reverse, a value outside `JobStatus` flows through the cast unchecked. mypy/pyright catch neither.
types.recommended_design: Make `JobStatus` the single source of truth and derive everything else from it. Replace the bare constants with a `StrEnum` (`class JobStatus(StrEnum): RUNNING='running'; COMPLETED='completed'; ...`) defined once in schemas, or keep the Literal and derive `JOB_STATUSES = frozenset(get_args(JobStatus))` so the frozenset is provably the Literal's members. Similarly type `TERMINAL_REASON_TO_STATUS: Mapping[TerminalReason, JobStatus]` and add a module-level assertion/test that `set(TERMINAL_REASON_TO_STATUS.values()) | {RUNNING}` exactly equals the JobStatus members. With a StrEnum, `require_job_status` becomes `JobStatus(status)` (raises on unknown) with no `cast`, turning the runtime cast into a type-level guarantee.

types.location: src/haute/routes/_job_store.py:80, 342, 360, 369, 382-388, 425-432, 458, 475, 534-541 (job record is dict[str, Any] throughout)
types.type_name: JobStore job record (dict[str, Any]) — the implicit Job entity
types.severity: high — the central state object of every long-running operation (train/optimise/explore) has zero structural typing; every field access is `.get("key")` returning Any, so misspelled keys, wrong-type values, and missing required fields (e.g. no `status`) are all constructible and only fail (if ever) deep downstream
types.title: The job record — the engine's core async-result type — is an untyped dict[str, Any] with stringly-keyed required fields
types.description: Every public JobStore method speaks `dict[str, Any]`: `create_job(initial_status: dict[str, Any])`, `get_job(...) -> dict[str, Any] | None`, `atomic_update(fields: dict[str, Any])`, `require_job(...) -> dict[str, Any]`. There is no type expressing that a job record *must* carry a `status: JobStatus` and `created_at: float`, *may* carry `terminal_reason: TerminalReason`, `completed_at`, `message`, `result`, `progress`, etc. The required-status invariant is enforced only by `require_job_status` reading `job.get("status")` (an `Any`) at one call site; `_job_eviction_timestamp_locked` (108) and `_clear_expired_heavy_objects_locked` (155) re-do `job.get("status") == "running"`/`"completed"` with bare literals, none type-checked. The seven `create_job` call sites (optimiser.py:254, _optimiser_service.py:2572/2923/2980, _train_service.py:436, _explore_service.py:561, modelling) each hand-build the dict with literal `"status": "running"` keys; a typo (`"staus"`) produces a job with NO status that passes `create_job` and only explodes later in `require_job_status`. This is the root primitive-obsession that all the other status findings (NodeResult, ExecutionMetricsPayload, terminal_reason mismatches catalogued in 02-findings #62) grow out of.
types.recommended_design: Introduce a typed record for the job — minimally a `TypedDict` with `Required[]`/`NotRequired[]` (e.g. `class JobRecord(TypedDict): status: JobStatus; created_at: float; terminal_reason: NotRequired[TerminalReason]; completed_at: NotRequired[float]; ...`) so `create_job(initial: JobRecord)` and `get_job(...) -> JobRecord | None` give key/type checking at every call site for free, or (stronger) a frozen dataclass `Job` with the heavy/lightweight split modelled explicitly and `atomic_update` taking a typed patch. Either way, `status` becomes `JobStatus` not `Any`, the seven construction sites get checked, and the `job.get("status") == "running"` literals become `record["status"] is JobStatus.RUNNING`.

types.location: src/haute/schemas.py:229-244 (NodeResult); constructed in src/haute/executor.py:1167-1204 (error shape) and 1189-1241 (ok shape)
types.severity: high — a single flat optional-everywhere model conflates two mutually-exclusive result shapes (ok / error); contradictory records like status='ok' with error set, or status='error' carrying row_count/preview, are freely constructible and cross the API boundary, and every consumer must defensively re-check `status` to know which fields are meaningful
types.title: NodeResult makes contradictory ok/error states representable (status: str + all-optional payload)
types.description: `NodeResult` flattens an OK result and an ERROR result into one model where `status: str` (not even a Literal) gates which fields are meaningful, and every distinguishing field is optional/defaulted. The executor itself builds it in two disjoint shapes — error: `NodeResult(status="error", error=..., error_line=...)` (1167) leaving `row_count=0, columns=[], preview=[]`; ok: `NodeResult(status="ok", row_count=len(df), columns=..., preview=...)` (1227) leaving `error=None`. Nothing in the type prevents `NodeResult(status="ok", error="boom")` or `NodeResult(status="error", row_count=999, preview=[...])`; the line-1249 consumer must re-derive intent via `r.status == "error"`, and the frontend (api/types.ts) re-declares the same loose shape. The `status: str` also admits any string (e.g. `"OK"`, `"failed"`) — only convention keeps it to `{"ok","error"}`.
types.recommended_design: Two complementary changes. (1) At minimum make `status: Literal["ok", "error"]` so the vocabulary is closed. (2) Better: model the sum type — `NodeOk(BaseModel)` (row_count, columns, available_columns, preview*, schema_warnings; no error fields) and `NodeError(BaseModel)` (error: str, error_line: int | None; no preview/columns), with `NodeResult = Annotated[NodeOk | NodeError, Field(discriminator="status")]` using a Pydantic discriminated union keyed on a `status` Literal per arm. Then an ok result cannot carry an error string and vice-versa — the illegal states stop being representable and consumers branch on the union, not a re-checked bare string.

types.severity: medium — the status/terminal-reason fields that the GUI keys memory-diagnostic logic off (see 02-findings frontend memory-limited branches) are untyped strings even though exact enums exist; a wrong/typo'd reason serialises silently and the consumer's `terminal_reason === 'memory_limited'` comparison just quietly fails to match
types.title: ExecutionMetricsPayload.status and .terminal_reason are bare str|None despite JobStatus / TerminalReason existing
types.description: `ExecutionMetricsPayload` carries `status: str | None` (200) and `terminal_reason: str | None` (201). These are exactly the `JobStatus` and `TerminalReason` vocabularies — the publisher in `_job_lifecycle.py` even calls `context.metrics_payload(status=RUNNING_STATUS, terminal_reason=None)` (80-84) with a value drawn from the lifecycle status constants, and the terminal-write path stamps `terminal_reason=to` where `to: TerminalReason`. By widening to `str` at the schema boundary the type system stops verifying that what gets serialised is a real status/reason; any string (including a stale or misspelled one) validates. The frontend then does equality checks like `terminal_reason === 'memory_limited'`, which silently no-ops on drift rather than failing loudly — precisely the brittleness the surrounding memory-diagnostic findings describe.
types.recommended_design: Type the fields with the existing closed vocabularies: `status: JobStatus | None` and `terminal_reason: TerminalReason | None` (importing the Literals, or the StrEnum from the consolidation in finding 1). Pydantic will then reject out-of-vocabulary values at validation time and `metrics_payload(...)` callers get checked at the call site. If a genuinely-open 'free text' status is ever needed it should be a separate explicitly-named field, not a widening of this one.

types.severity: medium — the optimistic-concurrency guard that prevents a timeout/late write from clobbering a completed job is keyed on a bare `str`; a mistyped expected_status never equals any stored status, so the guard silently skips every update and returns None, and the caller's race-handling path fires unconditionally with no error
types.title: Optimistic-concurrency `expected_status` guard is a bare str, not JobStatus
types.description: The compare-and-set guard parameter is `expected_status: str | None` on `atomic_update` (387), `atomic_update_if_heavy_present` (431), and `JobLifecycle.transition` (112). The guard is load-bearing: `if old.get("status") != expected_status: return None` is what stops a timeout from overwriting a job that already completed (per the docstring at 403-406). Because the parameter is an unconstrained string, passing a value that is not a real `JobStatus` (a typo, or a constant that drifted from the lifecycle set per finding 1) compares unequal to every stored status, so the update is *always* skipped and `None` is returned — the very failure mode the guard exists to prevent, now triggered silently by a type error the compiler would have caught.
types.recommended_design: Type the parameter `expected_status: JobStatus | None` (Literal or StrEnum). Every call site passing a status constant is then checked, and an out-of-vocabulary value is a compile error rather than a silent always-skip. This converts a runtime-only invariant ('expected_status must be a real status or the guard misbehaves') into a type-level guarantee.

types.type_name: artifact handle (dict[str, Any]) + ArtifactCleaner registry keyed on str 'kind'
types.severity: medium — artifact handles are untyped dicts probed at cleanup time with isinstance/get; a handle with a missing/misspelled 'kind' or absent 'directory'/'path' is fully constructible and surfaces only as a warning-logged skipped cleanup (leaked files), never a construction-time error
types.title: Artifact handles are untyped dicts and cleaner registry is keyed on a bare 'kind' string
types.description: `register_artifact_cleaner(kind: str, ...)` (40) registers cleanup hooks in a `dict[str, ArtifactCleaner]` keyed by an arbitrary string, and `_cleanup_artifact_handles` (121-150) reconstructs handle semantics entirely at runtime: `handles = job.get("artifact_handles")`; `if not isinstance(handles, dict)`; per handle `if not isinstance(handle, dict)`, `kind = handle.get("kind")`, `cleaner = _ARTIFACT_CLEANERS.get(kind) if isinstance(kind, str) else None`, then path via `handle.get("directory") or handle.get("path")`. Nothing types a handle as `{kind: <known kind>, directory|path: str}`; a producer can store a handle with no `kind`, an unknown `kind`, or neither path key, and the only feedback is a `job_artifact_cleanup_unknown_handle_kind` warning while the on-disk artifact silently leaks. The set of valid kinds is open and unvalidated at registration.
types.recommended_design: Model the handle as a typed structure — a `TypedDict ArtifactHandle { kind: ArtifactKind; directory: NotRequired[str]; path: NotRequired[str] }` (or a small frozen dataclass), where `ArtifactKind` is a Literal/StrEnum of the registered kinds, and store `artifact_handles: dict[str, ArtifactHandle]` on the (now typed, per finding 2) job record. Have `register_artifact_cleaner` take `kind: ArtifactKind` so registration is checked against the closed set. The cleanup loop then drops the `isinstance`/`get` probing and the 'unknown kind' branch becomes unreachable-by-construction rather than a logged leak.

types.location: src/haute/routes/_job_store.py:30-32, 196-198 (heavy-object sentinel/bookkeeping keys), 524-531 (clear_result_data) — keys live inside the same flat job dict[str, Any]
types.type_name: JobStore heavy-object lifecycle bookkeeping keys (heavy_objects_expires_at / heavy_objects_cleared_at / heavy_objects_retention_seconds)
types.severity: low-medium — engine-owned lifecycle bookkeeping is stored as magic string keys in the same untyped dict that holds caller-supplied fields (config, result, message...), so a caller passing a field of one of these reserved names corrupts eviction scheduling; the namespace collision is unrepresentable-by-type to detect
types.title: Heavy-object lifecycle bookkeeping shares the job dict namespace with caller domain fields
types.description: The job dict mixes two ownership domains in one flat `dict[str, Any]`: caller domain fields (`status`, `config`, `result`, `message`, `progress`, the heavy objects `solver`/`solve_result`/`quote_grid`/...) and JobStore-private lifecycle bookkeeping written as bare string keys — `_HEAVY_OBJECT_EXPIRES_AT_KEY = "heavy_objects_expires_at"` (32), and in `_clear_heavy_objects_locked` the injected `"heavy_objects_cleared_at"` / `"heavy_objects_retention_seconds"` (197-198). Because both share the namespace, a `create_job`/`update_job` caller that happens to pass a field named `heavy_objects_expires_at` (e.g. surfacing one in a status payload) directly perturbs the expiry the store computes in `_heavy_objects_expires_at` (202-208), and the heavy-key tuple `_HEAVY_OBJECT_KEYS` (30-31) being a list of bare strings means the same collision risk applies to the heavy payload keys. The store's invariants about its own bookkeeping are not encapsulated away from caller-controlled keys.
types.recommended_design: Separate the two domains structurally. Promote the job record to a typed object (finding 2) with an explicit, non-dict-keyed sub-structure for lifecycle bookkeeping — e.g. a `HeavyObjectPolicy` dataclass (`expires_at: float | None`, `cleared_at: float | None`, `retention_seconds: int`) held in a dedicated field, kept in a side-table (`dict[job_id, HeavyObjectPolicy]` like the existing `_running_activity_at`/`_heavy_object_timers`), so caller fields and engine bookkeeping can never collide in one namespace. Heavy-object key membership should likewise be a typed/closed set rather than a bare-string tuple compared against arbitrary caller keys.

types.title: Model flavour is stringly-typed and its valid set is duplicated across 4 independent sites
types.severity: high
types.description: The scoring flavour is passed as a bare `str` through every scoring surface (`score_frame(flavor: str)`, `_score_eager_unified`, `_score_batched_unified`, `_prepare_predict_frame(flavor='pyfunc')`, `ScoringModel.flavor: str = 'pyfunc'`). The authoritative set of legal values is encoded FOUR separate times with no shared source of truth: (1) `_SUPPORTED_FLAVORS = frozenset({'catboost','pyfunc','rustystats'})` (_model_scorer.py:32); (2) the membership check + error message in `score_frame` (:779-785); (3) a *second*, independently hard-coded check `if flavor not in ('catboost','pyfunc')` plus the `rustystats` early-return in `_prepare_predict_frame` (_mlflow_io.py:1078-1085); (4) the constructor `_flavor_from_artifact` (_mlflow_io.py:64-76) which maps extensions to the flavour strings. Each branch (`flavor == 'catboost'`, `== 'rustystats'`, `== 'pyfunc'`) is a literal string compared by eye. Nothing prevents constructing a `ScoringModel(flavor='catbost')` (typo) — the type checker is blind, and the failure only surfaces deep in `score_frame`/`_prepare_predict_frame` as a runtime `ConfigError`/`ValueError`. Adding a new flavour requires editing all four sites and there is no compiler signal if one is missed (e.g. `_prepare_predict_frame`'s `('catboost','pyfunc')` tuple is a known divergence risk from `_SUPPORTED_FLAVORS`). This is squarely against the project's own established pattern: `NodeType`, `ExecutionProfile`, `SourceFormat`, `ChunkCapabilityKind`, `_CheckpointAction` are all `StrEnum`s.
types.recommended_design: Introduce `class ModelFlavor(StrEnum): CATBOOST='catboost'; PYFUNC='pyfunc'; RUSTYSTATS='rustystats'` in `_mlflow_io.py` (or a shared modelling types module). Type every flavour parameter and `ScoringModel.flavor` as `ModelFlavor`. Replace `_SUPPORTED_FLAVORS` with `frozenset(ModelFlavor)` (or just iterate the enum). Make `_prepare_predict_frame` dispatch with `match flavor:` / `if flavor is ModelFlavor.RUSTYSTATS` so a missing case is a single source of truth, and drop the independently-spelled `('catboost','pyfunc')` tuple. Because `StrEnum` members compare equal to their string value, JSON/config reads (`_flavor_from_artifact`, `cfg.get(...)`) can coerce via `ModelFlavor(raw)` at the boundary — which then *fails loudly at the edge* on an unknown value instead of silently flowing a bad string inward. This removes the entire class of typo/desync bugs and makes 'add a flavour' a single-enum-plus-exhaustive-match change.

types.type_name: task — bare `str` in scorer & algorithms vs existing `Task = Literal['classification','regression']`
types.title: `task` is `str` across the scorer/algorithm surface even though a `Task` literal alias already exists and is used elsewhere
types.severity: high
types.description: `_feature_contract.py:29` defines `Task = Literal['classification','regression']` and `_signature.py:36` already types its parameter as `Literal['classification','regression']`. Yet the entire scoring/training hot path types `task` as a bare `str`: `score_frame(task: str = 'regression')`, `_score_eager_unified`, `_score_batched_unified`, `_run_score_pipeline`, `ModelScorer.__init__(task: str)`, `BaseAlgorithm.fit(task: str)`, `CatBoostAlgorithm.fit`, `GLMAlgorithm.fit`, and `resolve_loss_function(task: str)`. Seven modules then branch on `task == 'classification'` / `task == 'regression'` (grep-confirmed: `_mlflow_io`, `_model_scorer`, `_training_job`, `_algorithms`, `_model_explainability`, `_mlflow_log`, `_signature`). Because the parameter is `str`, a typo like `task='regresion'` type-checks and silently routes through the *else* arm (e.g. in `score_frame` it skips the `_proba` column; in `resolve_loss_function` it selects `CLASSIFICATION_LOSSES` for any non-'regression' string — line 231 `valid = REGRESSION_LOSSES if task == 'regression' else CLASSIFICATION_LOSSES`, so 'regresion' is silently treated as classification). The `Task` alias is already the right abstraction; it is simply not threaded through.
types.recommended_design: Promote the existing `Task` literal to a shared location (e.g. a small `haute/modelling/_types.py` or reuse the one in `_feature_contract.py`) and annotate every `task` parameter and `ScoringModel`/`ModelScorer` field with `Task`. Optionally upgrade to `class Task(StrEnum)` for richer call-sites; the `Literal` alone already makes mypy/pyright reject the typo at every call boundary. In `resolve_loss_function`, branch on the exhaustive literal so a 4th task value would be a type error, and replace the `else` fallthrough with an explicit `task == 'classification'` check so a non-'regression' string can never be silently misclassified.

types.title: ScoringModel is a 'uniform interface' carrier with mutable public fields — its invariants (flavour ∈ supported set, feature ordering, cat ⊆ features) can be broken after construction
types.severity: medium
types.description: `ScoringModel` is the central uniform-interface object the whole scoring layer trusts: `_validate_features` keys its cache on `(id(model), tuple(model.feature_names), frozenset(model.cat_feature_names))` (_model_scorer.py:119-124) and CatBoost positional categorical-index alignment depends on `feature_names` ordering being exactly training order. Yet `feature_names: list[str]`, `cat_feature_names: frozenset[str]`, and `flavor: str` are plain writable attributes (it uses `__slots__` but is not frozen and exposes no read-only views). Any code holding a cached/shared `ScoringModel` (these are cached in `_model_cache` and shared across threads — see the eviction-cascade machinery) can do `model.feature_names.append('x')` or `model.flavor = 'pyfunc'` and (a) silently desync the feature-validation cache from reality (the cache key snapshots a tuple at call time, so a later in-place `list.append` is invisible until the next key recompute), and (b) violate the documented invariant that `flavor` is one of the supported dispatch targets. There is also no construction-time guarantee that `cat_feature_names ⊆ set(feature_names)`; a stray cat name simply never matches.
types.recommended_design: Make `ScoringModel` an immutable value object: `@dataclass(frozen=True, slots=True)` (or keep the hand-written class but store `feature_names` as a `tuple[str, ...]` and validate in `__post_init__`/`__init__`). Type `flavor: ModelFlavor` (per the flavour-enum finding) so an illegal flavour is unconstructable. Validate the cross-field invariant `cat_feature_names <= set(feature_names)` at construction and raise a named error otherwise — turning the silent 'cat name never matches' failure into a loud one. With `feature_names` as a tuple, the cache key derivation is honestly stable and `list.append`-style mutation is impossible.

types.location: src/haute/modelling/_feature_contract.py:53-64 (FeatureContract); construction at :96-134; consumed by hash at :91-93, 116-124
types.title: FeatureContract is `frozen=True` but stores mutable list/dict fields, so its content-hash invariant can be silently desynced by in-place mutation
types.severity: medium
types.description: `FeatureContract` is documented as an 'Immutable record' and uses `@dataclasses.dataclass(frozen=True)`, but `frozen=True` only blocks *attribute rebinding* — it does nothing about mutation of the contained containers. The fields `features: list[str]`, `feature_types: dict[str,str]`, `categorical_features: list[str]`, `categorical_levels: dict[str, list[str|None]]` are all mutable, and the central invariant of the type is that `contract_hash == sha256(canonical(all other fields))`. A holder can do `contract.features.append('leaked')` or `contract.categorical_levels['x'].append('y')` and the object now carries a `contract_hash` that no longer matches its own content, which is exactly the corruption `load_contract(verify_hash=True)` exists to catch on disk — but the in-memory object provides no such protection. Because `load_contract_cached` returns a *process-wide shared* instance across threads (the docstring says 'shared across callers and threads — treat it as immutable'), a single accidental in-place mutation poisons the contract for every concurrent scorer, and `assert_contracts_match` (which compares field-by-field) would then compare against mutated state. The immutability is by-convention only.
types.recommended_design: Make the contents genuinely immutable so the hash invariant is structurally guaranteed: store `features`/`categorical_features` as `tuple[str, ...]`, `feature_types` as an immutable mapping (e.g. wrap in `types.MappingProxyType` or a frozen mapping), and `categorical_levels` as `Mapping[str, tuple[str|None, ...]]`. Keep `build_contract`/`load_contract` accepting plain lists/dicts at the boundary and freezing on the way in (they already copy). With frozen contents, `contract_hash` cannot drift from content for the lifetime of the object, eliminating the 'shared mutable contract' hazard entirely and letting the on-disk `verify_hash` be the *only* place corruption can enter.

types.title: CatBoost loss names are validated at runtime from bare string sets instead of being a typed closed union
types.severity: medium
types.description: `REGRESSION_LOSSES = {'RMSE','MAE','Poisson','Tweedie'}` and `CLASSIFICATION_LOSSES = {'Logloss','CrossEntropy'}` are bare `set[str]` module constants, and `resolve_loss_function(loss_name: str, task: str, ...)` validates membership purely at runtime (raising `ValueError` on a miss). The legal-loss vocabulary is therefore invisible to the type system: callers pass an arbitrary `str`, and the only signal that 'RMS' (typo) or 'logloss' (wrong case) is invalid is a runtime exception during training-config assembly. Combined with the `task: str` weakness above, the selector at line 231 (`valid = REGRESSION_LOSSES if task == 'regression' else CLASSIFICATION_LOSSES`) means a bad `task` value silently changes *which* loss set is considered valid. The valid set is small, closed, and known at authoring time — a textbook candidate for a literal union / enum.
types.recommended_design: Define `RegressionLoss = Literal['RMSE','MAE','Poisson','Tweedie']` and `ClassificationLoss = Literal['Logloss','CrossEntropy']` (or `StrEnum`s), derive the runtime sets from them (`frozenset(get_args(RegressionLoss))`) so there is a single source of truth, and type `resolve_loss_function(loss_name: RegressionLoss | ClassificationLoss | None, task: Task, ...)`. The runtime check stays as a belt-and-braces guard for config-file inputs, but in-code callers now get a compile-time error for an unknown loss, and the regression/classification split is enforced by `Task` being a closed union.

types.type_name: GLM family / link — bare `str` read from an untyped `params: dict[str, Any]`
types.title: GLM `family` and `link` are stringly-typed and pulled from an untyped params dict, with behaviour-changing string equality (`family == 'tweedie'`) unguarded by the type system
types.severity: medium
types.description: The GLM distribution `family` and `link` flow as bare `str` (`_build_glm_builder_kwargs(family: str, link: str | None)`), read out of an opaque `params: dict[str, Any]` in `GLMAlgorithm.fit` via `params.get('family', 'gaussian')` / `params.get('link') or None`. Behaviour branches on exact string equality — `if family == 'tweedie': kwargs['var_power'] = var_power` (line 135) — so a miscapitalised or misspelled `family` ('Tweedie', 'tweedy') silently skips the `var_power` wiring and is forwarded verbatim to `rs.glm_dict`, where it either errors cryptically or (worse) is interpreted differently than intended. There is no enumeration of supported families/links anywhere in the Python layer, so neither the type checker nor a reader can see the legal vocabulary, and the train-config surface accepts any string. This is the GLM analogue of the CatBoost-loss issue and the flavour issue.
types.recommended_design: Introduce `GLMFamily = Literal['gaussian','poisson','gamma','tweedie', ...]` and `GLMLink = Literal[...]` (enumerate against what RustyStats actually accepts) and type `_build_glm_builder_kwargs(family: GLMFamily, link: GLMLink | None)`. Validate/coerce `params['family']`/`params['link']` to these at the `fit` boundary (the one place untyped config becomes typed) so an unknown family fails loudly there rather than inside the Rust layer, and so the `family == 'tweedie'` branch is checked against a closed set. This makes the supported-distribution set discoverable and the `var_power` coupling robust to typos.

types.location: src/haute/_model_scorer.py:1015-1019 (source_type, version) and 980-989 docstring; consumed in _mlflow_io.load_mlflow_model:852-875
types.title: `source_type` ('run' | 'registered') and `version` ('latest' | digits) are stringly-typed across the MLflow loading surface
types.severity: low
types.description: `ModelScorer.__init__(source_type: str, version: str = 'latest')` and `load_mlflow_model(source_type: str, ...)` accept bare strings whose only legal values are `'run'`/`'registered'` (source_type) and `'latest'` or a version-number string (version). `load_mlflow_model` branches on `source_type == 'run'` (line 893) and the docstrings enumerate the two values, but nothing in the type system enforces them: `source_type='registerd'` type-checks and would fall into the non-'run' path, attempting a registered-model lookup with an empty `registered_model`. The required *companion* field also differs by `source_type` (run_id for 'run', registered_model for 'registered'), so this is also a latent illegal-states issue — a `ModelScorer(source_type='run')` with empty `run_id` and a populated `registered_model` is representable and meaningless.
types.recommended_design: Type `source_type` as `Literal['run','registered']` (or a `ModelSource` StrEnum). For the stronger fix, model the source as a small tagged union so the run-vs-registered companion fields cannot be mismatched — e.g. `RunSource(run_id: str, artifact_path: str)` vs `RegisteredSource(name: str, version: str | Literal['latest'])` — making 'run source with no run_id' unrepresentable. At minimum the literal on `source_type` catches the typo and the wrong-path-with-empty-id failure mode.

types.title: ScoreWriteProjection is already well-designed (frozen, slots, frozenset fields, documented sentinel) — no change recommended
types.severity: info
types.description: Recording the positive: `ScoreWriteProjection` is an exemplary small value object for this codebase. It is `@dataclass(frozen=True, slots=True)`; its collection fields are `frozenset[str]` (immutable, no in-place mutation hazard like the ScoringModel/FeatureContract findings above); the `passthrough_columns: frozenset[str] | None = None` sentinel is explicitly documented ('None passthrough means preserve the full scored input; a concrete set means write exactly those'), so the `Optional` here encodes a genuine two-state choice rather than hiding a required invariant. The defaults (`frozenset()` for optional/required) are correct empty-set identities. No illegal state is constructible. I reviewed it specifically because the surface brief flags optional-everywhere and encapsulation risks — this type does NOT exhibit them and should be left as-is (and is a good template for tightening ScoringModel/FeatureContract).
types.recommended_design: No change. Use as the reference pattern (frozen + slots + frozenset/tuple fields + a single documented sentinel) when tightening `ScoringModel` and `FeatureContract` per the other findings.

types.severity: low-medium
types.title: SinkResponse omits execution_metrics the backend always returns
types.description: Backend SinkResponse (schemas.py:375-381) has execution_metrics like all other long-running payloads; FE type lacks it (distinct from B131 which only flags the missing parseSinkResponse guard).
